chapters.title: 1. Never Talk to Strangers
paragraphs: “...So who are you, then?” — “I am a part of that force which forever wants evil and forever does good.” Goethe, Faust

At the hour of a hot spring sunset, two citizens appeared at Patriarch’s Ponds. The first of them—about forty, dressed in a grayish summer suit—was short, dark-haired, plump and bald; he carried his respectable pork-pie hat in his hand, and his neatly shaven face was adorned with glasses of supernatural size in black horn-rimmed frames. The second—a broad-shouldered, reddish, tousle-haired young man with a checked cap pushed to the back of his head—wore a cowboy shirt, crumpled white trousers and black canvas shoes.

The first was none other than Mikhail Alexandrovich Berlioz, editor of a thick literary magazine and chairman of the board of one of Moscow’s largest literary associations, known for short as Massolit; his young companion was the poet Ivan Nikolayevich Ponyrev, who wrote under the pen name Bezdomny.
Reaching the shade of the lindens, which were just turning green, the writers first of all made a dash for a gaily painted kiosk with the sign “Beer and Soft Drinks.”

Yes, we must note the first oddity of that terrible May evening. Not only at the kiosk but along the whole avenue running parallel to Malaya Bronnaya Street, there was not a single person. At that hour, when it seemed there was no strength left even to breathe, when the sun, having baked Moscow through, was sinking in a dry haze somewhere beyond the Garden Ring, nobody came under the lindens, nobody sat down on a bench; the avenue was empty.
“Give us some Narzan,” Berlioz asked.
“There isn’t any Narzan,” the woman in the kiosk replied, and for some reason took offense.
“Is there any beer?” Bezdomny inquired in a hoarse voice.
“The beer’s coming this evening,” the woman replied.
“Then what is there?” asked Berlioz.
“Apricot soda, only it’s warm,” said the woman.
“Well, let’s have it, let’s have it, let’s have it!..”

The apricot soda produced a rich yellow foam, and the air began to smell of a barbershop. Having drunk, the writers immediately started hiccuping; they paid and sat down on a bench facing the pond, with their backs to the Bronnaya.

Here a second oddity occurred, concerning Berlioz alone. He suddenly stopped hiccuping, his heart thumped and for an instant dropped away somewhere, then came back, but with a blunt needle lodged in it. What was more, Berlioz was seized by a fear so groundless, yet so strong, that he wanted to run from Patriarch’s that very moment without looking back.

Berlioz looked around in anguish, not understanding what had frightened him. He went pale, wiped his forehead with his handkerchief, and thought: “What’s the matter with me? This has never happened before... my heart’s acting up... I’m overworked... Maybe it’s time to send everything to the devil and go to Kislovodsk...”

And then the sultry air thickened in front of him, and out of this air a transparent citizen of the strangest appearance was woven. On his little head, a jockey’s cap; a skimpy little checked jacket, also made of air... The citizen was seven feet tall but narrow in the shoulders, incredibly thin, and his face, kindly note, was a jeering one.
Berlioz’s life had been arranged in such a way that he was not used to extraordinary phenomena. Turning paler still, he goggled and thought in dismay: “This cannot be!..”
But, alas, it was, and the long citizen, whom one could see right through, swayed before him to the left and to the right without touching the ground.

At this, terror so overpowered Berlioz that he shut his eyes. And when he opened them, he saw that it was all over: the mirage had dissolved, the checked figure had vanished, and with it the blunt needle had popped out of his heart.

“Phew, the devil!” the editor exclaimed. “You know, Ivan, I nearly had a heatstroke just now! I even had something like a hallucination...” He tried to smile, but alarm was still jumping in his eyes, and his hands were trembling. Little by little, however, he calmed down, fanned himself with his handkerchief and, saying quite cheerfully, “Well now, as I was saying...,” resumed the talk that the apricot soda had interrupted.

This talk, as was learned later, was about Jesus Christ. The point was that the editor had commissioned the poet to write a long anti-religious poem for the next issue of the magazine. Ivan Nikolayevich had written this poem, and in a very short time, but unfortunately it had not satisfied the editor in the least. Bezdomny had painted the main character of his poem, that is, Jesus, in very black colors, and yet, in the editor’s opinion, the whole poem had to be written over again. And so now the editor was giving the poet something like a lecture on Jesus, in order to bring home the poet’s basic mistake.

It is hard to say what exactly had let Ivan Nikolayevich down—the descriptive power of his talent or his complete ignorance of the subject he was writing about—but his Jesus had come out, well, completely alive, a Jesus who had once existed, only, true, a Jesus equipped with every negative trait.

Berlioz, on the other hand, wanted to prove to the poet that the main thing was not what Jesus had been like, bad or good, but that this Jesus had never existed in the world at all as a person, and that all the stories about him were mere inventions, the most ordinary myth.

It must be said that the editor was a well-read man and very skillfully pointed in his talk to the ancient historians—for instance, to the famous Philo of Alexandria and the brilliantly educated Josephus Flavius—who never said a single word about the existence of Jesus. Displaying solid erudition, Mikhail Alexandrovich also informed the poet, among other things, that the passage in the fifteenth book, chapter 44, of Tacitus’s famous Annals, where the execution of Jesus is mentioned, is nothing but a later forged insertion.

The poet, for whom everything the editor told him was news, listened attentively to Mikhail Alexandrovich, fixing his lively green eyes on him, and only now and then hiccuped, cursing the apricot soda under his breath.

“There is not a single Eastern religion,” Berlioz was saying, “in which, as a rule, an immaculate virgin did not give birth to a god. And the Christians, without inventing anything new, created their Jesus in exactly the same way, a Jesus who in fact never lived at all. That’s where the main emphasis has to go...”

Berlioz’s high tenor rang out in the deserted avenue, and as Mikhail Alexandrovich pushed into thickets that only a very educated man can enter without risk of breaking his neck, the poet learned more and more interesting and useful things: about the Egyptian Osiris, benevolent god and son of Heaven and Earth, about the Phoenician god Tammuz, about Marduk, and even about a lesser-known, fearsome god, Vitzliputzli, once greatly revered by the Aztecs in Mexico.
And just when Mikhail Alexandrovich was telling the poet how the Aztecs used to mold a figurine of Vitzliputzli out of dough, the first person appeared in the avenue.

Later, when, frankly speaking, it was already too late, various agencies submitted reports describing this person. Comparing them cannot fail to cause astonishment. Thus the first of them states that the man was short, had gold teeth and limped on his right leg. The second, that the man was enormously tall, had platinum crowns and limped on his left leg. The third tersely reports that the man had no distinguishing features.
One has to admit that not one of these reports is any good.

First of all: the man described did not limp on either leg, and he was neither short nor enormous, but simply tall. As for his teeth, on the left side he had platinum crowns, and on the right, gold ones. He wore an expensive gray suit and foreign shoes the same color as the suit. His gray beret was jauntily cocked over one ear, and under his arm he carried a walking stick with a black knob in the shape of a poodle’s head. He looked a little over forty. His mouth was somehow crooked. Clean-shaven. Dark-haired. His right eye was black, his left, for some reason, green. Black eyebrows, but one higher than the other. In a word, a foreigner.
Passing the bench where the editor and the poet were sitting, the foreigner gave them a sidelong look, stopped, and suddenly sat down on the next bench, two steps away from the friends.
“A German...” thought Berlioz.
“An Englishman...” thought Bezdomny. “Look at that, he isn’t even hot in those gloves.”
The foreigner, meanwhile, ran his eyes over the tall buildings that framed the pond in a square, and it was clear that he was seeing the place for the first time and that it interested him.

He let his gaze rest on the upper floors, whose windows dazzlingly reflected the broken sun that was leaving Mikhail Alexandrovich forever, then lowered it to where the windows were beginning to darken toward evening, smiled condescendingly at something, narrowed his eyes, placed his hands on the knob of his stick and his chin on his hands.

“You, Ivan,” Berlioz was saying, “portrayed the birth of Jesus, the Son of God, for instance, very well and satirically, but the whole point is that a whole line of sons of God had been born before Jesus—the Phoenician Adonis, say, the Phrygian Attis, the Persian Mithras. In short, not one of them was ever born and none of them existed, Jesus included, and what you need to do, instead of depicting the birth or, let’s say, the coming of the Magi, is to depict the absurd rumors about that coming. Otherwise, the way you tell it, he really was born!..”

At this point Bezdomny tried to stop the hiccups that were tormenting him by holding his breath, which only made him hiccup more painfully and loudly, and at that very moment Berlioz broke off his speech, because the foreigner suddenly got up and walked over to the writers.
They looked at him in surprise.

“Do forgive me,” said the newcomer, speaking with a foreign accent but without mangling his words, “for taking the liberty, without being acquainted... but the subject of your learned conversation is so interesting that...”
Here he politely took off his beret, and the friends had no choice but to half rise and bow.
“No, a Frenchman, more likely...” thought Berlioz.
“A Pole?..” thought Bezdomny.

It must be added that from his very first words the foreigner made a repulsive impression on the poet, whereas Berlioz rather liked him—that is, not liked exactly, but... how should one put it... was intrigued by him, perhaps.
“May I sit down?” the foreigner asked politely, and the friends somehow involuntarily moved apart; the foreigner deftly settled between them and at once joined the conversation:
“If I heard correctly, you were pleased to say that Jesus never existed?” the foreigner asked, turning his green left eye to Berlioz.
“No, you heard correctly,” Berlioz answered courteously. “That is exactly what I was saying.”
“Ah, how interesting!” the foreigner exclaimed.
“What the devil does he want?” thought Bezdomny, and frowned.
“And you agreed with your companion?” inquired the stranger, turning to his right, toward Bezdomny.
“A hundred percent!” the latter confirmed, being fond of fancy, figurative expressions.

“Amazing!” exclaimed the uninvited conversationalist, and, glancing around furtively for some reason and lowering his deep voice, he said: “Forgive my being intrusive, but do I understand that, on top of everything else, you also don’t believe in God?” He made frightened eyes and added: “I swear I won’t tell anyone.”
“That’s right, we don’t believe in God,” Berlioz answered, smiling slightly at the foreign tourist’s alarm, “but one can speak about that perfectly freely.”
The foreigner leaned back against the bench and asked, even squealing a little with curiosity:
“You are atheists?!”
“Yes, we are atheists,” Berlioz answered with a smile, and Bezdomny thought angrily: “Now he’s latched on, the foreign goose!”
“Oh, how delightful!” cried the astonishing foreigner, and began turning his head, looking from one writer to the other.
“In our country atheism surprises no one,” Berlioz said with diplomatic politeness. “The majority of our population consciously stopped believing the fairy tales about God long ago.”
At this the foreigner pulled the following stunt: he stood up and shook the astonished editor’s hand, pronouncing these words as he did so:
“Allow me to thank you from the bottom of my heart!”
“What are you thanking him for?” Bezdomny inquired, blinking.
“For a very important piece of information, which is of extraordinary interest to me as a traveler,” the foreign eccentric explained, raising a finger significantly.
The important information had evidently made a strong impression on the traveler, because he glanced fearfully around at the buildings, as if afraid of seeing an atheist in every window.
“No, he’s not an Englishman...” thought Berlioz, while Bezdomny thought: “Where did he learn to speak Russian so well, that’s what I’d like to know!”—and frowned again.
“But allow me to ask you,” the foreign visitor began after some anxious reflection, “what about the proofs of the existence of God, of which, as is well known, there are exactly five?”

“Alas!” Berlioz answered with regret. “Not one of those proofs is worth anything, and humanity filed them away in the archive long ago. You must agree that in the realm of reason there can be no proof of the existence of God.”

“Bravo!” cried the foreigner. “Bravo! You have repeated exactly the idea of restless old Immanuel on this point. But here’s the curious thing: he utterly demolished all five proofs, and then, as if mocking himself, constructed a sixth proof of his own!”

“Kant’s proof,” the educated editor objected with a subtle smile, “is also unconvincing. Not for nothing did Schiller say that Kant’s reasoning on the question could satisfy only slaves, and Strauss simply laughed at that proof.”
Berlioz talked, and all the while he was thinking: “But who is he, after all? And why does he speak Russian so well?”
“Somebody ought to take that Kant and give him three years in Solovki for proofs like that!” Ivan Nikolayevich blurted out completely unexpectedly.
“Ivan!” Berlioz whispered, embarrassed.
But the proposal to send Kant to Solovki not only failed to shock the foreigner, it even delighted him.

“Exactly, exactly,” he cried, and his green left eye, turned to Berlioz, flashed. “That’s just the place for him! Didn’t I tell him at breakfast that time: ‘Say what you like, Professor, but you’ve come up with something awkward! It may be clever, but it’s awfully hard to understand. People will make fun of you.’”
Berlioz’s eyes bulged. “At breakfast... to Kant?.. What is he babbling about?” he thought.

“But,” the foreigner went on, unembarrassed by Berlioz’s astonishment and turning to the poet, “it’s impossible to send him to Solovki, for the simple reason that for over a hundred years now he has been residing in places considerably more remote than Solovki, and there’s no way whatever to get him out of there, I assure you!”
“Too bad!” responded the pugnacious poet.

“I think it’s too bad, too,” the stranger agreed, his eye flashing, and went on: “But here is a question that troubles me: if there is no God, then, one asks, who governs human life and the whole order of things on earth?”
“Man governs it himself,” Bezdomny hurried to answer angrily to this, admittedly, not very clear question.

“Pardon me,” the stranger responded gently, “but in order to govern, one needs, after all, to have a precise plan for some at least reasonably decent stretch of time. Allow me to ask you, then: how can man govern if he is not only deprived of the possibility of drawing up any plan even for a ridiculously short period—well, say, a thousand years—but cannot even vouch for his own tomorrow? And indeed,” here the stranger turned to Berlioz, “imagine that you, for instance, start governing, giving orders to others and to yourself, generally, so to speak, acquiring a taste for it, and suddenly you get... ahem... ahem... a sarcoma of the lung...” here the foreigner smiled sweetly, as if the thought of a sarcoma of the lung gave him pleasure, “yes, a sarcoma,” he repeated the sonorous word, squinting like a cat, “and there goes your governing! Nobody’s fate but your own interests you any longer. Your family start lying to you. Sensing that something is wrong, you rush to learned doctors, then to quacks, and sometimes even to fortune-tellers. The first, the second and the third are all completely pointless, as you yourself understand. And it all ends tragically: the man who only recently thought he was governing something suddenly turns out to be lying motionless in a wooden box, and the people around him, realizing that the man lying there is of no more use whatsoever, burn him in an oven. And sometimes it’s worse still: a man has just made up his mind to go to Kislovodsk,” here the foreigner squinted at Berlioz, “a trifling matter, you’d think, but he can’t manage even that, because suddenly, nobody knows why, he up and slips and falls under a tram! Surely you won’t tell me he arranged that for himself? Isn’t it more correct to think that someone else entirely arranged things for him?”—and here the stranger laughed a strange little laugh.

Berlioz listened with great attention to the unpleasant story about the sarcoma and the tram, and some alarming thoughts began to torment him. “He’s not a foreigner... he’s not a foreigner...” he thought. “He’s a very strange character... but, wait, who is he, then?..”
“You’d like a smoke, I see?” the stranger turned unexpectedly to Bezdomny. “Which kind do you prefer?”
“What, you’ve got different kinds?” asked the poet gloomily; he had run out of cigarettes.
“Which kind do you prefer?” the stranger repeated.
“Well, ‘Our Brand,’” Bezdomny answered spitefully.
The stranger immediately took a cigarette case out of his pocket and offered it to Bezdomny:
“‘Our Brand.’”

What struck the editor and the poet alike was not so much that the case contained precisely Our Brand as the case itself. It was of enormous size, made of red gold, and on its lid, as it opened, a diamond triangle flashed with blue and white fire.
Here the writers thought different things. Berlioz: “No, a foreigner!” And Bezdomny: “Well, devil take him, eh!..”
The poet and the owner of the cigarette case lit up, while Berlioz, a non-smoker, declined.
“I’ll have to answer him like this,” Berlioz decided. “Yes, man is mortal, nobody disputes that. But the point is that...”
But before he could utter these words, the foreigner spoke:

“Yes, man is mortal, but that would be only half the trouble. The bad thing is that he is sometimes suddenly mortal—that’s the catch! And generally he can’t even say what he’ll be doing this evening.”
“What an absurd way of putting the question...” Berlioz reflected, and objected:
“Well, now, that’s an exaggeration. I know more or less exactly what I’m doing this evening. It goes without saying that if a brick should fall on my head on the Bronnaya...”

“A brick never falls on anyone’s head out of the blue,” the stranger interrupted impressively. “And you in particular, I assure you, are in no danger from one whatsoever. You will die a different death.”
“Perhaps you know which one exactly?” Berlioz inquired with perfectly natural irony, being drawn into a truly absurd conversation. “And you’ll tell me?”

“Gladly,” the stranger responded. He sized Berlioz up as though he were about to make him a suit, muttered through his teeth something like: “One, two... Mercury in the second house... the moon has gone... six—misfortune... evening—seven...” and announced loudly and joyfully: “Your head will be cut off!”
Bezdomny goggled wildly and angrily at the cheeky stranger, while Berlioz asked with a crooked smile:
“And by whom exactly? Enemies? Interventionists?”
“No,” his companion answered, “a Russian woman, a Komsomol girl.”
“Hm...” Berlioz grunted, irritated by the stranger’s little joke. “Well, that, excuse me, is rather unlikely.”
“I must ask you to excuse me as well,” the foreigner answered, “but that is how it is. Oh yes, I’d like to ask you what you’ll be doing this evening, if it’s not a secret?”
“It’s no secret. I’m going home to Sadovaya now, and then at ten this evening there’s a meeting at Massolit, and I’ll be chairing it.”
“No, that cannot possibly be,” the foreigner objected firmly.
“And why not?”

“Because,” the foreigner answered, looking with narrowed eyes at the sky, where black birds, sensing the cool of evening, were silently tracing their lines, “Annushka has already bought the sunflower oil, and not only bought it, but spilled it too. So the meeting will not take place.”
At this, as is quite understandable, silence fell under the lindens.
“Excuse me,” Berlioz said after a pause, glancing at the foreigner who was talking such nonsense, “but what has sunflower oil got to do with it... and which Annushka?”

“Here’s what sunflower oil has got to do with it,” Bezdomny suddenly spoke up, evidently having decided to declare war on their uninvited companion. “Have you ever happened, citizen, to be in a hospital for the mentally ill?”
“Ivan!..” Mikhail Alexandrovich exclaimed quietly.
But the foreigner was not offended in the least and laughed merrily.

“I have, I have, and more than once!” he cried, laughing, but without taking his unlaughing eye off the poet. “Where haven’t I been! The only pity is that I never found the time to ask the professor what schizophrenia is. So you’ll have to find that out from him yourself, Ivan Nikolayevich!”
“How do you know my name?”

“Good heavens, Ivan Nikolayevich, who doesn’t know you?” Here the foreigner pulled yesterday’s issue of the Literary Gazette out of his pocket, and Ivan Nikolayevich saw his own picture on the very front page, and beneath it his very own verses. But this proof of fame and popularity, which had delighted him only yesterday, did not delight the poet in the least this time.
“Excuse me,” he said, and his face darkened, “could you wait a minute? I want to have a couple of words with my comrade.”
“Oh, with pleasure!” exclaimed the stranger. “It’s so nice here under the lindens, and I’m in no hurry to go anywhere, as it happens.”
“Listen, Misha,” the poet whispered, pulling Berlioz aside, “he’s no foreign tourist, he’s a spy. He’s a Russian émigré who’s slipped back across to us. Ask for his papers, or he’ll get away...”
“You think so?” Berlioz whispered anxiously, and thought to himself: “He’s right, you know...”

“Take my word for it,” the poet rasped into his ear, “he’s playing the fool so he can worm things out of us. You hear how he speaks Russian,” the poet talked and kept glancing sideways to make sure the stranger didn’t slip away, “come on, let’s detain him, or he’ll get away...”
And the poet pulled Berlioz by the arm back to the bench.
The stranger was not sitting but standing beside it, holding some sort of booklet in a dark gray binding, a thick envelope of good paper, and a visiting card.

“Forgive me for forgetting, in the heat of our argument, to introduce myself. Here is my card, my passport and an invitation to come to Moscow for consultation,” the stranger said weightily, looking penetratingly at both writers.

They were embarrassed. “Damn, he heard everything...” thought Berlioz, and indicated with a polite gesture that there was no need to show any documents. While the foreigner was pushing them at the editor, the poet managed to make out on the card the word “Professor” printed in foreign letters, and the first letter of the surname—a double “V”: “W.”
“A pleasure,” the editor was meanwhile muttering in embarrassment, and the foreigner put the documents back in his pocket.
Relations having thus been restored, all three sat down on the bench again.
“You’ve been invited here as a consultant, Professor?” asked Berlioz.
“Yes, as a consultant.”
“Are you German?” inquired Bezdomny.
“Me?..” the professor asked back, and suddenly grew thoughtful. “Yes, I suppose I am German...” he said.
“You speak Russian awfully well,” Bezdomny remarked.
“Oh, I’m a polyglot in general and know a very great number of languages,” the professor answered.
“And what is your field?” inquired Berlioz.
“I am a specialist in black magic.”
“There you go!..” thudded in Mikhail Alexandrovich’s head.
“And... and you were invited here in that field?” he asked, stammering.

“Yes, that is the field they invited me in,” the professor confirmed, and explained: “Genuine manuscripts of the tenth-century necromancer Gerbert of Aurillac have been discovered here in the State Library. So I am needed to decipher them. I am the only specialist in the world.”
“Ah! You’re a historian?” Berlioz asked with great relief and respect.
“I am a historian,” the scholar confirmed, and added, apropos of nothing: “There will be some interesting history at Patriarch’s this evening!”
And again the editor and the poet were both extremely surprised, and the professor beckoned them both closer and, when they leaned toward him, whispered:
“Bear in mind that Jesus existed.”
“You see, Professor,” Berlioz responded with a forced smile, “we respect your great learning, but on this question we hold a different point of view.”
“There’s no need for any points of view,” the strange professor answered. “He simply existed, and that’s all there is to it.”
“But surely some proof is required...” Berlioz began.

“And no proofs are required either,” the professor answered, and began speaking quietly, and for some reason his accent had vanished: “It’s all very simple: in a white cloak with a blood-red lining, with the shuffling gait of a cavalryman, early in the morning of the fourteenth day of the spring month of Nisan...”

chapters.title: 2. Pontius Pilate
paragraphs: In a white cloak with a blood-red lining, with the shuffling gait of a cavalryman, early in the morning of the fourteenth day of the spring month of Nisan, the procurator of Judea, Pontius Pilate, came out into the covered colonnade between the two wings of the palace of Herod the Great.

More than anything in the world the procurator hated the smell of rose oil, and everything now foretold a bad day, because that smell had been pursuing the procurator since dawn. It seemed to the procurator that the cypresses and palms in the garden were giving off the scent of roses, that the cursed stream of roses was mingling with the smell of leather gear and of the escort’s sweat. From the outbuildings at the back of the palace, where the first cohort of the Twelfth Lightning Legion, which had come to Yershalaim with the procurator, was quartered, wisps of smoke drifted into the colonnade across the upper terrace of the garden, and that bitterish smoke, which showed that the cooks in the centuries had begun preparing the midday meal, was mixed with the same greasy rose scent.

“O gods, gods, why are you punishing me?.. Yes, there’s no doubt, it’s her, her again, the invincible, terrible illness... hemicrania, when half the head aches... there is no remedy for it, no escape at all... I’ll try not to move my head...”

On the mosaic floor by the fountain an armchair had already been set out, and the procurator, without looking at anyone, sat down in it and stretched out his hand to one side. The secretary respectfully placed a piece of parchment in that hand. Unable to hold back a grimace of pain, the procurator glanced sidelong over what was written, handed the parchment back to the secretary and said with difficulty:
“The accused from Galilee? Was the case sent to the tetrarch?”
“Yes, Procurator,” the secretary answered.
“And what did he do?”
“He declined to give an opinion on the case and sent the Sanhedrin’s death sentence to you for confirmation,” the secretary explained.
The procurator’s cheek twitched, and he said quietly:
“Bring in the accused.”

And at once two legionaries led a man of about twenty-seven from the garden terrace, under the columns and onto the balcony, and stood him in front of the procurator’s chair. The man was dressed in an old, torn blue chiton. His head was covered with a white cloth held by a strap around his forehead, and his hands were tied behind his back. Under his left eye he had a large bruise, and at the corner of his mouth a scrape caked with dried blood. The man who had been brought in looked at the procurator with anxious curiosity.
The procurator was silent for a while, then asked quietly in Aramaic:
“So it was you who incited the people to destroy the temple of Yershalaim?”

As he spoke, the procurator sat as if made of stone, and only his lips moved slightly as he pronounced the words. The procurator was like stone because he was afraid to move his head, which was blazing with hellish pain.
The man with bound hands leaned forward a little and began to speak:
“Good man! Believe me...”
But the procurator, still motionless and without raising his voice in the least, interrupted him at once:

“Is it me you are calling a good man? You are mistaken. All Yershalaim whispers that I am a ferocious monster, and that is perfectly true.” And in the same monotone he added: “Centurion Ratslayer to me.”

It seemed to everyone that the balcony grew darker when the centurion of the first century, Mark, nicknamed Ratslayer, appeared before the procurator. Ratslayer was a head taller than the tallest soldier in the legion and so broad in the shoulders that he completely blocked out the still-low sun.
The procurator addressed the centurion in Latin:
“The criminal calls me ‘good man.’ Take him out of here for a minute and explain to him how he is to speak to me. But no maiming.”
And everyone except the motionless procurator followed with their eyes Mark Ratslayer, who waved to the prisoner to show that he was to follow him.

Everyone always followed Ratslayer with their eyes wherever he appeared, because of his height, and those who saw him for the first time also because the centurion’s face was disfigured: his nose had once been smashed by a blow from a Germanic club.

Mark’s heavy boots thudded across the mosaic, the bound man followed him without a sound, complete silence fell in the colonnade, and one could hear the pigeons cooing on the garden terrace by the balcony, and the water singing an intricate, pleasant song in the fountain.
The procurator felt like getting up, putting his temple under the jet of water and staying like that, without moving. But he knew that even this would not help him.

Having led the prisoner out from under the columns into the garden, Ratslayer took a whip from the hands of a legionary standing at the foot of a bronze statue and, with an easy swing, struck the prisoner across the shoulders. The centurion’s movement was careless and light, but the bound man instantly crashed to the ground as if his legs had been cut from under him; he choked on the air, the color drained from his face, and his eyes went blank.
With his left hand alone, as lightly as if he were lifting an empty sack, Mark jerked the fallen man up into the air, set him on his feet and spoke in a nasal voice, mangling the Aramaic words:
“Roman procurator you call—hegemon. Other words not say. Stand straight. You understand me, or I hit you?”
The prisoner staggered but got control of himself; the color came back, he caught his breath and answered hoarsely:
“I understand you. Don’t beat me.”
A minute later he was standing before the procurator again.
A dull, sick voice sounded:
“Name?”
“Mine?” the prisoner responded hastily, his whole being expressing his readiness to answer sensibly and not provoke any more anger.
The procurator said quietly:
“Mine I know. Don’t pretend to be stupider than you are. Yours.”
“Yeshua,” the prisoner answered hurriedly.
“Do you have a byname?”
“Ha-Notsri.”
“Where are you from?”
“From the town of Gamala,” the prisoner answered, motioning with his head to show that somewhere far away, to his right, in the north, there was a town called Gamala.
“Who are you by blood?”
“I don’t know exactly,” the prisoner answered readily. “I don’t remember my parents. I was told my father was a Syrian...”
“Where do you live permanently?”
“I have no permanent home,” the prisoner answered shyly. “I travel from town to town.”
“That can be put more briefly, in one word: a vagrant,” said the procurator, and asked: “Any family?”
“None at all. I am alone in the world.”
“Can you read and write?”
“Yes.”
“Do you know any language besides Aramaic?”
“I do. Greek.”
A swollen eyelid lifted, and an eye clouded with a haze of suffering fixed itself on the prisoner. The other eye remained closed.
Pilate spoke in Greek:
“So it was you who meant to destroy the temple building and called on the people to do it?”
At this the prisoner brightened again, his eyes stopped showing fear, and he spoke in Greek:

“I, goo...”—here horror flashed in the prisoner’s eyes because he had nearly slipped—“I, hegemon, have never in my life meant to destroy the temple building, and I never incited anyone to such a senseless act.”
Surprise showed on the face of the secretary, who was hunched over a low table writing down the testimony. He raised his head, but immediately bent it again over the parchment.

“A great many different people flock to this city for the feast. Among them there are magicians, astrologers, soothsayers and murderers,” the procurator said in a monotone, “and one also comes across liars. You, for instance, are a liar. It is written down clearly: incited the destruction of the temple. That is what people testify.”

“These good people,” the prisoner began, and, hurriedly adding “hegemon,” went on: “never learned anything, and they got everything I said muddled. In fact I’m beginning to fear that this muddle will go on for a very long time. And all because he writes down what I say wrongly.”
Silence fell. Now both sick eyes were looking heavily at the prisoner.

“I repeat to you, but for the last time: stop pretending to be mad, you robber,” Pilate said softly and monotonously. “Not much has been written down against you, but what has been written is enough to hang you.”

“No, no, hegemon,” the prisoner said, straining all over in his wish to convince, “there’s one who goes around, goes around with a goatskin parchment and writes all the time. But once I looked into that parchment and was horrified. I said absolutely nothing of what is written there. I begged him: for God’s sake, burn your parchment! But he snatched it out of my hands and ran away.”
“Who is he?” Pilate asked with distaste, and touched his temple with his hand.

“Levi Matvei,” the prisoner explained willingly. “He was a tax collector, and I first met him on the road in Bethphage, where the fig orchard juts out at the corner, and got to talking with him. At first he treated me with hostility and even insulted me—that is, he thought he was insulting me by calling me a dog,” here the prisoner smiled, “but I personally see nothing bad in that animal that I should be offended by the word...”
The secretary stopped writing and stealthily cast a surprised glance—not at the prisoner, but at the procurator.
“...however, after he had listened to me, he began to soften,” Yeshua went on, “and in the end he threw his money out onto the road and said he would go traveling with me...”
Pilate grinned with one cheek, baring yellow teeth, and said, turning his whole body toward the secretary:
“Oh, city of Yershalaim! The things one hears in it! A tax collector, do you hear, threw his money out onto the road!”
Not knowing how to respond to this, the secretary thought it best to copy Pilate’s smile.
“And he said that from then on money had become hateful to him,” Yeshua explained Levi Matvei’s strange behavior, and added: “And ever since then he has been my companion.”

Still baring his teeth, the procurator looked at the prisoner, then at the sun, rising steadily over the equestrian statues of the hippodrome, which lay far below to the right, and suddenly, in a kind of sickening torment, thought that the simplest thing would be to drive this strange robber off the balcony with just two words: “Hang him.” To drive out the escort as well, to leave the colonnade for the inside of the palace, order the room darkened, collapse onto the couch, call for cold water, call his dog Banga in a plaintive voice and complain to her about the hemicrania. And the thought of poison suddenly flashed temptingly through the procurator’s aching head.

He looked at the prisoner with clouded eyes and was silent for some time, trying painfully to remember why, in the merciless morning sun of Yershalaim, a prisoner with a face disfigured by beatings was standing before him, and what other useless questions he would have to ask him.
“Levi Matvei?” the sick man asked in a hoarse voice, and closed his eyes.
“Yes, Levi Matvei,” came the high voice that tormented him.
“But what was it, all the same, that you said about the temple to the crowd in the market?”
The voice of the one answering seemed to stab Pilate in the temple; it was inexpressibly painful, and this voice was saying:
“I said, hegemon, that the temple of the old faith would fall and a new temple of truth would be built. I put it that way so it would be easier to understand.”
“And why, you vagrant, did you stir up the people in the market, telling them about the truth, of which you have no notion? What is truth?”

And here the procurator thought: “O my gods! I’m asking him something unnecessary at a trial... My mind no longer serves me...” And again he seemed to see a cup of dark liquid. “Poison, give me poison...”
And again he heard the voice:

“The truth, first of all, is that your head aches, and aches so badly that you are faint-heartedly thinking of death. You are not only too weak to talk to me, it is hard for you even to look at me. And right now I am, against my will, your torturer, which grieves me. You can’t even think about anything, and you only dream that your dog will come, apparently the only creature you are attached to. But your torment will end now; your headache will go away.”
The secretary goggled at the prisoner and left a word unfinished.

Pilate raised his martyred eyes to the prisoner and saw that the sun already stood quite high over the hippodrome, that a ray had made its way into the colonnade and was creeping toward Yeshua’s worn-out sandals, and that Yeshua was moving out of the sun.

At this the procurator rose from his chair and clutched his head in his hands, and horror showed on his yellowish, shaven face. But he at once suppressed it by force of will and sank back into the chair.
Meanwhile the prisoner went on talking, but the secretary wrote nothing more down; he only stretched out his neck like a goose, trying not to miss a single word.

“There, it’s all over,” the arrested man was saying, glancing benevolently at Pilate, “and I’m extremely glad of it. I’d advise you, hegemon, to leave the palace for a while and take a walk somewhere in the surrounding country, say, in the gardens on the Mount of Olives. The storm will begin...” the prisoner turned and squinted at the sun, “...later, toward evening. A walk would do you a great deal of good, and I would gladly go with you. Some new thoughts have come into my head which might, I think, interest you, and I’d willingly share them with you, all the more since you give the impression of being a very intelligent man.”
The secretary turned deathly pale and dropped the scroll on the floor.

“The trouble is,” the bound man went on, with no one stopping him, “that you are too closed off and have lost faith in people entirely. After all, you’ll agree, one can’t place all one’s affection in a dog. Your life is meager, hegemon”—and here the speaker allowed himself to smile.

The secretary now thought of only one thing: whether to believe his ears or not. He had to believe them. Then he tried to imagine exactly what bizarre form the hot-tempered procurator’s anger would take at this unheard-of insolence from the prisoner. And this the secretary could not imagine, although he knew the procurator well.
Then the cracked, hoarse voice of the procurator rang out, saying in Latin:
“Untie his hands.”

One of the legionaries of the escort rapped his spear on the floor, handed it to another, went over and took the ropes off the prisoner. The secretary picked up the scroll and decided for the time being to write nothing down and be surprised at nothing.
“Admit it,” Pilate asked quietly in Greek, “you are a great physician?”
“No, Procurator, I am not a physician,” the prisoner answered, rubbing his crushed, swollen, purple wrist with relish.
Glowering from under his brows, Pilate bored into the prisoner with his eyes, and there was no longer any murk in those eyes; the sparks everyone knew had appeared in them.
“I didn’t ask you,” said Pilate, “perhaps you know Latin as well?”
“Yes, I do,” the prisoner answered.
Color rose to Pilate’s yellowish cheeks, and he asked in Latin:
“How did you know I wanted to call my dog?”
“That’s very simple,” the prisoner answered in Latin. “You were moving your hand through the air,” and the prisoner repeated Pilate’s gesture, “as if you wanted to stroke something, and your lips...”
“Yes,” said Pilate.
They were silent for a while. Then Pilate asked a question in Greek:
“So, you are a physician?”
“No, no,” the prisoner answered quickly, “believe me, I’m not a physician.”

“Very well. If you want to keep it a secret, keep it. It has no direct bearing on the case. So you maintain that you did not call for the temple to be destroyed... or set on fire, or done away with in any other way?”
“I, hegemon, have not called anyone to such acts, I repeat. Do I look like a feeble-minded man?”
“Oh yes, you don’t look feeble-minded,” the procurator answered quietly, and smiled a terrible sort of smile. “Then swear that it did not happen.”
“What do you want me to swear by?” asked the untied man, becoming very animated.
“Well, by your life, say,” the procurator answered. “It’s just the time to swear by it, since it hangs by a thread, you may as well know.”
“You don’t suppose it was you who hung it there, hegemon?” the prisoner asked. “If you do, you are very much mistaken.”
Pilate started and answered through his teeth:
“I can cut that thread.”
“There too you are mistaken,” the prisoner objected, smiling radiantly and shading his eyes from the sun with his hand. “You’ll agree that surely only the one who hung the thread can cut it?”

“So, so,” Pilate said with a smile, “now I have no doubt that the idle gapers of Yershalaim followed at your heels. I don’t know who hung your tongue, but it’s hung well. By the way, tell me: is it true that you came into Yershalaim through the Susa Gate riding on a donkey, accompanied by a rabble that shouted greetings to you as if to some prophet?” Here the procurator pointed to the parchment scroll.
The prisoner looked at the procurator in bewilderment.

“I don’t even have a donkey, hegemon,” he said. “I did come into Yershalaim through the Susa Gate, but on foot, with only Levi Matvei for company, and nobody shouted anything at me, because nobody in Yershalaim knew me then.”
“Do you happen to know,” Pilate continued, not taking his eyes off the prisoner, “a certain Dismas, another called Gestas, and a third called Bar-Rabban?”
“I don’t know these good people,” the prisoner answered.
“Truly?”
“Truly.”
“And now tell me, why is it that you keep using the words ‘good people’? Is that what you call everyone?”
“Everyone,” the prisoner answered. “There are no evil people in the world.”

“That’s the first I’ve heard of it,” Pilate said with a smile. “But perhaps I know too little of life!.. You need not record what follows,” he told the secretary, although the latter was not recording anything anyway, and went on to the prisoner: “Did you read that in some Greek book?”
“No, I arrived at it with my own mind.”
“And you preach it?”
“Yes.”
“And what about, for instance, the centurion Mark, the one they nicknamed Ratslayer—is he good?”
“Yes,” the prisoner answered. “He is, it’s true, an unhappy man. Ever since good people disfigured him, he has become cruel and hard. I wonder who maimed him.”

“I can tell you that gladly,” Pilate responded, “for I was a witness to it. Good people threw themselves at him like dogs at a bear. Germans fastened on his neck, his arms, his legs. An infantry maniple had been caught in a trap, and if a cavalry turma had not cut its way in from the flank—and I commanded it—you, philosopher, would not have had the chance to talk with Ratslayer. That was at the battle of Idistaviso, in the Valley of the Maidens.”
“If one could only talk with him,” the prisoner suddenly said dreamily, “I’m sure he would change completely.”

“I suspect,” Pilate responded, “that you would bring little joy to the legate of the legion if you took it into your head to talk with any of his officers or soldiers. However, that will not happen, fortunately for everyone, and I shall be the first to see to it.”

At that moment a swallow darted swiftly into the colonnade, circled under the golden ceiling, swooped down, nearly brushed the face of a bronze statue in a niche with its sharp wing, and vanished behind the capital of a column. Perhaps it had the idea of building a nest there.

While it was flying, a formula took shape in the procurator’s head, which was now clear and light. It went like this: the hegemon has examined the case of the wandering philosopher Yeshua, called Ha-Notsri, and found no grounds in it for a criminal charge. In particular, he has found not the slightest connection between Yeshua’s actions and the disturbances that recently took place in Yershalaim. The wandering philosopher has proved to be mentally ill. Consequently the procurator does not confirm the death sentence passed on Ha-Notsri by the Lesser Sanhedrin. But in view of the fact that Ha-Notsri’s mad, utopian speeches may cause unrest in Yershalaim, the procurator removes Yeshua from Yershalaim and will have him confined in Strato’s Caesarea on the Mediterranean Sea, that is, precisely where the procurator’s residence is.
It remained to dictate this to the secretary.

The swallow’s wings whirred just above the hegemon’s head; the bird shot over to the basin of the fountain and flew out into the open. The procurator raised his eyes to the prisoner and saw that a column of dust had caught fire in the sunlight beside him.
“Is that everything on him?” Pilate asked the secretary.
“No, unfortunately,” the secretary answered unexpectedly, and handed Pilate another piece of parchment.
“What else is there?” Pilate asked, frowning.

When he had read what he was handed, his face changed even more. Whether it was dark blood rushing to his neck and face or something else that happened, his skin lost its yellowness and turned brown, and his eyes seemed to sink.

Again it was probably the blood that was to blame, rushing to his temples and pounding in them, but something happened to the procurator’s sight. He imagined that the prisoner’s head floated away somewhere and another appeared in its place. On this bald head sat a gold crown with sparse teeth. On the forehead was a round ulcer, eating into the skin and smeared with ointment. A sunken, toothless mouth with a drooping, capricious lower lip. It seemed to Pilate that the pink columns of the balcony and the roofs of Yershalaim far below, beyond the garden, had disappeared, and everything around had drowned in the dense greenery of the gardens of Capreae. And something strange happened to his hearing as well—it was as if trumpets had sounded far away, softly and menacingly, and a nasal voice was heard very distinctly, haughtily drawling the words: “The law of lèse-majesté...”

Thoughts rushed by, short, incoherent and extraordinary: “Lost!..” then: “All lost!..” And among them one quite absurd thought about some sort of immortality, and the immortality, for some reason, brought on an unbearable anguish.
Pilate made an effort, drove the vision away, returned his gaze to the balcony, and again the prisoner’s eyes were before him.

“Listen, Ha-Notsri,” the procurator began, looking at Yeshua rather strangely: the procurator’s face was menacing, but his eyes were anxious, “did you ever say anything about the great Caesar? Answer! Did you?.. Or... did you... not?” Pilate drew out the word “not” a little longer than is proper at a trial, and in his glance he sent Yeshua some thought that he seemed to want to plant in the prisoner’s mind.
“Telling the truth is easy and pleasant,” the prisoner remarked.

“I don’t need to know,” Pilate responded in a stifled, angry voice, “whether it is pleasant or unpleasant for you to tell the truth. But you will have to tell it. And as you tell it, weigh every word, if you want to avoid a death that is not only inevitable but agonizing.”

No one knows what had happened to the procurator of Judea, but he allowed himself to raise his hand as if shielding himself from a ray of sun, and from behind that hand, as from behind a shield, to send the prisoner a look full of hints.
“So,” he said, “answer: do you know a certain Judas from Kiriath, and what exactly did you say to him about Caesar, if you said anything?”

“It was like this,” the prisoner began readily. “The evening before last, near the temple, I met a young man who called himself Judas, from the town of Kiriath. He invited me to his house in the Lower City and offered me a meal...”
“A good man?” asked Pilate, and a diabolical fire flashed in his eyes.
“A very good and inquisitive man,” the prisoner confirmed. “He showed the greatest interest in my thoughts and received me most cordially...”
“He lit the lamps...” Pilate said through his teeth, in the same tone as the prisoner, and his eyes glimmered as he said it.
“Yes,” Yeshua went on, a little surprised at how well informed the procurator was, “and asked me to tell him my views on state power. The question interested him extremely.”
“And what did you say?” asked Pilate. “Or will you tell me you’ve forgotten what you said?”—but there was already hopelessness in Pilate’s tone.

“Among other things I said,” the prisoner related, “that all power is violence done to people, and that a time will come when there will be no power of the Caesars, nor any other power. Man will pass into the kingdom of truth and justice, where no power at all will be needed.”
“Go on!”
“There was nothing more,” said the prisoner. “At that point people ran in, began tying me up and took me off to prison.”
The secretary, trying not to miss a word, was rapidly scratching words onto the parchment.
“There has never been, there is not, and there never will be in the world a greater or finer power for people than the power of the emperor Tiberius!” Pilate’s cracked, sick voice swelled.
For some reason the procurator was looking with hatred at the secretary and the escort.

“And it is not for you, you mad criminal, to reason about it!” Here Pilate shouted: “Take the escort off the balcony!” And, turning to the secretary, he added: “Leave me alone with the criminal. This is a matter of state.”
The escort raised their spears and, their hobnailed caligae thudding in step, went out from the balcony into the garden, and after the escort the secretary went out too.

For some time the silence on the balcony was broken only by the song of the water in the fountain. Pilate watched the dome of water swell above the spout, its edges break off and fall in thin streams.
The prisoner was the first to speak:
“I see that some misfortune has come about because I talked with that young man from Kiriath. I have a foreboding, hegemon, that something terrible will happen to him, and I am very sorry for him.”

“I think,” the procurator answered with a strange smile, “that there is someone else in the world whom you ought to pity more than Judas from Kiriath, and who will fare far worse than Judas!.. So then: Mark Ratslayer, a cold and convinced executioner; the people who, as I see,” the procurator pointed at Yeshua’s disfigured face, “beat you for your preaching; the robbers Dismas and Gestas, who with their accomplices killed four soldiers; and, finally, the dirty traitor Judas—they are all good people?”
“Yes,” the prisoner answered.
“And the kingdom of truth will come?”
“It will come, hegemon,” Yeshua answered with conviction.

“It will never come!” Pilate suddenly shouted in such a terrible voice that Yeshua recoiled. So, many years before, in the Valley of the Maidens, Pilate had shouted to his horsemen: “Cut them down! Cut them down! The giant Ratslayer is trapped!” He raised his voice, worn ragged by shouting commands, higher still, calling out the words so that they would be heard in the garden: “Criminal! Criminal! Criminal!”
And then, lowering his voice, he asked:
“Yeshua Ha-Notsri, do you believe in any gods?”
“There is one God,” Yeshua answered. “I believe in him.”
“Then pray to him! Pray hard! However...” here Pilate’s voice gave out, “that won’t help. No wife?” Pilate asked, for some reason in anguish, not understanding what was happening to him.
“No, I’m alone.”

“Hateful city...” the procurator suddenly muttered for no apparent reason, and twitched his shoulders as if he were cold, and rubbed his hands as if washing them. “If they had cut your throat before your meeting with Judas from Kiriath, truly, it would have been better.”
“Why don’t you let me go, hegemon,” the prisoner asked unexpectedly, and his voice grew anxious. “I see that they want to kill me.”
Pilate’s face was distorted by a spasm; he turned the inflamed, red-veined whites of his eyes on Yeshua and said:

“Do you suppose, you wretch, that a Roman procurator will let go a man who has said what you have said? O gods, gods! Or do you think I’m ready to take your place? I do not share your ideas! And listen to me: if from this moment you utter so much as a word, if you speak to anyone at all, beware of me! I repeat: beware!”
“Hegemon...”
“Silence!” Pilate cried, and his furious gaze followed the swallow, which had fluttered onto the balcony again. “Here!” Pilate shouted.

And when the secretary and the escort had returned to their places, Pilate announced that he confirmed the death sentence passed at the session of the Lesser Sanhedrin on the criminal Yeshua Ha-Notsri, and the secretary wrote down what Pilate had said.

A minute later Mark Ratslayer stood before the procurator. The procurator ordered him to hand the criminal over to the head of the secret service and to pass on to him the procurator’s instructions that Yeshua Ha-Notsri be kept apart from the other condemned men, and also that the men of the secret service detail be forbidden, under threat of severe punishment, to talk to Yeshua about anything at all or to answer any of his questions.
At a sign from Mark the escort closed around Yeshua and led him off the balcony.

Next there appeared before the procurator a handsome, fair-bearded man with eagle feathers in the crest of his helmet, gold lions’ heads gleaming on his chest and gold studs on his sword belt as well, in triple-soled boots laced up to the knee, with a crimson cloak thrown over his left shoulder. This was the legate in command of the legion.

The procurator asked him where the Sebastian cohort was at present. The legate reported that the Sebastians were holding a cordon on the square in front of the hippodrome, where the sentence on the criminals would be announced to the people.

Then the procurator ordered the legate to detach two centuries from the Roman cohort. One of them, under Ratslayer’s command, was to escort the criminals, the carts carrying the implements of execution, and the executioners on their way to Bald Mountain, and on arriving there to join the upper cordon. The other was to be sent to Bald Mountain at once and to begin the cordon immediately. For the same purpose, that is, to guard the Mountain, the procurator asked the legate to send an auxiliary cavalry regiment, the Syrian ala.

When the legate had left the balcony, the procurator ordered the secretary to invite to the palace the president of the Sanhedrin, two of its members and the head of the temple guard of Yershalaim, but added that he wished it to be arranged so that, before conferring with all these people, he could speak with the president first and in private.

The procurator’s order was carried out quickly and precisely, and the sun, which in those days was scorching Yershalaim with an extraordinary fury, had not yet come near its highest point when, on the upper terrace of the garden, by the two white marble lions that guarded the stairs, the procurator met the acting president of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish high priest Joseph Caiaphas.

It was quiet in the garden. But as he came out from under the colonnade onto the sun-flooded upper level of the garden, with its palms on monstrous elephant legs—the level from which the whole of Yershalaim, which he hated, spread out before the procurator, with its hanging bridges, its fortresses and, above all, that indescribable mass of marble with golden dragon scales instead of a roof, the temple of Yershalaim—the procurator’s keen ear caught, far below, where a stone wall separated the lower terraces of the palace garden from the city square, a low rumbling, above which there rose now and then faint, thin sounds that were half moans, half cries.

The procurator understood that a countless crowd of the inhabitants of Yershalaim, stirred up by the recent disturbances, had already gathered there on the square, that this crowd was impatiently waiting for the sentence to be pronounced, and that restless water sellers were crying their wares in it.

The procurator began by inviting the high priest onto the balcony, to take shelter from the merciless heat, but Caiaphas politely excused himself and explained that he could not do so on the eve of the feast. Pilate pulled a hood over his slightly balding head and began the conversation. The conversation was in Greek.
Pilate said that he had examined the case of Yeshua Ha-Notsri and confirmed the death sentence.

Thus, three robbers were condemned to death, the execution to be carried out today: Dismas, Gestas and Bar-Rabban, and in addition this Yeshua Ha-Notsri. The first two, who had taken it into their heads to incite the people to revolt against Caesar, had been captured in a fight by the Roman authorities, were under the procurator’s jurisdiction, and consequently were not under discussion here. The last two, however, Bar-Rabban and Ha-Notsri, had been seized by the local authorities and condemned by the Sanhedrin. According to the law, according to custom, one of these two criminals was to be set free in honor of the great feast of Passover, which began today.
And so the procurator wished to know which of the two criminals the Sanhedrin intended to release: Bar-Rabban or Ha-Notsri?
Caiaphas inclined his head to show that the question was clear to him, and answered:
“The Sanhedrin asks for the release of Bar-Rabban.”
The procurator knew very well that this was exactly how the high priest would answer, but his task was to show that such an answer astonished him.
And Pilate did this with great skill. The eyebrows on his haughty face went up, and the procurator looked straight into the high priest’s eyes in surprise.
“I confess, this answer has astounded me,” the procurator began softly. “I fear there may be some misunderstanding here.”

Pilate explained himself. The Roman authorities had no wish whatever to encroach on the rights of the local spiritual authorities, as the high priest well knew, but in the present case there was an obvious error. And the Roman authorities were, of course, interested in having that error corrected.

Indeed: the crimes of Bar-Rabban and Ha-Notsri were not at all comparable in gravity. If the latter, clearly a madman, was guilty of uttering absurd speeches that had stirred up the people in Yershalaim and in certain other places, the former bore a far heavier burden of guilt. Not only had he allowed himself to make direct calls to rebellion, he had also killed a guard when they tried to arrest him. Bar-Rabban was incomparably more dangerous than Ha-Notsri.

In view of all the foregoing, the procurator asked the high priest to reconsider the decision and to set free whichever of the two condemned men was the less harmful, and that, beyond doubt, was Ha-Notsri. Well then?..
Caiaphas said in a quiet but firm voice that the Sanhedrin had studied the case carefully and informed him a second time that it intended to release Bar-Rabban.
“What? Even after my petition? The petition of the man through whom Roman authority speaks? High priest, repeat it a third time.”
“And for the third time I inform you that we are releasing Bar-Rabban,” Caiaphas said quietly.

It was all over, and there was nothing more to talk about. Ha-Notsri was going away forever, and there was no one to cure the procurator’s terrible, savage pains; there is no remedy for them but death. But it was not this thought that struck Pilate now. The same incomprehensible anguish that had already come over him on the balcony pierced his whole being. He at once tried to explain it, and the explanation was a strange one: it seemed to the procurator, dimly, that he had left something unsaid to the condemned man, or perhaps had not heard something out.

Pilate drove the thought away, and it flew off in an instant, just as it had flown in. It flew off, but the anguish remained unexplained, for it could hardly be explained by some other brief thought that flashed like lightning and went out at once: “Immortality... immortality has come...” Whose immortality had come? The procurator did not understand that, but the thought of this mysterious immortality made him go cold in the blazing sun.
“Very well,” said Pilate, “so be it.”

At this he looked around, took in the world that was visible to him, and was surprised at the change that had come over it. The bush heavy with roses had vanished, the cypresses bordering the upper terrace had vanished, and the pomegranate tree, and the white statue in the greenery, and the greenery itself. In place of all this a kind of crimson murk came floating by; seaweed swayed in it and drifted off somewhere, and Pilate himself drifted with it. He was being carried away now, suffocated and scorched, by the most terrible anger there is—the anger of powerlessness.
“I can’t breathe,” Pilate uttered, “I can’t breathe!”
With a cold, damp hand he tore the clasp from the collar of his cloak, and it fell onto the sand.

“It is close today; there’s a storm somewhere,” Caiaphas responded, not taking his eyes off the procurator’s reddened face and foreseeing all the torments still to come. “Oh, what a terrible month of Nisan it is this year!”
“No,” said Pilate, “it’s not the closeness; it is you, Caiaphas, who leave me no air.” And, narrowing his eyes, Pilate smiled and added: “Take care of yourself, high priest.”
The high priest’s dark eyes flashed, and, no less skillfully than the procurator had done earlier, he expressed surprise on his face.

“What do I hear, Procurator?” Caiaphas answered proudly and calmly. “You threaten me, after a sentence has been passed that you yourself confirmed? Can this be? We are used to the Roman procurator choosing his words before he speaks. What if someone should overhear us, hegemon?”
Pilate looked at the high priest with dead eyes and, baring his teeth, produced a smile.

“Come now, high priest! Who could possibly overhear us here now? Do I look like the young wandering holy fool who is being executed today? Am I a boy, Caiaphas? I know what I am saying and where I am saying it. The garden is cordoned off, the palace is cordoned off, so that not a mouse could slip through any crack! And not only a mouse—not even that one, what’s his name... from the town of Kiriath, could get in. By the way, do you know him, high priest? Yes... if such a man did get in here, he would bitterly regret it—you’ll surely believe me there? Know, then, high priest, that from now on you will have no peace! Neither you nor your people”—and Pilate pointed far off to the right, where the temple blazed on the heights—“it is I who tell you this, Pilate of Pontus, the knight Golden Spear!”

“I know, I know!” the black-bearded Caiaphas answered fearlessly, and his eyes flashed. He raised his hand to the sky and went on: “The Jewish people know that you hate them with a fierce hatred and will cause them much torment, but you will never destroy them! God will protect them! The almighty Caesar will hear us, he will hear, and he will shelter us from Pilate the destroyer!”

“Oh no!” Pilate exclaimed, and with every word it became easier and easier for him: there was no more need to pretend, no need to choose his words. “You have complained about me to Caesar too often, and now my hour has come, Caiaphas! Now a message will fly from me—and not to the governor in Antioch, and not to Rome, but straight to Capreae, to the emperor himself—a message about how you are sheltering known rebels in Yershalaim from death. And then it will not be with water from Solomon’s Pool, as I wanted for your own good, that I give Yershalaim to drink! No, not with water! Remember how because of you I had to take the shields bearing the emperor’s monograms down from the walls, move troops, how, you see, I had to come here myself to look into what is going on among you! Remember my words: it is not one cohort you will see here in Yershalaim, high priest, no! The whole Fulminata legion will come up under the city walls, the Arab cavalry will arrive, and then you will hear bitter weeping and lamentation! Then you will remember the Bar-Rabban you saved, and you will regret that you sent the philosopher with his peaceful preaching to his death!”
The high priest’s face broke out in blotches; his eyes burned. Like the procurator, he smiled, baring his teeth, and answered:

“Do you believe what you are saying now yourself, Procurator? No, you don’t! It was not peace, not peace that the seducer of the people brought us here in Yershalaim, and you, knight, understand that perfectly well. You wanted to release him so that he would stir up the people, defile the faith and bring the people under Roman swords! But I, the high priest of the Jews, as long as I live, will not let the faith be defiled, and I will protect the people! Do you hear, Pilate?” And here Caiaphas raised his hand menacingly: “Listen, Procurator!”

Caiaphas fell silent, and the procurator heard again what sounded like the noise of the sea, rolling up to the very walls of the garden of Herod the Great. The noise rose from below to the procurator’s feet and into his face. And behind his back, beyond the wings of the palace, came anxious trumpet calls, the heavy crunch of hundreds of feet, the clank of iron—and here the procurator understood that the Roman infantry was already marching out, as he had ordered, hurrying to the parade before death that is so terrible for rebels and robbers.

“Do you hear, Procurator?” the high priest quietly repeated. “Will you really tell me that all this”—here the high priest raised both hands, and the dark hood fell from his head—“was caused by the wretched robber Bar-Rabban?”

The procurator wiped his wet, cold forehead with the back of his hand, looked at the ground, then, squinting up at the sky, saw that the red-hot ball was almost directly overhead and that Caiaphas’s shadow had shrunk to almost nothing beside the lion’s tail, and said quietly and indifferently:
“It is getting on for noon. We have let ourselves be carried away by our conversation, and meanwhile there is business to continue.”

Having apologized to the high priest in exquisitely chosen words, he asked him to sit down on a bench in the shade of a magnolia and wait while he summoned the other persons needed for a last brief conference and gave one more order connected with the execution.

Caiaphas bowed politely, laying his hand on his heart, and remained in the garden, while Pilate returned to the balcony. There he told the secretary, who was waiting for him, to invite into the garden the legate of the legion and the tribune of the cohort, as well as the two members of the Sanhedrin and the head of the temple guard, who were waiting to be summoned on the lower terrace of the garden, in a round gazebo with a fountain. To this Pilate added that he would come out into the garden himself directly, and withdrew into the palace.

While the secretary was assembling the conference, the procurator, in a room screened from the sun by dark curtains, met with a certain man whose face was half covered by a hood, although in that room the sun’s rays could not have troubled him. The meeting was extremely short. The procurator said a few words to the man quietly, after which the man withdrew, and Pilate went through the colonnade into the garden.

There, in the presence of everyone he wished to see, the procurator solemnly and dryly confirmed that he upheld the death sentence on Yeshua Ha-Notsri, and officially inquired of the members of the Sanhedrin which of the criminals it was their pleasure to leave alive. On receiving the answer that it was Bar-Rabban, the procurator said:
“Very good,” and told the secretary to enter it in the record at once, clenched in his hand the clasp the secretary had picked up from the sand, and said solemnly: “It is time!”

At this, all those present set off down the broad marble staircase between walls of roses that gave off a stupefying fragrance, going lower and lower toward the palace wall, toward the gate that led out onto a large, smoothly paved square, at the far end of which could be seen the columns and statues of the Yershalaim racecourse.

As soon as the group had come out of the garden onto the square and climbed onto the broad stone platform that dominated it, Pilate, looking around through narrowed eyelids, took stock of the situation. The space he had just crossed, that is, the space between the palace wall and the platform, was empty, but in front of him Pilate could no longer see the square at all: the crowd had devoured it. It would have flooded the platform itself and the cleared space too, if a triple row of Sebastian soldiers on Pilate’s left and soldiers of the Ituraean auxiliary cohort on his right had not held it back.

And so Pilate climbed onto the platform, mechanically clutching the useless clasp in his fist and squinting. The procurator was squinting not because the sun was burning his eyes, no! For some reason he did not want to see the group of condemned men who, as he knew perfectly well, were now being brought up onto the platform behind him.

As soon as the white cloak with the crimson lining appeared high up on that stone crag above the edge of the human sea, a wave of sound struck the unseeing Pilate’s ears: “Ha-a-a...” It began softly, rising somewhere far off near the hippodrome, then grew thunderous and, after holding for a few seconds, began to subside. “They’ve seen me,” the procurator thought. The wave did not reach its lowest point but unexpectedly began to grow again and, swaying, rose higher than the first, and on this second wave, as foam boils up on a sea swell, there boiled up whistling and, distinguishable through the thunder, the separate moans of women. “They’ve brought them onto the platform...” Pilate thought. “And the moans are because several women were crushed when the crowd surged forward.”
He waited a while, knowing that no power on earth could silence the crowd until it had breathed out everything that had built up inside it and fell silent of its own accord.
And when that moment came, the procurator flung up his right hand, and the last of the noise was blown away from the crowd.
Then Pilate drew as much of the hot air into his chest as he could and shouted, and his cracked voice was carried out over thousands of heads:
“In the name of Caesar the emperor!..”
At this an iron, chopped-off cry struck his ears several times over: in the cohorts the soldiers, flinging up their spears and standards, shouted terribly:
“Long live Caesar!!”
Pilate threw back his head and thrust it straight into the sun. Green fire flared under his eyelids, his brain caught fire from it, and hoarse Aramaic words flew out over the crowd:

“Four criminals, arrested in Yershalaim for murder, incitement to rebellion and contempt for the laws and the faith, have been sentenced to a shameful death—hanging on posts! And this execution will take place shortly on Bald Mountain! The names of the criminals are Dismas, Gestas, Bar-Rabban and Ha-Notsri. Here they stand before you!”
Pilate pointed with his hand to the right, not seeing any criminals, but knowing that they were there, in the place where they were supposed to be.
The crowd answered with a long rumble, as if of surprise or relief. When it had died away, Pilate continued:

“But only three of them will be executed, for, according to law and custom, in honor of the feast of Passover, to one of the condemned, chosen by the Lesser Sanhedrin and approved by the Roman authorities, the magnanimous Caesar the emperor returns his contemptible life!”

Pilate shouted out the words and at the same time listened as the rumble gave way to a great silence. Now not a sigh, not a rustle reached his ears, and there even came a moment when it seemed to Pilate that everything around him had vanished altogether. The city he hated had died, and only he was standing there, alone, scorched by the vertical rays, his face pressed against the sky. Pilate held the silence a moment longer, and then began to shout:
“The name of the one who will now be set free before your eyes...”

He made one more pause, holding back the name, checking whether he had said everything, because he knew that the dead city would come back to life once the lucky man’s name was spoken, and no further words would be heard.
“Is that all?” Pilate whispered soundlessly to himself. “That’s all. The name!”
And, rolling the letter “r” out over the silent city, he shouted:
“Bar-Rabban!”
Here it seemed to him that the sun burst with a ringing sound above him and flooded his ears with fire. In this fire raged roars, shrieks, moans, laughter and whistling.

Pilate turned and walked back across the platform toward the steps, looking at nothing but the many-colored squares of the paving under his feet, so as not to stumble. He knew that now, behind his back, bronze coins and dates were raining down on the platform, that in the howling crowd people, crushing one another, were climbing onto shoulders to see the miracle with their own eyes—how a man who had already been in the hands of death had broken free of those hands! How the legionaries were taking the ropes off him, unwittingly causing him burning pain in the arms that had been dislocated under interrogation, and how he, wincing and groaning, was nevertheless smiling a senseless, crazed smile.

He knew that at the same time the escort was already leading the three men with bound hands to the side steps, to take them out onto the road that ran west, out of the city, to Bald Mountain. Only when he was behind the platform, at its back, did Pilate open his eyes, knowing that he was safe now: he could no longer see the condemned men.

Mingled with the moaning of the crowd, which was beginning to quiet down, and distinguishable through it, were the piercing cries of the heralds, repeating, some in Aramaic, others in Greek, everything that the procurator had shouted from the platform. Besides that, there reached his ears the rapid, rattling, approaching clatter of hooves and a trumpet that blared something short and cheerful. These sounds were answered by the shrill whistling of boys on the rooftops of the street that led from the market to the hippodrome square, and by cries of “Look out!”

A soldier standing alone in the cleared space of the square with a standard in his hand waved it in alarm, and at that the procurator, the legate of the legion, the secretary and the escort came to a halt.

The cavalry ala, lengthening its trot more and more, flew out onto the square, so as to cross it at one side, avoiding the mass of people, and then, by a lane under a stone wall overgrown with vines, gallop by the shortest road to Bald Mountain.

Flying along at a trot, the commander of the ala, a Syrian, small as a boy and dark as a mulatto, drew level with Pilate, shouted something in a high voice and snatched his sword from its sheath. His vicious, sweat-soaked black horse shied and reared. Thrusting the sword back into its sheath, the commander struck the horse across the neck with his whip, brought it under control and rode off into the lane, breaking into a gallop. After him, three abreast, horsemen came flying in a cloud of dust, the tips of their light bamboo lances bobbing, and past the procurator rushed faces that looked especially swarthy under white turbans, with gleaming teeth bared in cheerful grins.
Raising dust to the sky, the ala burst into the lane, and the last to gallop past Pilate was a soldier with a trumpet blazing in the sun on his back.

Shielding himself from the dust with his hand and wrinkling his face in displeasure, Pilate moved on, heading for the gates of the palace garden, and after him came the legate, the secretary and the escort.
It was about ten o’clock in the morning.

chapters.title: 3. The Seventh Proof
paragraphs: “Yes, it was about ten o’clock in the morning, most esteemed Ivan Nikolayevich,” said the professor.
The poet passed his hand over his face like a man who has only just come to, and saw that it was evening at Patriarch’s.

The water in the pond had turned black, and a light little boat was already gliding over it, and one could hear the splash of an oar and the giggles of some citizeness in the boat. People had appeared on the benches along the avenues, but again on all three sides of the square except the one where our two companions were.

The sky over Moscow seemed to have faded, and the full moon could be seen quite distinctly high up, not yet golden but white. It had become much easier to breathe, and the voices under the lindens now sounded softer, as they do in the evening.

“How did I not notice that he had managed to spin a whole story?..” Bezdomny thought in amazement. “Why, it’s already evening! Or maybe it wasn’t him telling it at all, and I simply fell asleep and dreamed the whole thing?”

But we must suppose that it was the professor telling it after all, or else we would have to admit that Berlioz had dreamed the very same thing, because Berlioz said, peering attentively into the foreigner’s face:
“Your story is extremely interesting, professor, although it does not coincide at all with the Gospel stories.”

“Come now,” the professor responded with a condescending smile, “you of all people ought to know that absolutely nothing of what is written in the Gospels ever actually happened, and if we start citing the Gospels as a historical source...” He smiled once more, and Berlioz stopped short, because this was word for word what he himself had been telling Bezdomny as they walked down the Bronnaya to Patriarch’s Ponds.
“That is so,” Berlioz replied, “but I am afraid nobody can confirm that what you have just told us actually happened either.”
“Oh no! There is one who can confirm it!” the professor responded with tremendous assurance, beginning to speak in broken Russian, and unexpectedly, mysteriously, beckoned the two friends closer.
They leaned toward him from both sides, and he spoke, but now without any accent at all, an accent which, the devil knows why, kept vanishing and reappearing:
