“The thing is...” here the professor glanced round fearfully and went on in a whisper, “that I was personally present at all of it. I was on the balcony with Pontius Pilate, and in the garden when he talked with Caiaphas, and on the platform, only secretly, incognito, so to speak, so I beg you—not a word to anyone, and the most absolute secrecy!.. Shh!”
A silence fell, and Berlioz went pale.
“You... how long have you been in Moscow?” he asked in a voice that shook.

“Why, I arrived in Moscow just this minute,” the professor answered in confusion, and only now did the friends think to look him properly in the eyes, and they made sure that his left eye, the green one, was completely mad, while the right one was empty, black and dead.
“So that explains everything!” Berlioz thought in dismay. “Either a madman of a German has come here, or he has only just gone off his head at Patriarch’s. Well, here’s a story!”

Yes, indeed, everything was explained: the most peculiar breakfast with the late philosopher Kant, and the idiotic talk about sunflower oil and Annushka, and the predictions about the head being cut off, and all the rest—the professor was mad.

Berlioz grasped at once what had to be done. Leaning back against the bench, he began winking at Bezdomny behind the professor’s back—don’t contradict him, that is—but the bewildered poet did not understand these signals.
“Yes, yes, yes,” Berlioz said excitedly, “after all, that’s all possible!.. Even very possible, Pontius Pilate, and the balcony, and so forth... And did you come alone, or with your wife?”
“Alone, alone, I am always alone,” the professor answered bitterly.
“And where are your things, professor?” Berlioz asked insinuatingly. “At the Metropol? Where are you staying?”
“I? Nowhere,” answered the half-witted German, his green eye wandering wildly and miserably over Patriarch’s Ponds.
“What? But... where are you going to live?”
“In your apartment,” the madman suddenly answered with a swagger, and winked.
“I... I’d be very glad,” Berlioz began to mumble, “but really, you would be uncomfortable at my place... And the Metropol has wonderful rooms, it’s a first-class hotel...”
“And there is no devil either?” the sick man suddenly inquired of Ivan Nikolayevich merrily.
“No devil either...”
“Don’t contradict him!” Berlioz whispered with his lips alone, dropping back behind the professor’s back and making faces.
“There isn’t any devil!” cried Ivan Nikolayevich, at a loss from all this rigmarole, saying exactly what he should not have. “What a punishment! Stop your raving!”
At this the madman burst out laughing so loudly that a sparrow fluttered out of the linden over their heads.

“Well, now, this is positively interesting,” the professor said, shaking with laughter. “What is it with you here—whatever one reaches for, there’s nothing there!” He stopped laughing suddenly and, as is quite understandable in a mental illness, went after the laughter to the other extreme: he grew irritated and shouted sternly: “So, then, there is simply none at all?”

“Calm down, calm down, calm down, professor,” Berlioz muttered, afraid of agitating the sick man. “You sit here for just a minute with Comrade Bezdomny, and I’ll just run to the corner and make a quick telephone call, and then we’ll see you wherever you want to go. After all, you don’t know the city...”

Berlioz’s plan must be acknowledged as the right one: he needed to run to the nearest public telephone and inform the foreigners’ bureau that, look here, a consultant from abroad was sitting at Patriarch’s Ponds in a clearly abnormal state. So measures had to be taken, or else some unpleasant nonsense would come of it.

“Telephone? Well, all right, go and telephone,” the sick man agreed sadly, and suddenly begged passionately: “But I implore you, as a parting favor, at least believe that the devil exists! I won’t ask anything more of you. Bear in mind that there is a seventh proof of it, and the most reliable one! And it will be presented to you shortly.”

“Fine, fine,” Berlioz said with false tenderness, and, winking at the upset poet, who did not at all relish the thought of guarding a mad German, he hurried toward the exit from Patriarch’s at the corner of the Bronnaya and Yermolayevsky Lane.
And the professor at once seemed to recover and brighten.
“Mikhail Alexandrovich!” he shouted after Berlioz.

Berlioz gave a start and turned round, but calmed himself with the thought that the professor had also learned his first name and patronymic from some newspaper or other. And the professor shouted, cupping his hands like a megaphone:
“Would you like me to have a telegram sent to your uncle in Kiev right away?”

And again Berlioz gave a jolt. How on earth does the madman know about the existence of an uncle in Kiev? That has surely not been mentioned in any newspaper. Aha, could Bezdomny be right after all? What if those documents are fakes? Ah, what a strange specimen... Telephone, telephone! Telephone at once! They’ll soon sort him out!
And, no longer listening to anything, Berlioz ran on.

Then, right at the exit onto the Bronnaya, there rose from a bench to meet the editor exactly the same citizen who earlier, in the sunlight, had taken shape out of the thick, greasy heat. Only now he was no longer made of air but ordinary, of flesh and blood, and in the gathering dusk Berlioz made out distinctly that his little mustache was like chicken feathers, his little eyes were small, ironic and half drunk, and his little checked trousers were hitched up so high that his dirty white socks showed.
Mikhail Alexandrovich actually backed away, but consoled himself with the reflection that this was a silly coincidence and that in any case there was no time to think about it now.

“Looking for the turnstile, citizen?” the checked type inquired in a cracked tenor. “This way, if you please! Straight on and you’ll come out where you need to be. Now, for the directions you might spare a little something toward a quarter-liter... to set myself right... for a former choirmaster!” Clowning, the specimen swept off his little jockey cap with a flourish.

Berlioz did not stop to listen to the cadging, posturing choirmaster but ran up to the turnstile and took hold of it. He had turned it and was about to step onto the rails when red and white light splashed into his face: in a glass box the sign lit up: “Beware of the Tram!”

And at once the tram came flying up, turning along the newly laid line from Yermolayevsky into the Bronnaya. Having turned and come out onto the straight, it suddenly lit up inside with electric light, howled and put on speed.

The cautious Berlioz, although he was standing in a safe place, decided to go back behind the barrier, shifted his hand on the turnstile and took a step back. And at once his hand slipped and lost its grip, his foot slid irresistibly, as if on ice, over the cobbles that sloped down to the rails, his other foot was flung up, and Berlioz was thrown onto the rails.

Trying to catch hold of something, Berlioz fell on his back, striking the back of his head lightly on the cobbles, and had time to see high above—but whether to the right or the left he could no longer make out—the gilded moon. He managed to turn onto his side, in the same instant pulling his legs up to his stomach with a frenzied movement, and, turning, he made out, rushing at him with irresistible force, the face of the woman driver, completely white with horror, and her scarlet armband. Berlioz did not cry out, but around him the whole street shrieked in desperate women’s voices. The driver jerked the electric brake, the car dug its nose into the ground, then instantly leaped up, and with a crash and a jingle the glass flew out of the windows. Here in Berlioz’s brain someone cried out in despair: “Can it be?..” Once more, and for the last time, the moon flashed, but already breaking into pieces, and then it went dark.
The tram covered Berlioz, and a round dark object was flung under the railings of the Patriarch’s avenue onto the cobbled slope. Rolling down this slope, it bounced along the cobbles of the Bronnaya.
It was Berlioz’s severed head.

chapters.title: 4. The Chase
paragraphs: The hysterical women’s screams died down, the police whistles finished drilling the air, two ambulances drove off—one taking the headless body and the severed head to the morgue, the other the beautiful tram driver, wounded by splinters of glass—the yardkeepers in white aprons swept up the broken glass and poured sand over the pools of blood, and Ivan Nikolayevich, who had collapsed onto a bench without reaching the turnstile, simply stayed there.
Several times he tried to get up, but his legs would not obey him: something like paralysis had befallen Bezdomny.

The poet had rushed toward the turnstile as soon as he heard the first scream, and had seen the head bouncing along the roadway. This drove him so out of his mind that, having collapsed onto the bench, he bit his own hand until it bled. He had forgotten about the mad German, of course, and was trying to understand only one thing: how could it be that a moment ago he had been talking to Berlioz, and a minute later—the head...
Agitated people ran past the poet along the avenue, exclaiming something, but Ivan Nikolayevich did not take in their words.
Unexpectedly, however, two women ran into each other right beside him, and one of them, sharp-nosed and bareheaded, shouted to the other right in the poet’s ear, like this:

“Annushka, our Annushka! From Sadovaya! It’s her doing! She got some sunflower oil at the grocer’s, and went and broke the bottle on the turnstile! Messed up her whole skirt... And how she swore, how she swore! And him, poor man, he must have slipped and gone sliding onto the rails...”
Out of everything the woman had shouted, one word fastened onto Ivan Nikolayevich’s disordered brain: “Annushka”...
“Annushka... Annushka?..” the poet began to mutter, looking around in alarm. “Wait, wait...”

To the word “Annushka” the words “sunflower oil” attached themselves, and then for some reason “Pontius Pilate.” The poet rejected Pilate and began to link up a chain, starting from the word “Annushka.” And this chain linked up very quickly and at once led to the mad professor.

Excuse me! But he did say the meeting would not take place because Annushka had spilled the oil. And, if you please, it will not take place! What’s more, he said straight out that Berlioz’s head would be cut off by a woman?! Yes, yes, yes! And the driver was a woman! What is all this? Eh?

There remained not a grain of doubt that the mysterious consultant had known in advance, and precisely, the whole picture of Berlioz’s terrible death. Here two thoughts pierced the poet’s brain. The first: “He is not mad at all! That’s all nonsense!” And the second: “Could he have arranged all this himself?!”
But, permit me to ask, how?!
“Oh, no! We’ll find that out!”
Making a great effort, Ivan Nikolayevich got up from the bench and rushed back to where he had been talking with the professor. And it turned out that the professor, fortunately, had not yet left.

The streetlamps were already lit on the Bronnaya, and over Patriarch’s a golden moon was shining, and in the moonlight, always deceptive, it seemed to Ivan Nikolayevich that the man was standing with a sword under his arm, not a cane.

The retired choirmaster, that sponger, was sitting in the very place where Ivan Nikolayevich himself had sat not long before. The choirmaster had now stuck on his nose a pince-nez he obviously did not need, one lens of which was missing altogether while the other was cracked. This made the checked citizen still more loathsome than he had been when he showed Berlioz the way onto the rails.
His heart turning cold, Ivan approached the professor and, looking into his face, made sure that there were not, and never had been, any signs of madness in it.
“Confess, who are you?” Ivan asked in a hollow voice.
The foreigner frowned, looked at him as if seeing the poet for the first time, and answered with hostility:
“No understand... Russian speak...”
“The gentleman doesn’t understand!” the choirmaster butted in from the bench, though nobody had asked him to explain the foreigner’s words.

“Stop pretending!” Ivan said menacingly, and felt a chill in the pit of his stomach. “A moment ago you were speaking Russian perfectly well. You’re no German and no professor! You’re a murderer and a spy! Your papers!” Ivan shouted furiously.
The mysterious professor squeamishly twisted his already twisted mouth and shrugged.

“Citizen!” the vile choirmaster butted in again. “What do you mean by upsetting a foreign tourist? You’ll be held most strictly to account for this!” And the suspicious professor put on a haughty face, turned, and walked away from Ivan.
Ivan felt he was losing his head. Gasping for breath, he turned to the choirmaster:
“Hey, citizen, help me detain the criminal! It’s your duty!”
The choirmaster came extraordinarily to life, jumped up and bawled:

“Which criminal? Where is he? A foreign criminal?” The choirmaster’s little eyes lit up with glee. “This one? If he’s a criminal, the first thing to do is shout ‘Help! Police!’ Or else he’ll get away. Come on, let’s do it together! All at once!” And here the choirmaster opened his maw wide.
The bewildered Ivan obeyed the trickster choirmaster and shouted “Help! Police!”—but the choirmaster had fooled him and shouted nothing.
Ivan’s lonely, hoarse cry did not bring good results. A couple of girls shied away from him, and he heard the word “Drunk!”
“Ah, so you’re in league with him?” Ivan shouted, flying into a rage. “What are you doing, making fun of me? Let me pass!”
Ivan darted to the right, and the choirmaster—to the right too! Ivan to the left, and the scoundrel went the same way.
“Are you getting under my feet on purpose?” Ivan shouted, turning savage. “I’ll hand you over to the police yourself!”
Ivan made an attempt to grab the villain by the sleeve, but missed and caught absolutely nothing. The choirmaster seemed to have sunk into the ground.

Ivan gasped, looked into the distance and saw the hated stranger. He was already at the exit into Patriarch’s Lane, and not alone, either. The more than dubious choirmaster had managed to join him. But that was not all: the third in this company turned out to be a cat that had appeared from nobody knew where, huge as a hog, black as soot or a rook, and with a dashing cavalryman’s mustache. The trio set off into Patriarch’s Lane, and the cat moved off on its hind legs.
Ivan rushed after the villains and at once made sure that it would be very hard to catch up with them.

The trio shot through the lane in a flash and came out on Spiridonovka. However much Ivan quickened his pace, the distance between him and the pursued did not shrink in the least. And before the poet could collect himself, he found himself, after quiet Spiridonovka, at the Nikitsky Gate, where his position got worse. Here there were already crowds, Ivan bumped into some of the passers-by and was sworn at. The villainous gang, what was more, decided to use a favorite bandit trick here: to scatter in different directions.

With great dexterity the choirmaster wormed his way, on the move, into a bus flying toward Arbat Square, and slipped away. Having lost one of the pursued, Ivan concentrated his attention on the cat, and saw this strange cat go up to the step of the motor car of an “A” tram standing at the stop, brazenly elbow aside a woman, who squealed, grab hold of the handrail and even try to shove a ten-kopeck piece at the conductress through the window, which was open because of the stuffiness.

The cat’s behavior so astounded Ivan that he froze motionless by a grocer’s shop on the corner, and here he was astounded a second time, but much more strongly, by the behavior of the conductress. As soon as she saw the cat climbing into the tram, she shouted, with a fury that actually made her shake:
“No cats! No cats allowed! Scat! Get off, or I’ll call the police!”
Neither the conductress nor the passengers were struck by the very heart of the matter: not that a cat was climbing into a tram, which would be only half the trouble, but that it was going to pay!

The cat turned out to be not only a solvent animal but a disciplined one. At the conductress’s very first shout it halted its advance, got down off the step and sat at the stop, rubbing its whiskers with the ten-kopeck piece. But as soon as the conductress yanked the cord and the tram moved off, the cat did what anyone does who is thrown off a tram but still needs to get somewhere. Letting all three cars go past, the cat jumped onto the rear coupling bow of the last one, gripped with its paw some hose that came out of the wall, and rolled away, thereby saving ten kopecks.

Busy with the vile cat, Ivan nearly lost the most important of the three, the professor. But, fortunately, the professor had not managed to slip away. Ivan saw the gray beret in the thick of the crowd at the beginning of Bolshaya Nikitskaya, or Herzen Street. In the twinkling of an eye Ivan was there himself. But he had no luck. The poet quickened his pace, and broke into a trot, shoving passers-by, and did not get one centimeter closer to the professor.

Upset as Ivan was, he was still struck by the supernatural speed at which the chase was proceeding. Not twenty seconds had passed after the Nikitsky Gate before Ivan Nikolayevich was already dazzled by the lights of Arbat Square. A few seconds more, and here was some dark lane with lopsided sidewalks, where Ivan Nikolayevich crashed down and hurt his knee. Again a brightly lit thoroughfare, Kropotkin Street, then a lane, then Ostozhenka, and another lane, dreary, nasty and meagerly lit. And it was here that Ivan Nikolayevich finally lost the one he needed so badly. The professor had vanished.
Ivan Nikolayevich was dismayed, but not for long, because he suddenly realized that the professor was bound to be in house No. 13, and without fail in apartment 47.

Bursting into the entrance, Ivan Nikolayevich flew up to the second floor, found the apartment at once and rang impatiently. He did not have to wait long: the door was opened to Ivan by some little girl of about five, who, without asking the visitor anything, immediately went off somewhere.

In the huge, extremely neglected entrance hall, feebly lit by a tiny carbon-filament bulb under a high ceiling black with grime, a bicycle without tires hung on the wall, a huge iron-bound chest stood there, and on the shelf above the coat rack lay a winter hat with its long earflaps hanging down. Behind one of the doors a booming male voice on the radio was angrily shouting something in verse.

Ivan Nikolayevich was not in the least taken aback by the unfamiliar surroundings and headed straight into the corridor, reasoning thus: “He’s hiding in the bathroom, of course.” The corridor was dark. Having bumped into the walls a few times, Ivan saw a feeble strip of light at the bottom of a door, groped for the handle and gave it a light jerk. The hook flew off, and Ivan found himself in precisely the bathroom, and thought that he was in luck.

But he was not in as much luck as he would have needed! A wave of damp warmth breathed on Ivan, and by the light of the coals smoldering in the boiler he made out large washtubs hanging on the wall and a bathtub covered all over in frightful black patches where the enamel had chipped off. Well, then, in this bathtub stood a naked citizeness, all in soap and with a bath sponge in her hands. She squinted nearsightedly at Ivan as he burst in and, evidently mistaking him for someone else in the infernal light, said quietly and merrily:
“Kiryushka! Stop fooling around! Have you gone out of your mind?.. Fyodor Ivanovich will be back any minute. Get out of here this instant!” And she waved the sponge at Ivan.

The misunderstanding was obvious, and the one to blame for it was, of course, Ivan Nikolayevich. But he did not wish to admit it and, exclaiming reproachfully, “Ah, you wanton woman!..”, at once, for some reason, found himself in the kitchen. There was no one in it, and on the stove in the semidarkness stood about ten extinguished Primus stoves in silence. A single moonbeam, seeping through a dusty window that had not been wiped for years, meagerly lit the corner where, in dust and cobwebs, a forgotten icon hung, from behind whose icon case stuck out the ends of two wedding candles. Under the large icon a small one, made of paper, was pinned.

No one knows what thought took hold of Ivan here, but before running out by the back stairs he appropriated one of these candles, and also the little paper icon. With these objects he left the unknown apartment, muttering something, embarrassed at the thought of what he had just been through in the bathroom, and involuntarily trying to guess who this insolent Kiryushka might be and whether the disgusting hat with the earflaps belonged to him.
In the deserted, cheerless lane the poet looked round, searching for the fugitive, but he was nowhere to be seen. Then Ivan said firmly to himself:
“Of course, he’s at the Moscow River! Forward!”

Perhaps one ought to have asked Ivan Nikolayevich why he supposed the professor was at the Moscow River precisely and not somewhere else. But the trouble was that there was nobody to ask him. The loathsome lane was completely empty.
In the shortest possible time, Ivan Nikolayevich could be seen on the granite steps of the Moscow River amphitheater.

Having taken off his clothes, Ivan entrusted them to some pleasant bearded man who was smoking a hand-rolled cigarette beside a torn white tolstovka smock and a pair of unlaced, worn-down boots. Waving his arms to cool off, Ivan dived into the water like a swallow. It took his breath away, so cold was the water, and the thought even flashed through his mind that he might not manage to come back up to the surface. But he did manage to come up, and, puffing and snorting, his eyes round with horror, Ivan Nikolayevich began swimming in the black, oil-smelling water among the broken zigzags of the lights along the embankment.

When the wet Ivan came dancing up the steps to the place where his clothes had been left in the bearded man’s care, it emerged that not only the former had been stolen, but the latter as well—that is, the bearded man himself. Exactly where the heap of clothes had been there remained a pair of striped long johns, the torn tolstovka, the candle, the little icon and a box of matches. Shaking his fist in impotent rage at someone in the distance, Ivan clad himself in what had been left.

Here two considerations began to trouble him: first, that his Massolit identity card, which he never parted with, had disappeared; and second, whether he would manage to get across Moscow unhindered in this state? Long johns, after all... True, whose business was it, but still, there might be some fault-finding or he might be stopped.

Ivan tore the buttons off the long johns where they fastened at the ankle, reckoning that in this form they might perhaps pass for summer trousers, gathered up the icon, the candle and the matches, and set off, saying to himself:
“To Griboyedov’s! Beyond all doubt, he’s there.”

The city was already living its evening life. Trucks flew by in the dust, their chains clanking, and on their platforms, on sacks, some men lay sprawled with their bellies to the sky. All the windows were open. In each of these windows a light burned under an orange lampshade, and from all the windows, from all the doors, from all the gateways, from roofs and attics, from basements and courtyards, burst the hoarse roar of the polonaise from the opera Eugene Onegin.

Ivan Nikolayevich’s fears were fully justified: passers-by paid attention to him, and laughed, and turned to look. As a result he made the decision to leave the big streets and make his way through the side lanes, where people were not so pushy, where there was less chance they would pester a barefoot man, tormenting him with questions about the long johns, which stubbornly refused to look like trousers.

That is what Ivan did, plunging into the mysterious network of the Arbat lanes and making his way along the walls, glancing about fearfully, looking back every minute, hiding in doorways from time to time and avoiding crossroads with traffic lights and the grand doors of embassy mansions.
And all along his difficult way he was for some reason inexpressibly tormented by the ubiquitous orchestra, to whose accompaniment a heavy bass sang of his love for Tatiana.

chapters.title: 5. It Happened at Griboyedov’s
paragraphs: The old two-story cream-colored house stood on the Boulevard Ring, at the back of a sickly garden separated from the sidewalk of the Ring by a wrought-iron railing. The small forecourt in front of the house was asphalted, and in wintertime a snowdrift with a shovel stuck in it towered there, while in summertime it turned into the most magnificent section of the summer restaurant, under a canvas awning.

The house was called “Griboyedov House” on the grounds that it had supposedly once belonged to an aunt of the writer Alexander Sergeyevich Griboyedov. Well, whether it belonged to her or not, we do not know for sure. One even recalls that, it seems, Griboyedov never had any such house-owning aunt... Still, that is what the house was called. What is more, a certain Moscow liar used to tell how, on the second floor, in the round hall with columns, the famous writer had supposedly read passages from Woe from Wit to this very aunt as she reclined on a sofa. But then, the devil knows, maybe he did read them; that is not important!
What is important is that at present this house belonged to that same Massolit which had been headed by the unfortunate Mikhail Alexandrovich Berlioz until his appearance at Patriarch’s Ponds.

Thanks to the members of Massolit, nobody called the house “Griboyedov House”; everybody simply said “Griboyedov’s”: “I spent two hours elbowing my way around at Griboyedov’s yesterday.” “And how did it go?” “I wangled a month in Yalta.” “Good for you!” Or: “Go and see Berlioz, he’s receiving at Griboyedov’s today from four to five...” and so on.

Massolit had installed itself at Griboyedov’s in a way that could not have been better or cozier. Anyone entering Griboyedov’s was first of all made acquainted, willy-nilly, with the notices of various sports clubs and with group and individual photographs of the members of Massolit, with which (photographs) the walls of the staircase leading to the second floor were hung.
On the door of the very first room on this upper floor a large sign could be seen, “Fishing and Dacha Section,” and next to it was a picture of a carp caught on a hook.
On the door of room No. 2 something not entirely comprehensible was written: “One-Day Creative Trip Vouchers. Apply to M. V. Podlozhnaya.”

The next door bore a brief but by now altogether incomprehensible sign: “Perelygino.” After that the chance visitor to Griboyedov’s would find his eyes darting about from the signs that dotted the aunt’s walnut doors: “Waiting List for Paper, See Poklevkina,” “Cash Desk. Personal Accounts of Sketch Writers”...
Cutting through an extremely long queue that began downstairs at the doorman’s lodge, one could see a sign on a door that people were storming every second: “Housing Question.”

Past the housing question there opened up a luxurious poster showing a cliff, along whose crest rode a horseman in a felt cloak with a rifle on his shoulder. Lower down, palm trees and a balcony; on the balcony, a seated young man with a forelock, gazing somewhere on high with very, very lively eyes and holding a fountain pen in his hand. The caption: “Full-Length Creative Leaves from Two Weeks (Short Story or Novella) to One Year (Novel, Trilogy). Yalta, Suuk-Su, Borovoye, Tsikhidziri, Makhindzhauri, Leningrad (Winter Palace).” There was a queue at this door too, but not an excessive one, some hundred and fifty people.

Then came, following the whimsical bends, rises and descents of the Griboyedov house, “Massolit Board,” “Cash Desks Nos. 2, 3, 4 and 5,” “Editorial Board,” “Chairman of Massolit,” “Billiard Room,” various auxiliary offices and, finally, that same hall with the colonnade where the aunt had relished the comedy of her genius nephew.

Every visitor, provided of course that he was not a complete dimwit, on getting into Griboyedov’s grasped at once how good life was for the lucky members of Massolit, and black envy immediately began to torment him. And immediately he would address bitter reproaches to heaven for not having endowed him at birth with literary talent, without which, naturally, there was no dreaming of acquiring a Massolit membership card—brown, smelling of expensive leather, with a wide gold border—a card known to all Moscow.

Who will say a word in defense of envy? It is a feeling of a rotten sort, but still, one must put oneself in the visitor’s position. For what he had seen on the upper floor was not everything, and far from everything. The entire ground floor of the aunt’s house was taken up by a restaurant, and what a restaurant! In all fairness it was considered the very best in Moscow. And not only because it was housed in two large halls with vaulted ceilings painted with lilac horses with Assyrian manes, not only because on every little table stood a lamp draped with a shawl, not only because it could not be entered by the first person who came in off the street, but also because in the quality of its provisions Griboyedov’s beat any restaurant in Moscow hollow, and these provisions were served at the most reasonable, by no means burdensome prices.
Hence there is nothing surprising in such a conversation as, for instance, the one the author of these most truthful lines once overheard by the wrought-iron railing of Griboyedov’s:
“Where are you having supper tonight, Amvrosy?”
“What a question, here of course, my dear Foka! Archibald Archibaldovich whispered to me today that there will be individual portions of zander au naturel. A virtuoso little item!”
“You know how to live, Amvrosy!” sighed Foka, skinny, neglected, with a carbuncle on his neck, to the red-lipped giant, golden-haired and plump-cheeked Amvrosy the poet.

“I have no special knack at all,” Amvrosy objected, “just an ordinary desire to live like a human being. You mean to say, Foka, that one can come across zander at the Coliseum too. But at the Coliseum a portion of zander costs thirteen roubles fifteen kopecks, and here—five fifty! Besides, at the Coliseum the zander is three days old, and besides that, you have no guarantee that you won’t get a bunch of grapes in the mug at the Coliseum from the first young man who bursts in off Teatralny Passage. No, I am categorically against the Coliseum!” the gastronome Amvrosy thundered for the whole boulevard to hear. “Don’t try to persuade me, Foka!”
“I’m not trying to persuade you, Amvrosy,” Foka squeaked. “One can have supper at home.”

“Your humble servant,” trumpeted Amvrosy. “I can just picture your wife trying to knock together individual portions of zander au naturel in a little saucepan in the communal kitchen of your building! Hee-hee-hee!.. Au revoir, Foka!” And, humming, Amvrosy headed for the veranda under the awning.

Oh-ho-ho... Yes, it was, it was!.. Old Muscovites remember the famous Griboyedov’s! What is boiled zander in portions! Cheap stuff, my dear Amvrosy! But sterlet, sterlet in a silvery saucepan, sterlet in pieces layered with crayfish tails and fresh caviar? And eggs cocotte with mushroom purée in little cups? And didn’t you like the little fillets of thrush? With truffles? Quails à la génoise? Nine and a half roubles! And the jazz, and the courteous service! And in July, when the whole family is at the dacha and urgent literary business keeps you in town—on the veranda, in the shade of the climbing vine, in a golden spot on the cleanest of tablecloths, a little plate of soupe printanière? Remember, Amvrosy? But why ask! I can see by your lips that you remember. What are your whitefish, your zander! What about great snipe, jack snipe, common snipe, woodcock in season, quails, sandpipers? Narzan fizzing in the throat?! But enough, you are getting distracted, reader! Follow me!..

At half past ten on the evening when Berlioz perished at Patriarch’s, only one room was lit upstairs at Griboyedov’s, and in it twelve writers were languishing, who had gathered for the meeting and were waiting for Mikhail Alexandrovich.

Those sitting on chairs, and on tables, and even on the two windowsills in the Massolit board room were suffering seriously from the stuffiness. Not a single fresh current of air came in through the open windows. Moscow was giving off the heat stored up during the day in its asphalt, and it was clear that the night would bring no relief. There was a smell of onions from the basement of the aunt’s house, where the restaurant kitchen was working, and everybody was thirsty, everybody was nervous and cross.

The fiction writer Beskudnikov—a quiet, decently dressed man with attentive and at the same time elusive eyes—took out his watch. The hand was creeping toward eleven. Beskudnikov tapped the dial with his finger and showed it to his neighbor, the poet Dvubratsky, who was sitting on the table and, out of boredom, swinging his feet, shod in yellow shoes with rubber soles.
“Well, really,” grumbled Dvubratsky.

“The lad must have got stuck on the Klyazma,” responded in a thick voice Nastasya Lukinishna Nepremenova, a Moscow merchant’s orphan who had become a writer and composed naval battle stories under the pen name “Navigator Georges.”

“Excuse me!” the author of popular sketches, Zagrivov, spoke up boldly. “I’d enjoy drinking a little tea on a balcony myself right now, instead of stewing in here. The meeting was set for ten, wasn’t it?”

“And it’s lovely on the Klyazma now,” Navigator Georges egged on those present, knowing that the writers’ dacha settlement of Perelygino on the Klyazma was everybody’s sore spot. “The nightingales must be singing by now. I always somehow work better out of town, especially in spring.”

“This is the third year I’ve been paying in my money to send my wife, who has Basedow’s disease, to this paradise, but there’s nothing to be seen on the horizon,” the short-story writer Ieronim Poprikhin said venomously and bitterly.
“That’s a matter of luck,” the critic Ababkov droned from the windowsill.
Joy lit up in Navigator Georges’s little eyes, and she said, softening her contralto:
“We mustn’t envy, comrades. There are only twenty-two dachas, and only seven more are being built, and there are three thousand of us in Massolit.”
“Three thousand one hundred and eleven,” someone put in from a corner.
“So you see,” the Navigator went on, “what can be done? Naturally, the dachas went to the most talented among us...”
“The generals!” Glukharev the screenwriter cut straight into the squabble.
Beskudnikov, with an artificial yawn, went out of the room.
“Five rooms all to himself in Perelygino,” Glukharev said after him.
“Lavrovich has six all to himself,” cried Deniskin, “and the dining room’s paneled in oak!”
“Eh, that’s not the point right now,” droned Ababkov, “the point is that it’s half past eleven.”

A hubbub began; something like a mutiny was brewing. They started telephoning the hated Perelygino, got the wrong dacha, Lavrovich’s, learned that Lavrovich had gone to the river, and were thoroughly upset by it. At random they called the Commission for Belles-Lettres on extension No. 930 and, of course, found no one there.
“He might have telephoned!” shouted Deniskin, Glukharev and Kvant.

Ah, they shouted in vain: Mikhail Alexandrovich could not telephone anywhere. Far, far from Griboyedov’s, in an enormous hall lit by thousand-candlepower lamps, on three zinc tables lay what until recently had been Mikhail Alexandrovich.

On the first, the naked body, caked with dried blood, with a broken arm and a crushed rib cage; on the second, the head, its front teeth knocked out, its clouded eyes open and unafraid of the harshest light; and on the third, a heap of stiffened rags.

Beside the headless body stood a professor of forensic medicine, a pathologist and his prosector, representatives of the investigation, and Mikhail Alexandrovich Berlioz’s deputy in Massolit, the writer Zheldybin, who had been summoned by telephone from the bedside of his sick wife.

A car had called for Zheldybin and first of all, together with the investigators, taken him (this was around midnight) to the dead man’s apartment, where his papers were sealed, and only then did they all go to the morgue.

And now those standing by the remains of the deceased were conferring on what would be best: to sew the severed head back onto the neck, or to lay the body out in the hall at Griboyedov’s, simply covering the dead man up to the chin with a black cloth?

Yes, Mikhail Alexandrovich could not telephone anywhere, and Deniskin, Glukharev and Kvant, along with Beskudnikov, were quite pointlessly indignant and shouting. At exactly midnight all twelve writers left the upper floor and went down to the restaurant. Here again they inwardly cursed Mikhail Alexandrovich: all the tables on the veranda, naturally, had already been taken, and they had to stay and have supper in those beautiful but stuffy halls.

And at exactly midnight in the first of them something crashed, rang out, showered down, leaped. And at once a thin male voice cried out desperately to the music: “Hallelujah!!” It was the famous Griboyedov jazz band striking up. Faces covered with perspiration seemed to light up, the horses painted on the ceiling seemed to come to life, the lamps seemed to give more light, and suddenly, as if breaking loose from a chain, both halls broke into dance, and after them the veranda broke into dance too.

Glukharev started dancing with the poetess Tamara Polumesyats, Kvant started dancing, Zhukopov the novelist started dancing with some film actress in a yellow dress. Dancing were: Dragunsky, Cherdakchi, little Deniskin with the gigantic Navigator Georges, the beautiful architect Semeikina-Gall was dancing, gripped tight by a stranger in white burlap trousers. Dancing were the regulars and invited guests, Muscovites and out-of-towners, the writer Johann from Kronstadt, a certain Vitya Kuftik from Rostov, a director, it seems, with a lilac lichen covering his whole cheek; dancing were the most prominent representatives of the poetry subsection of Massolit, that is, Pavianov, Bogokhulsky, Sladky, Shpichkin and Adelfina Buzdyak; dancing were young men of unknown profession, with crew cuts and cotton-padded shoulders; dancing was a very elderly man with a beard in which a bit of green onion had got stuck, and dancing with him was a sickly girl, being eaten up by anemia, in a crumpled little orange silk dress.

Streaming with sweat, the waiters carried sweating mugs of beer above their heads, shouting hoarsely and with hatred: “Excuse me, citizen!” Somewhere through a megaphone a voice was commanding: “Kars shashlik, one! Zubrik, two! Tripe hospodar-style!!” The thin voice was no longer singing but howling: “Hallelujah!” The crash of the golden cymbals in the jazz band was sometimes drowned by the crash of dishes, which the dishwashers were sending down an inclined chute into the kitchen. In a word, hell.

And at midnight there was an apparition in hell. Onto the veranda came a black-eyed handsome man with a dagger-shaped beard, in tails, and cast a regal gaze over his domain. It was said, the mystics said, that there was a time when the handsome man did not wear tails but was girded with a broad leather belt with pistol butts sticking out of it, and his raven-black hair was tied up in scarlet silk, and under his command a brig sailed the Caribbean Sea under a black coffin flag with a death’s-head.

But no, no! The mystics, those seducers, lie; there are no Caribbean Seas in the world, and no desperate freebooters sail them, and no corvette gives chase, no cannon smoke drifts over the waves. There is nothing, and there never was anything! There is a sickly linden over there, there is a wrought-iron railing, and beyond it the boulevard... And the ice is melting in the little bowl, and at the next table someone’s bloodshot, bull-like eyes can be seen, and it is frightening, frightening... O gods, my gods, poison, give me poison!..

And suddenly at a table a word fluttered up: “Berlioz!!” Suddenly the jazz fell apart and went silent, as though someone had banged it with a fist. “What, what, what, what?!!” “Berlioz!!!” And they started jumping up, started crying out...

Yes, a wave of grief surged up at the terrible news about Mikhail Alexandrovich. Someone was bustling about, shouting that it was necessary right now, right here, on the spot, to draw up some sort of collective telegram and send it off at once.

But what telegram, we may ask, and where to? And why send it? Indeed, where to? And what use is any telegram whatever to him whose flattened skull is now being squeezed in the prosector’s rubber hands, whose neck is now being pierced by the professor’s curved needles? He has perished, and he needs no telegram. It is all over; let us not overload the telegraph any further.
Yes, he has perished, perished... But we, after all, are alive!

Yes, a wave of grief surged up, but it held, held, and began to subside, and here and there someone had already gone back to his table and—at first on the sly, then openly—drunk a little vodka and had a bite. Really, should the chicken cutlets de volaille go to waste? How will we help Mikhail Alexandrovich? By staying hungry? Why, we are alive, after all!

Naturally, the piano was locked, the jazz band dispersed, a few journalists left for their offices to write obituaries. It became known that Zheldybin had arrived from the morgue. He installed himself in the late man’s office upstairs, and at once a rumor rolled through that it was he who would replace Berlioz. Zheldybin summoned all twelve board members from the restaurant, and at the meeting urgently begun in Berlioz’s office they proceeded to discuss the pressing questions of decorating the columned hall of Griboyedov’s, of transferring the body from the morgue to that hall, of opening it to the public, and other matters connected with the sad event.

And the restaurant went on living its usual nighttime life, and would have gone on living it until closing, that is, until four in the morning, had something not happened that was by now quite out of the ordinary and that struck the restaurant’s guests far more than the news of Berlioz’s death.
The first to grow agitated were the cabbies on duty at the gates of the Griboyedov house. One of them could be heard, half rising on his box, shouting:
“Whoa! Just look at that!”

Following this, from out of nowhere, a little light flared up by the wrought-iron railing and began to approach the veranda. Those sitting at the tables began to rise and peer, and saw that a white ghost was proceeding toward the restaurant together with the little light. When it came right up to the trellis, everyone sat as if petrified at their tables, with bits of sterlet on their forks and their eyes popping. The doorman, who had come out of the restaurant’s cloakroom door into the courtyard at that moment for a smoke, stamped out his cigarette and started toward the ghost with the clear aim of barring its way into the restaurant, but for some reason did not do so and stopped, smiling foolishly.

And the ghost, passing through the opening in the trellis, stepped unhindered onto the veranda. Here everyone saw that this was no ghost at all, but Ivan Nikolayevich Bezdomny, the very well-known poet.

He was barefoot, in a torn, whitish tolstovka, to which, on the chest, a paper icon with the rubbed-off image of an unknown saint was fastened with a safety pin, and in striped white long johns. In his hand Ivan Nikolayevich carried a lit wedding candle. Ivan Nikolayevich’s right cheek was freshly scratched. It is hard even to measure the depth of the silence that reigned on the veranda. One could see beer flowing onto the floor from a mug tilted to one side in the hand of one of the waiters.
The poet raised the candle above his head and said loudly:
“Hail, friends!” after which he looked under the nearest table and exclaimed miserably: “No, he’s not here!”
Two voices were heard. A bass said pitilessly:
“That’s it, then. Delirium tremens.”
And a second, a woman’s, frightened, spoke these words:
“How could the police let him go through the streets like that?”
Ivan Nikolayevich heard this and responded:

“They tried to stop me twice, in Skatertny Lane and here on the Bronnaya, but I swung over a fence and, as you see, tore my cheek!” Here Ivan Nikolayevich raised the candle and cried out: “Brethren in literature!” (His hoarse voice grew stronger and more fervent.) “Listen to me, all of you! He has appeared! Catch him at once, or he’ll do untold harm!”
“What? What? What did he say? Who has appeared?” voices came from all sides.
“The consultant!” Ivan answered. “And this consultant has just killed Misha Berlioz at Patriarch’s.”
Here people came pouring out of the inner hall onto the veranda, and a crowd closed in around Ivan’s flame.
“Excuse me, excuse me, be more precise,” a quiet and polite voice said right by Ivan Nikolayevich’s ear. “Tell us, what do you mean, killed? Who killed him?”
“A foreign consultant, a professor and a spy!” Ivan responded, looking around.
“And what is his name?” someone asked quietly in his ear.

“That’s just it, the name!” Ivan cried in anguish. “If only I knew the name! I didn’t make out the name on the visiting card... All I remember is the first letter, ‘W,’ the name begins with ‘W’! What name could that be, beginning with ‘W’?” Ivan asked himself, clutching his forehead, and suddenly began to mutter: “W, w, w... Wa... Wo... Wagner? Wagner? Weiner? Wegner? Winter?” The hair on Ivan’s head began to crawl from the strain.
“Wolf?” some woman cried out pitifully.
Ivan got angry.

“You fool!” he shouted, searching for the woman with his eyes. “What has Wolf got to do with it? Wolf isn’t to blame for anything! Wo, wo... No! I won’t remember it this way! Now look here, citizens: telephone the police at once, have them send out five motorcycles with machine guns to catch the professor. And don’t forget to tell them there are two more with him: some long checked fellow... cracked pince-nez... and a black cat, a fat one. And meanwhile I’ll search Griboyedov’s... I sense that he’s here!”

Ivan grew restless, shoved aside those around him, began waving the candle, pouring wax all over himself, and looking under the tables. Here the word was heard: “A doctor!” and someone’s kindly, fleshy face, shaven and well fed, in horn-rimmed glasses, appeared in front of Ivan.

“Comrade Bezdomny,” this face began in a jubilee-speech voice, “calm down! You are upset by the death of our beloved Mikhail Alexandrovich... no, simply Misha Berlioz. We all understand that perfectly. You need rest. Our comrades will now see you to bed, and you will forget...”
“Do you,” Ivan interrupted, baring his teeth, “understand that the professor has to be caught? And you come pestering me with your nonsense! Cretin!”
“Comrade Bezdomny, for pity’s sake,” the face replied, turning red, backing away and already regretting it had got mixed up in this business.
“No, you of all people are the one I’ll show no pity,” Ivan Nikolayevich said with quiet hatred.
A spasm distorted his face; he quickly shifted the candle from his right hand to his left, swung wide and struck the sympathetic face on the ear.

Here it dawned on them to throw themselves on Ivan—and they did. The candle went out, and the glasses that had jumped off the face were instantly trampled. Ivan let out a terrible war cry, audible, to the general scandal, even on the boulevard, and began to defend himself. Dishes rang as they fell from the tables, women screamed.
While the waiters were tying up the poet with towels, a conversation was going on in the cloakroom between the commander of the brig and the doorman.
“Did you see he was in his underpants?” the pirate asked coldly.
“But, Archibald Archibaldovich,” the doorman answered, cowering, “how can I refuse them entry, if the gentleman is a member of Massolit?”
“Did you see he was in his underpants?” the pirate repeated.
“For pity’s sake, Archibald Archibaldovich,” the doorman said, turning crimson, “what can I do? I understand myself, there are ladies sitting on the veranda...”

“The ladies have nothing to do with it, it’s all the same to the ladies,” the pirate answered, literally burning the doorman up with his eyes, “but it is not all the same to the police! A man in his underwear may proceed through the streets of Moscow in only one case, if he is going under police escort, and to only one place—the police station! And you, if you are a doorman, ought to know that on seeing such a man you must, without delaying a second, start blowing your whistle. Do you hear? Do you hear what is going on on the veranda?”
Here the frantic doorman heard a sort of whooping coming from the veranda, the smashing of dishes and women’s screams.
“Well, what am I to do with you for this?” the freebooter asked.

The skin on the doorman’s face took on a typhoid tinge, and his eyes went dead. It seemed to him that the black hair, now combed into a parting, was covered with flaming silk. The shirtfront and tails vanished, and the butt of a pistol appeared behind a leather belt. The doorman pictured himself hanged from the fore-topsail yard. With his own eyes he saw his own tongue sticking out and his lifeless head drooping onto his shoulder, and even heard the splash of a wave against the side. The doorman’s knees gave way. But here the freebooter took pity on him and dimmed his piercing gaze.

“Watch out, Nikolai! This is the last time. We wouldn’t take doormen like you in this restaurant for free. Go and get yourself a job as a church watchman.” Having said this, the commander commanded precisely, clearly, quickly: “Panteley from the bar. A policeman. A report. A car. To the psychiatric hospital.” And he added: “Whistle!”

A quarter of an hour later, an extremely astonished public, not only in the restaurant but on the boulevard itself and in the windows of the houses overlooking the restaurant garden, saw Panteley, the doorman, a policeman, a waiter and the poet Ryukhin carry out of the gates of Griboyedov’s a young man swaddled like a doll, who, dissolving in tears, kept spitting, trying to hit Ryukhin in particular, and shouting for the whole boulevard to hear:
“Swine!.. Swine!..”
The driver of a truck, with a vicious face, was starting the engine. Next to him a cabby was getting his horse worked up, slapping it on the croup with lilac reins and shouting:
“Here, take a racehorse! I’ve driven ’em to the psychiatric before!”

All around, the crowd buzzed, discussing the unprecedented incident. In a word, there was a nasty, vile, juicy, swinish scandal, which ended only when the truck carried away from the gates of Griboyedov’s the unfortunate Ivan Nikolayevich, the policeman, Panteley and Ryukhin.

chapters.title: 6. Schizophrenia, as Was Foretold
paragraphs: It was half past one in the morning when a man with a pointed beard, clad in a white coat, came out into the reception room of the famous psychiatric clinic recently built outside Moscow on the bank of the river. Three orderlies did not take their eyes off Ivan Nikolayevich, who was sitting on a couch. The extremely agitated poet Ryukhin was there too. The towels with which Ivan Nikolayevich had been tied up lay in a heap on that same couch. Ivan Nikolayevich’s hands and feet were free.
Seeing the man come in, Ryukhin turned pale, coughed and said timidly:
“Hello, doctor.”

The doctor bowed to Ryukhin, but as he bowed he looked not at him but at Ivan Nikolayevich. Ivan was sitting perfectly still, with an angry face and knitted brows, and did not even stir when the doctor came in.

“Here, doctor,” Ryukhin began, for some reason in a mysterious whisper, glancing fearfully at Ivan Nikolayevich, “the well-known poet Ivan Bezdomny... well, you see... we’re afraid it may be delirium tremens...”
“Was he drinking heavily?” the doctor asked through his teeth.
“No, he drank a bit, but not so as to...”
“Was he catching cockroaches, rats, little devils or scurrying dogs?”
“No,” Ryukhin answered with a start, “I saw him yesterday and this morning. He was perfectly healthy...”
“And why is he in long johns? Was he taken from his bed?”
“He came to the restaurant like that, doctor...”
“Aha, aha,” the doctor said, very satisfied, “and why the scratches? Was he fighting with someone?”
“He fell off a fence, and then in the restaurant he hit somebody... and somebody else as well...”
“So, so, so,” said the doctor, and, turning to Ivan, added: “Hello!”
“Hi there, wrecker!” Ivan answered loudly and spitefully.

Ryukhin was so embarrassed that he did not dare raise his eyes to the courteous doctor. But the doctor was not offended in the least; with a practiced, deft gesture he took off his glasses, lifted the skirt of his coat, put them away in the back pocket of his trousers, and then asked Ivan:
“How old are you?”
“Go to the devil, all of you, really!” Ivan shouted rudely, and turned away.
“But why are you angry? Did I say anything unpleasant to you?”
“I’m twenty-three,” Ivan began excitedly, “and I’m going to lodge a complaint against all of you. And against you in particular, you louse!” This he addressed to Ryukhin separately.
“And what is it you want to complain about?”
“About the fact that I, a healthy man, was seized and dragged by force into a madhouse!” Ivan answered in a rage.

Here Ryukhin took a close look at Ivan and went cold: there was absolutely no madness in his eyes. From being clouded, as they had been at Griboyedov’s, they had turned clear again, as they used to be.
“Good heavens!” Ryukhin thought in fright. “Is he really normal? What nonsense! Why on earth did we drag him here, then? Normal, normal, only his mug’s scratched...”
“You are,” the doctor began calmly, sitting down on a white stool with a shiny leg, “not in a madhouse but in a clinic, where nobody is going to keep you if there is no need for it.”
Ivan Nikolayevich gave him a sidelong, distrustful look, but still grumbled:
“Thank the Lord! At last there’s one normal man among the idiots, and the first of them is that dolt and no-talent Sashka!”
“Who is this no-talent Sashka?” the doctor inquired.
“Him there, Ryukhin!” Ivan answered, and jabbed a dirty finger in Ryukhin’s direction.
Ryukhin flushed with indignation.
“That’s what he gives me instead of a thank-you!” he thought bitterly. “For taking an interest in him! What a rotten creature, really!”

“A typical little kulak by his psychology,” Ivan Nikolayevich began, evidently itching to expose Ryukhin, “and, what’s more, a little kulak carefully disguising himself as a proletarian. Look at his sanctimonious face and compare it with the resounding verses he composed for the holiday on the first! Heh-heh-heh... ‘Soar on high!’ and ‘Unfurl and fly!’... but just take a look inside him—what he thinks in there... you’ll gasp!” And Ivan Nikolayevich laughed ominously.

Ryukhin was breathing heavily, red in the face, and thinking of only one thing: that he had nursed a viper in his bosom, that he had taken an interest in someone who had turned out on inspection to be a vicious enemy. And the main thing was that nothing could be done about it: one could hardly start a quarrel with a mental patient!
“And why, exactly, have you been brought to us?” the doctor asked, having listened attentively to Bezdomny’s denunciations.
“The devil take them, the blockheads! They grabbed me, tied me up with some rags and dragged me off in a truck!”
“May I ask you why you came to the restaurant in nothing but your underwear?”

“There’s nothing surprising in that,” Ivan answered. “I went for a swim in the Moscow River, and they swiped my clothes and left this rubbish! I could hardly go across Moscow naked! I put on what there was, because I was in a hurry to get to the restaurant, to Griboyedov’s.”
The doctor glanced questioningly at Ryukhin, who muttered sullenly:
“That’s the name of the restaurant.”
“Aha,” said the doctor, “and why were you in such a hurry? Some business appointment?”
“I’m trying to catch the consultant,” Ivan Nikolayevich answered, and looked round anxiously.
“What consultant?”
“Do you know Berlioz?” Ivan asked meaningfully.
“That’s... the composer?”
Ivan was upset.
“What composer? Ah, yes... No, no! The composer just has the same name as Misha Berlioz.”
Ryukhin had no wish to say anything, but he had to explain:
“Berlioz, the secretary of Massolit, was run over by a tram this evening at Patriarch’s.”
“Don’t you lie about things you know nothing about!” Ivan said angrily to Ryukhin. “It was me, not you, who was there! He set him up under the tram on purpose!”
“Pushed him?”

“What has ‘pushed’ got to do with it?” Ivan exclaimed, angered by the general obtuseness. “Someone like him doesn’t need to push! He can pull off tricks that make you hold on to your hat! He knew in advance that Berlioz would fall under a tram!”
“And did anyone besides you see this consultant?”
“That’s just the trouble, only Berlioz and I did.”

“I see. And what measures did you take to catch this murderer?” Here the doctor turned and cast a glance at a woman in a white coat sitting at a table off to one side. She took out a sheet of paper and began filling in the blanks in its columns.
“The measures were these. I took a little candle from the kitchen...”
“This one?” the doctor asked, pointing to a broken candle lying on the table next to the icon in front of the woman.
“That very one, and...”
“And why the icon?”

“Well, yes, the icon...” Ivan turned red. “It was the icon that frightened them most of all,” he again jabbed his finger toward Ryukhin, “but the thing is that he, the consultant, he... let’s speak plainly... has dealings with the unclean powers... and you won’t catch him that easily.”
The orderlies for some reason stood with their arms straight at their sides and did not take their eyes off Ivan.

“Yes,” Ivan went on, “he has dealings with them! That’s an irrefutable fact. He talked with Pontius Pilate in person. And there’s no need to look at me like that! I’m telling the truth! He saw everything—the balcony and the palms. In a word, he was with Pontius Pilate, I’ll vouch for that.”
“Go on, go on...”
“Well, so I pinned the icon on my chest and ran...”
Here the clock suddenly struck twice.
“Oho!” exclaimed Ivan, getting up from the couch. “Two o’clock, and I’m wasting time with you! Beg pardon, where’s the telephone?”
“Let him get to the telephone,” the doctor ordered the orderlies.
Ivan seized the receiver, and meanwhile the woman quietly asked Ryukhin:
“Is he married?”
“Single,” Ryukhin answered fearfully.
“Member of a trade union?”
“Yes.”

“Police?” Ivan shouted into the receiver. “Police? Comrade officer on duty, give orders at once for five motorcycles with machine guns to be sent out to capture a foreign consultant. What? Come and pick me up, I’ll go with you myself... This is the poet Bezdomny speaking, from the madhouse... What’s your address?” Bezdomny asked the doctor in a whisper, covering the receiver with his palm, and then shouted into the receiver again: “Are you listening? Hello!.. Outrageous!” Ivan suddenly howled, and flung the receiver at the wall. Then he turned to the doctor, held out his hand to him, said “good-bye” curtly, and made to leave.
“For pity’s sake, where do you mean to go?” the doctor began, peering into Ivan’s eyes. “In the dead of night, in your underwear... You are not feeling well, stay with us!”
“Let me through,” Ivan said to the orderlies, who had closed ranks at the door. “Are you going to let me through or not?” the poet shouted in a terrible voice.
Ryukhin began to tremble, and the woman pressed a button in the table, and out onto its glass surface popped a shiny little box and a sealed ampoule.
“Oh, so that’s it?!” said Ivan, looking around wildly, like a hunted animal. “All right, then! Farewell!!” And he hurled himself headfirst at the window blind.
There was a rather loud crash, but the glass behind the blind did not crack, and an instant later Ivan Nikolayevich was thrashing in the hands of the orderlies. He wheezed, tried to bite, shouted:
“So that’s the kind of glass you’ve got in here!.. Let go! Let go!..”

A syringe flashed in the doctor’s hands; with a single stroke the woman slit open the decrepit sleeve of the tolstovka and seized the arm with unwomanly strength. There was a smell of ether, Ivan went limp in the hands of four people, and the deft doctor took advantage of this moment and stuck the needle into Ivan’s arm. They held Ivan for a few more seconds and then lowered him onto the couch.

“Bandits!” Ivan shouted, and jumped up from the couch, but was put back on it again. As soon as they let go of him he started to jump up again, but this time sat back down by himself. He was silent for a while, looking around somewhat wildly, then unexpectedly yawned, then smiled spitefully.

“So you’ve locked me up after all,” he said, yawned once more, unexpectedly lay down, put his head on the pillow, his fist under his cheek like a child, and began to mutter in an already sleepy voice, without spite: “Well, so much the better... you’ll pay for it all yourselves. I’ve warned you, and now do as you like!.. What interests me most of all right now is Pontius Pilate... Pilate...” Here he closed his eyes.

“A bath, private room one hundred and seventeen, and a nurse on watch,” the doctor ordered, putting on his glasses. Here Ryukhin gave a start again: the white doors opened noiselessly, and beyond them a corridor could be seen, lit by blue night-lights. Out of the corridor rolled a couch on rubber wheels, the quieted Ivan was moved onto it, and he rolled away into the corridor, and the doors closed behind him.
“Doctor,” the shaken Ryukhin asked in a whisper, “so he really is ill?”
“Oh, yes,” the doctor answered.
“But what is it he has?” Ryukhin asked timidly.
The weary doctor looked at Ryukhin and answered listlessly:
“Motor and speech agitation... delusional interpretations... a complicated case, apparently... Schizophrenia, one must suppose. And alcoholism on top of it...”
Ryukhin understood nothing of the doctor’s words except that things were evidently pretty bad for Ivan Nikolayevich. He sighed and asked:
“But why does he keep talking about some consultant?”
“He probably saw someone who struck his disordered imagination. Or perhaps he was hallucinating...”

A few minutes later the truck was carrying Ryukhin off to Moscow. Day was breaking, and the light of the streetlamps along the highway, not yet put out, was no longer needed and was unpleasant. The driver was angry at having lost the night, drove the truck as hard as he could, and it skidded on the bends.

And now the forest fell away, was left somewhere behind, and the river went off somewhere to one side; all manner of odds and ends came pouring toward the truck: fences with sentry boxes and stacks of firewood, very tall poles and some sort of masts, with spools strung on the masts, heaps of crushed stone, earth striped with channels—in a word, one felt that here it was, any minute now, Moscow, right there, just beyond the bend, about to tumble down on you and engulf you.

Ryukhin was shaken and tossed about; some stump of wood on which he had settled kept trying to slip out from under him. The restaurant towels, thrown in by the policeman and Panteley, who had left earlier by trolleybus, were sliding all over the platform. Ryukhin tried to gather them up, but, hissing for some reason with spite, “Oh, the devil take them! Why am I, really, fussing about like a fool?..”, he kicked them away and stopped looking at them.

The traveler’s state of mind was dreadful. It was becoming clear that his visit to the house of sorrow had left a very grievous mark on him. Ryukhin tried to understand what was tormenting him. The corridor with the blue lamps, stuck in his memory? The thought that there is no worse misfortune in the world than losing one’s reason? Yes, yes, of course, that too. But that—well, that was a general thought. There was something else. What was it? Hurt pride, that was it. Yes, yes, the hurtful words Bezdomny had flung right in his face. And the trouble was not that they were hurtful, but that there was truth in them.
The poet no longer looked about him, but, staring at the dirty, shaking floor, began to mutter something, to whine, gnawing at himself.

Yes, poems... He was thirty-two years old! Really, what next? And next he would go on composing a few poems a year. Until old age? Yes, until old age. And what would these poems bring him? Fame? “What rubbish! At least don’t fool yourself. Fame will never come to someone who writes bad poems. Why are they bad? He told the truth, the truth!” Ryukhin addressed himself mercilessly. “I don’t believe in anything I write!..”

Poisoned by this outburst of neurasthenia, the poet swayed, and the floor beneath him stopped shaking. Ryukhin raised his head and saw that he had long been in Moscow and, what was more, that dawn was over Moscow, that a cloud was lit up with gold, that his truck was standing, stuck in a column of other vehicles at the turn onto the boulevard, and that very close to him, on a pedestal, stood a metal man, his head slightly bowed, looking indifferently at the boulevard.

Some strange thoughts flooded into the ailing poet’s head. “There’s an example of real luck...” Here Ryukhin rose to his full height on the platform of the truck and raised his arm, for some reason attacking the cast-iron man, who was bothering no one. “Whatever step he took in life, whatever happened to him, it all went to his advantage, it all turned to his glory! But what did he do? I can’t comprehend it... Is there anything special in these words: ‘The storm with darkness veils...’? I don’t understand!.. Luck, luck!” Ryukhin suddenly concluded venomously, and felt the truck stir under him. “He shot, that White Guard shot at him, and shattered his hip, and secured him immortality...”

The column moved off. Completely ill, and even aged, the poet walked onto the veranda of Griboyedov’s no more than two minutes later. It was already deserted. In a corner some company was finishing its drinks, and in the middle of it a familiar master of ceremonies in a skullcap, with a glass of Abrau in his hand, was bustling about.

Ryukhin, burdened with towels, was greeted cordially by Archibald Archibaldovich and at once relieved of the cursed rags. Had Ryukhin not been so worn out in the clinic and on the truck, he would probably have taken pleasure in telling how everything had gone at the hospital and embellishing the story with invented details. But just now he was in no mood for it, and besides, unobservant as Ryukhin was, now, after the torture in the truck, for the first time he looked sharply at the pirate and understood that although he asked questions about Bezdomny and even exclaimed “Tut-tut-tut!”, in essence he was completely indifferent to Bezdomny’s fate and did not pity him in the least. “Good for him! Quite right!” Ryukhin thought with cynical, self-annihilating spite, and, breaking off his story about schizophrenia, he asked:
“Archibald Archibaldovich, I could do with a little vodka...”
The pirate put on a sympathetic face and whispered:
“I understand... this very minute...” And he waved to a waiter.

A quarter of an hour later Ryukhin, entirely alone, sat hunched over a smoked rybets, drinking glass after glass, understanding and admitting that nothing in his life could be put right any more, it could only be forgotten.

The poet had wasted his night while others feasted, and now understood that it could not be brought back. He had only to raise his head from the lamp to the sky to understand that the night was lost irretrievably. The waiters were hurriedly snatching the tablecloths off the tables. The cats prowling near the veranda had a morning look. Day was bearing down on the poet irresistibly.

chapters.title: 7. The Bad Apartment
paragraphs: If on the following morning someone had said to Styopa Likhodeyev, “Styopa! You’ll be shot if you don’t get up this minute!” Styopa would have answered in a languid, barely audible voice, “Shoot me, do whatever you like with me, but I’m not getting up.”

Getting up was out of the question—it seemed to him that he could not even open his eyes, because the moment he did, lightning would flash and his head would instantly be blown to pieces. A heavy bell was booming inside that head, brown spots with fiery green rims were floating between his eyeballs and his closed lids, and to crown it all he felt sick, and it seemed to him that the nausea was somehow connected with the sounds of an insistent gramophone.

Styopa tried to remember something, but only one thing came back to him—that yesterday, apparently, in some unknown place, he had stood with a napkin in his hand and tried to kiss some lady, and had promised her that he would come and visit her the next day, at noon sharp. The lady had declined, saying, “No, no, I won’t be at home!”—but Styopa had stubbornly insisted: “And I’ll just up and come anyway!”

Who the lady was, what time it was now, what day it was and of what month—Styopa had absolutely no idea, and, worst of all, he could not work out where he was. He tried to establish at least the last of these, and to that end he unstuck the gummed-up lids of his left eye. Something was gleaming dully in the half-dark. At last Styopa recognized the pier glass and understood that he was lying on his back in his own bed—that is, in the jeweler’s widow’s former bed—in the bedroom. At this something struck him so hard in the head that he closed the eye and groaned.

Let us explain: Styopa Likhodeyev, director of the Variety Theatre, had come to that morning in his own home, in the very apartment he shared with the late Berlioz, in a large six-story building laid out in a U on Sadovaya Street.

It must be said that this apartment—No. 50—had long enjoyed a reputation that was, if not bad, then at any rate strange. As recently as two years before, its owner had been the widow of the jeweler de Fougeray. Anna Frantsevna de Fougeray, a respectable and very businesslike lady of fifty, let three of its five rooms to lodgers: one, whose name was apparently Belomut, and another whose name has been lost.
And then, two years ago, inexplicable events began in the apartment: people started disappearing from it without a trace.

One day off, a policeman turned up at the apartment, called the second lodger (the one whose name has been lost) out into the hall, and said he was requested to drop by the police station for a minute to sign something. The lodger told Anfisa, Anna Frantsevna’s devoted housekeeper of many years, to say, in case anyone telephoned, that he would be back in ten minutes, and left together with the correct policeman in white gloves. But he did not come back in ten minutes; in fact he never came back at all. Most surprising of all, the policeman had evidently vanished along with him.

The pious—or, to put it more frankly, superstitious—Anfisa told the very upset Anna Frantsevna straight out that this was witchcraft and that she knew perfectly well who had carried off both the lodger and the policeman, only she did not want to say it with night coming on.

Well, witchcraft, as everyone knows, has only to begin, and after that there is no stopping it. The second lodger disappeared, as I recall, on a Monday, and on Wednesday Belomut vanished as if the earth had swallowed him, though under different circumstances, true. In the morning a car called for him as usual to take him to work, and it took him, but it brought no one back and never returned itself.

Madame Belomut’s grief and horror are beyond description. But, alas, neither the one nor the other lasted long. That same night, on returning with Anfisa from the dacha, where for some reason Anna Frantsevna had gone in a hurry, she found Citizen Belomut no longer in the apartment. And that was not all: the doors of both rooms occupied by the Belomut couple turned out to be sealed!
Two days passed somehow or other. On the third day Anna Frantsevna, who had suffered from insomnia all this time, again left in a hurry for the dacha... Need it be said that she did not come back!

Anfisa, left alone, had a good long cry and went to bed after one in the morning. What happened to her after that is not known, but the tenants of other apartments said that knocking of some sort was supposedly heard in No. 50 all night and that the electric light supposedly burned in the windows until morning. In the morning it turned out that Anfisa was gone too!

For a long time all kinds of legends were told in the building about the vanished people and the accursed apartment—for instance, that this dried-up, pious Anfisa supposedly carried on her withered chest, in a little suede bag, twenty-five large diamonds belonging to Anna Frantsevna. That in the woodshed at that very dacha to which Anna Frantsevna had made her hurried trips, some untold treasures had supposedly turned up all by themselves, in the form of those same diamonds, as well as gold coins of tsarist minting... And so on, in the same vein. Well, what we do not know, we cannot vouch for.

Be that as it may, the apartment stood empty and sealed for only a week, and then it was moved into—by the late Berlioz and his wife, and by this same Styopa, also with his wife. Quite naturally, as soon as they got into the accursed apartment, the devil knows what began happening to them too. Namely, within a single month both wives disappeared. But these did not vanish without a trace. Of Berlioz’s wife it was said that she had supposedly been seen in Kharkov with some ballet master, while Styopa’s wife allegedly turned up on Bozhedomka Street, where, so the gossip went, the director of the Variety, using his countless connections, had contrived to get her a room, but on one condition: that there be not a whiff of her on Sadovaya Street...

And so Styopa groaned. He wanted to call the housekeeper Grunya and demand some Pyramidon from her, but he was still able to realize that this was nonsense, that Grunya of course had no Pyramidon. He tried calling Berlioz for help, groaned twice, “Misha... Misha...” but, as you can imagine, got no answer. The apartment was utterly silent.

Wiggling his toes, Styopa guessed that he was lying there in his socks; he ran a trembling hand down his hip to determine whether he had his trousers on or not, and could not determine it. At last, seeing that he was abandoned and alone, that there was no one to help him, he decided to get up, whatever inhuman effort it might cost him.

Styopa unstuck his gummed lids and saw himself reflected in the pier glass as a man with hair sticking out in all directions, with a puffy face covered in black stubble, with swollen eyes, in a dirty shirt with collar and tie, in his underpants and socks.
That was how he saw himself in the pier glass, and next to the mirror he saw an unknown man, dressed in black and wearing a black beret.
Styopa sat up on the bed and goggled his bloodshot eyes at the stranger as far as he could.
It was the stranger who broke the silence, pronouncing the following words in a low, heavy voice with a foreign accent:
“Good day, most charming Stepan Bogdanovich!”
There was a pause, after which, making a terrible effort, Styopa got out:
“What can I do for you?”—and was himself astonished, not recognizing his own voice. He pronounced the word “what” as a treble, “can I” as a bass, and “do for you” did not come out at all.
The stranger smiled amiably, took out a large gold watch with a diamond triangle on the lid, let it chime eleven times, and said:
“Eleven! And it’s exactly an hour that I have been waiting for you to wake up, since you made an appointment with me for ten. Here I am!”
Styopa felt for his trousers on the chair beside the bed and whispered:
“Excuse me...” He put them on and asked hoarsely: “Would you tell me your name, please?”
Speaking was hard for him. With every word someone stuck a needle into his brain, causing him hellish pain.
“What? You’ve forgotten my name too?” At this the stranger smiled.

“Forgive me...” Styopa croaked, feeling that his hangover was presenting him with a new symptom: it seemed to him that the floor beside the bed had gone off somewhere and that any minute now he would fly headfirst to the devil’s mother, down into the underworld.

“My dear Stepan Bogdanovich,” the visitor began, with a shrewd smile, “no Pyramidon will help you. Follow the wise old rule: treat like with like. The only thing that will bring you back to life is two shots of vodka with something sharp and hot to eat.”
Styopa was a cunning man and, ill as he was, realized that since he had been caught in this state, he had better confess everything.
“To be frank,” he began, barely able to move his tongue, “yesterday I had a bit...”
“Not another word!” the visitor replied, and moved off to one side with his armchair.

Styopa, goggling, saw that a tray had been laid on a little table, and on it there was sliced white bread, pressed caviar in a little bowl, pickled porcini mushrooms on a little plate, something in a small saucepan, and, finally, vodka in the jeweler’s widow’s capacious decanter. What particularly struck Styopa was that the decanter was misted with cold. That, however, was understandable—it stood in a slop bowl packed with ice. In a word, the table had been laid neatly and expertly.
The stranger did not allow Styopa’s amazement to develop to a morbid degree and deftly poured him half a shot of vodka.
“And you?” Styopa squeaked.
“With pleasure!”
With a jumping hand Styopa raised the glass to his lips, while the stranger swallowed the contents of his in one gulp. Chewing on a bit of caviar, Styopa squeezed out the words:
“And you... won’t you have a bite?”
“Thank you kindly, I never take a bite,” the stranger replied, and poured a second round. They opened the saucepan—it held frankfurters in tomato sauce.

And then the cursed green before his eyes melted away, words began to come out, and, above all, Styopa remembered something. Namely, that yesterday’s affair had taken place at Skhodnya, at the dacha of the sketch writer Khustov, where this Khustov had taken Styopa in a taxi. He even remembered hiring the taxi outside the Metropol, and there had been some actor or other, or not an actor... with a gramophone in a little suitcase. Yes, yes, yes, it had been at the dacha! And he remembered, too, the dogs howling at that gramophone. Only the lady Styopa had wanted to kiss remained unexplained... the devil knows who she was... she worked in radio, it seemed, or maybe not.

Yesterday, then, was gradually becoming clearer, but just now Styopa was far more interested in today, and in particular in the appearance of a stranger in his bedroom, complete with snacks and vodka. That would be nice to have explained!
“Well, then, I hope you’ve remembered my name now?”
But Styopa only smiled sheepishly and spread his hands.
“Well, really! I sense that after the vodka you drank port! For pity’s sake, how can anyone do that!”
“I’d like to ask you to keep this between us,” Styopa said ingratiatingly.
“Oh, of course, of course! But for Khustov, needless to say, I cannot vouch.”
