“Why, actually, did I get so worked up because Berlioz fell under a tram?” the poet reasoned. “When all’s said and done, the swamp can have him! What am I to him, really, his godfather or his in-law? If you give the question a proper airing, it turns out that, in essence, I didn’t even really know the deceased. Truly, what did I know about him? Why, nothing, except that he was bald and terribly eloquent. And further, citizens,” Ivan went on with his speech, addressing someone, “let’s get to the bottom of this: explain to me, why did I fly into such a rage at this mysterious consultant, magician and professor with the empty black eye? What was the point of that whole absurd chase after him in my underpants with a little candle in my hand, and then that wild farce in the restaurant?”

“Now, now, now,” the former Ivan suddenly said sternly to the new Ivan, somewhere either inside him or just above his ear, “he did know in advance, though, that Berlioz would have his head cut off, didn’t he? How could anyone not get worked up?”

“What is there to discuss, comrades!” the new Ivan objected to the old, former Ivan. “That there’s something unclean about this business is clear even to a child. He’s an extraordinary and mysterious personality, a hundred percent. But that’s exactly what’s most interesting about it! The man was personally acquainted with Pontius Pilate—what could you want that’s more interesting than that? And instead of kicking up the stupidest fuss at Patriarch’s, wouldn’t it have been smarter to ask him politely what happened next with Pilate and that prisoner Ha-Notsri? And instead I got up to the devil knows what! A great event, really—a magazine editor got run over! What of it, is the magazine going to close down because of it? Well, what can you do? Man is mortal, and, as was so rightly said, suddenly mortal. Well, may he rest in the kingdom of heaven! Well, there’ll be another editor, maybe even more eloquent than the last one.”
After dozing a little, the new Ivan asked the old Ivan snidely:
“So what does that make me, in this case?”
“A fool!” a bass voice said distinctly somewhere, a voice that belonged to neither of the Ivans and was extremely like the consultant’s bass.

Ivan, who for some reason was not offended by the word “fool” but was even pleasantly surprised by it, smiled and, half asleep, grew quiet. Sleep was stealing up on Ivan, and already he seemed to see the palm tree on its elephant’s foot, and the cat walked past—not frightening, but cheerful—and, in a word, sleep was just about to cover Ivan when suddenly the grille slid noiselessly aside, and on the balcony appeared a mysterious figure, hiding from the moonlight, and shook a finger at Ivan.
Ivan raised himself in bed without the slightest fright and saw that there was a man on the balcony. And this man, pressing a finger to his lips, whispered:
“Shhh!”

chapters.title: 12. Black Magic and Its Exposure
paragraphs: A little man in a battered yellow bowler with holes in it, with a pear-shaped crimson nose, checked trousers and patent-leather shoes, rode out onto the stage of the Variety on an ordinary two-wheeled bicycle. To the strains of a foxtrot he rode a circle, and then let out a triumphant yell, at which the bicycle reared up on its hind wheel. After riding a stretch on the back wheel alone, the little man turned upside down, contrived to unscrew the front wheel while still moving and send it rolling off into the wings, and then went on his way on one wheel, turning the pedals with his hands.

A plump blonde in tights and a short skirt strewn with silver stars rode out on a tall metal mast with a saddle on top and a single wheel, and began to ride around in a circle. Each time he passed her, the little man gave a cry of greeting and took the bowler off his head with his foot.
Finally a tot of about eight with an old man’s face rolled in and began darting among the grown-ups on a tiny two-wheeler to which an enormous motor-car horn had been attached.

After making several loops, the whole company, to an anxious drumroll from the orchestra, rolled up to the very edge of the stage, and the spectators in the front rows gasped and recoiled, because it seemed to the audience that the whole trio, machines and all, was about to come crashing down into the orchestra pit.

But the bicycles stopped at the very moment when the front wheels were already threatening to slip into the abyss onto the musicians’ heads. With a loud cry of “Hup!” the cyclists leaped off their machines and bowed, the blonde blowing kisses to the audience and the tot sounding a funny call on his horn.

Applause shook the building, the blue curtain moved in from both sides and hid the cyclists, the green lights with the word “Exit” over the doors went out, and in the web of trapezes beneath the dome white globes lit up like the sun. The intermission before the last part of the program had begun.

The only person in whom the marvels of cycling technique performed by the Giulli family aroused no interest whatsoever was Grigory Danilovich Rimsky. He sat all alone in his office, biting his thin lips, and every so often a spasm passed across his face. To the extraordinary disappearance of Likhodeyev had now been added the wholly unforeseen disappearance of the house manager, Varenukha.
Rimsky knew where he had gone, but he had gone and... had not come back! Rimsky kept shrugging and whispering to himself:
“But what for?!”

And, strange to say, for so businesslike a man as the financial director, the simplest thing, of course, would have been to telephone the place where Varenukha had gone and find out what had happened to him, and yet until ten o’clock in the evening he could not bring himself to do it.

At ten, however, having done himself regular violence, Rimsky lifted the receiver and at once discovered that his telephone was dead. A messenger reported that the other telephones in the building were out of order too. This event—unpleasant, of course, but not supernatural—for some reason shook the financial director to the core, and yet at the same time it gladdened him: the need to telephone had dropped away.

Just as the red lamp above the financial director’s head flashed on and began to blink, announcing the start of the intermission, the messenger came in and informed him that the foreign artiste had arrived. For some reason the financial director gave a shudder, and, now looking blacker than a thundercloud, he went backstage to receive the visiting performer, since there was no one else left to receive him.

Under various pretexts, curious people kept peering into the large dressing room from the corridor, where the warning bells were already ringing. There were conjurers in bright robes and turbans, a roller skater in a white knitted jacket, a monologist pale with powder, and a make-up man.

The celebrity who had arrived struck everyone with his tailcoat, of a marvelous cut and of a length never seen before, and with the fact that he had come in a black half mask. But most astonishing of all were the black magician’s two companions: a long checked fellow in cracked pince-nez, and a fat black cat, which, entering the dressing room on its hind legs, sat down on the sofa perfectly at its ease, squinting at the bare make-up lights.

Rimsky tried to put a smile on his face, which only made it sour and spiteful, and bowed to the silent magician sitting beside the cat on the sofa. There was no handshake. Instead, the overfamiliar checked fellow introduced himself to the financial director, calling himself “assistant to their honor.” This circumstance surprised the financial director, and again unpleasantly: the contract made absolutely no mention of any assistant.
Very stiffly and drily, Grigory Danilovich inquired of the checked fellow who had landed on his head where the artiste’s equipment was.

“Our heavenly diamond, most precious Mister Director,” the magician’s assistant answered in a rattling voice, “our equipment is always with us. Here it is! Ein, zwei, drei!” And, twiddling his knobbly fingers before Rimsky’s eyes, he suddenly pulled out from behind the cat’s ear Rimsky’s own gold watch and chain, which until that moment had been in the financial director’s waistcoat pocket under his buttoned jacket, with the chain threaded through the buttonhole.
Rimsky involuntarily clutched at his belly, those present gasped, and the make-up man, peering in at the door, grunted his approval.
“Your little watch? Kindly take it back,” said the checked fellow, smiling overfamiliarly, and on his dirty palm he handed the bewildered Rimsky his property.
“Don’t get on a tram with that one,” the monologist whispered quietly and merrily to the make-up man.

But the cat pulled a trick even neater than the number with someone else’s watch. Unexpectedly getting up from the sofa, it walked on its hind legs to the dressing table, pulled the stopper out of the carafe with its front paw, poured water into a glass, drank it, put the stopper back in its place and wiped its whiskers with a make-up rag.
This time nobody even gasped; they simply opened their mouths, and the make-up man whispered rapturously:
“Oh, class!”
At this point the bells rang out anxiously for the third time, and everyone, excited and anticipating an interesting act, poured out of the dressing room.

A minute later the globes in the auditorium went out, the footlights flared up and cast a reddish glow on the bottom of the curtain, and in the lit gap of the curtain there appeared before the audience a plump man, merry as a child, with a clean-shaven face, in a rumpled tailcoat and none-too-fresh linen. It was the master of ceremonies Georges Bengalsky, well known to all Moscow.

“And now, citizens,” Bengalsky began, smiling an infant’s smile, “appearing before you will be...” Here Bengalsky interrupted himself and began speaking in a different tone: “I see the size of the audience has grown still further for the third part. We have half the city here tonight! The other day I run into a friend and say to him: ‘Why don’t you ever come and see us? Yesterday we had half the city.’ And he answers me: ‘But I live in the other half!’” Bengalsky paused, expecting an explosion of laughter, but since no one laughed, he went on: “...And so, appearing will be the famous foreign artiste Monsieur Woland with a séance of black magic! Well, you and I understand,” here Bengalsky smiled a wise smile, “that there’s no such thing in the world, that it’s nothing but superstition, and that Maestro Woland is simply a supreme master of the technique of conjuring, as will be seen from the most interesting part, that is, the exposure of that technique, and since we are all, to a man, both for technique and for its exposure, let us ask Mr. Woland to come on!”
Having uttered all this rubbish, Bengalsky clasped both hands palm to palm and waved them in greeting through the slit in the curtain, at which the curtain, rustling softly, parted to either side.
The entrance of the magician with his long assistant and the cat, which stepped onto the stage on its hind legs, pleased the audience very much.

“An armchair,” Woland ordered quietly, and that very second, no one knew how or from where, an armchair appeared on the stage, and the magician sat down in it. “Tell me, my dear Fagot,” Woland inquired of the checked buffoon, who evidently bore another name besides “Koroviev,” “in your opinion, the population of Moscow has changed considerably, hasn’t it?”
The magician looked at the audience, which had fallen silent, stunned by the appearance of an armchair out of thin air.
“Just so, messire,” Fagot-Koroviev answered quietly.

“You are right. The townspeople have changed a great deal... outwardly, I mean, as has the city itself, for that matter. Not to mention the clothes, but now these... what do you call them... trams have appeared, automobiles...”
“Buses,” Fagot prompted respectfully.

The audience listened attentively to this conversation, assuming it was a prelude to the magic tricks. The wings were packed with performers and stagehands, and among their faces could be seen Rimsky’s tense, pale face.
The physiognomy of Bengalsky, who had taken shelter at the side of the stage, began to express bewilderment. He raised one eyebrow very slightly and, taking advantage of the pause, spoke up:

“Our foreign artiste is expressing his admiration for Moscow, which has grown so much technically, and also for Muscovites,” and here Bengalsky smiled twice, first at the stalls and then at the gallery.
Woland, Fagot and the cat turned their heads toward the master of ceremonies.
“Did I express admiration?” the magician asked Fagot.
“By no means, messire, you expressed no admiration whatsoever,” the latter answered.
“Then what is this man saying?”
“Why, he simply told a lie!” the checked assistant announced resoundingly, for the whole theater to hear, and, turning to Bengalsky, he added: “Congratulations, citizen, you been and gone and lied!”
A splash of laughter came from the gallery, while Bengalsky gave a start and his eyes bulged.
“But of course I am not so much interested in buses, telephones and other...”
“Equipment!” the checked one prompted.
“Quite right, thank you,” the magician said slowly in a heavy bass, “as in a far more important question: have these townspeople changed inwardly?”
“Yes, that is the most important question, sir.”
In the wings people began exchanging glances and shrugging; Bengalsky stood there red in the face, and Rimsky was pale. But here, as if guessing at the alarm that was beginning, the magician said:
“However, we have been talking too long, my dear Fagot, and the audience is beginning to get bored. Show us something simple to start with.”
The hall stirred with relief. Fagot and the cat went off in different directions along the footlights. Fagot snapped his fingers and shouted dashingly:

“Three, four!” He caught a deck of cards out of the air, shuffled it and sent it flying to the cat in a ribbon. The cat intercepted the ribbon and sent it back. The satiny snake snorted, Fagot opened his mouth like a fledgling and swallowed the whole of it, card by card.
After this the cat bowed, scraping its right hind paw, and drew incredible applause.
“Class! Class!” came rapturous shouts from the wings.
And Fagot jabbed a finger at the stalls and announced:

“This here deck, esteemed citizens, is now in row seven, in the possession of Citizen Parchevsky, right between a three-ruble note and a summons to appear in court in the matter of alimony payments to Citizen Zelkova.”

People in the stalls stirred and began to rise, and at last a certain citizen, whose name was indeed Parchevsky, flushed crimson all over with astonishment, extracted the deck from his wallet and began poking the air with it, not knowing what to do with it.
“Let it stay with you as a souvenir!” shouted Fagot. “Not for nothing did you say at supper yesterday that if it weren’t for poker your life in Moscow would be utterly unbearable.”
“Old trick,” came a voice from the gallery. “That one in the stalls is from the same gang.”
“You think so?” bawled Fagot, squinting up at the gallery. “In that case you’re in our gang too, because the deck is in your pocket!”
There was a stir in the gallery, and a joyful voice was heard:
“It’s true! He’s got it! Here, here... Wait! Why, it’s tenners!”

The people in the stalls turned their heads. Up in the gallery a flustered citizen had found in his pocket a wad tied up the way banks do it, with the words “One thousand rubles” written on the wrapper.
His neighbors piled onto him, while he, in amazement, picked at the wrapper with his fingernail, trying to find out whether these were real ten-ruble notes or some sort of magic ones.
“God’s truth, they’re real! Tenners!” came joyful shouts from the gallery.
“Play a game with a deck like that with me too,” a fat man in the middle of the stalls requested merrily.

“Avec plaisir!” responded Fagot. “But why with you alone? Everyone will take part with enthusiasm!” And he commanded: “Kindly look up!.. One!” A pistol appeared in his hand. He shouted: “Two!” The pistol jerked upward. He shouted: “Three!” There was a flash and a bang, and at once, from under the dome, diving between the trapezes, white slips of paper began falling into the hall.

They twirled, they were carried off to the sides, blown into the gallery, tossed back into the orchestra pit and onto the stage. In a few seconds the rain of money, growing ever thicker, reached the seats, and the spectators began catching the slips.

Hundreds of hands went up; the spectators held the slips up to the lit stage and saw the most genuine and upright of watermarks. The smell, too, left no doubt whatsoever: it was the smell of freshly printed money, incomparable in its delightfulness. First merriment and then amazement seized the whole theater. Everywhere the word “tenners, tenners” hummed, cries of “Oh, oh!” and merry laughter were heard. Some were already crawling in the aisle, groping under the seats. Many stood on their seats, catching the fidgety, capricious slips.
Little by little bewilderment began to show on the faces of the police, and the performers unceremoniously began sticking their heads out of the wings.

In the dress circle a voice was heard: “What are you grabbing for? That one’s mine! It was flying to me!” and another voice: “Don’t you shove me, or I’ll shove you so you’ll know it!” And suddenly the sound of a slap was heard. At once a policeman’s helmet appeared in the dress circle, and someone was led out of the dress circle.
On the whole the excitement was mounting, and there is no knowing what it all might have come to if Fagot had not stopped the rain of money by suddenly blowing into the air.

Two young men, exchanging a meaningful and merry look, left their seats and headed straight for the buffet. The theater was humming; the eyes of every spectator shone with excitement. Yes, yes, there is no knowing what it all might have come to if Bengalsky had not found the strength in himself to stir. Trying to get a firmer grip on himself, he rubbed his hands out of habit and, in his most resonant voice, began as follows:

“There, citizens, we have just witnessed a case of so-called mass hypnosis. A purely scientific experiment, proving as clearly as could be that no miracles or magic exist. Let us ask Maestro Woland to expose this experiment for us. Now, citizens, you will see how these supposedly monetary slips of paper will vanish just as suddenly as they appeared.”
Here he began to applaud, but entirely alone, and while a confident smile played on his face, there was no confidence at all in his eyes; if anything, they expressed entreaty.
The audience did not like Bengalsky’s speech. A total silence fell, which was broken by the checked Fagot.
“This is yet another case of so-called fibbing,” he announced in a loud, goatish tenor. “The slips, citizens, are real!”
“Bravo!” barked a bass voice abruptly somewhere up high.
“By the way, this one here,” and Fagot pointed at Bengalsky, “bores me. He keeps poking his nose in where nobody asked him, spoiling the séance with false remarks! What shall we do with him?”
“Tear his head off!” someone said sternly in the gallery.
“What’s that you say? Eh?” Fagot responded at once to this outrageous suggestion. “Tear his head off? That’s an idea! Behemoth!” he shouted to the cat. “Do it! Ein, zwei, drei!!”

And an unheard-of thing happened. The black cat’s fur stood on end, and it gave a heart-rending miaow. Then it shrank into a ball and, like a panther, sprang straight at Bengalsky’s chest and from there leaped onto his head. Growling, the cat sank its plump paws into the master of ceremonies’ thin hair and, with a wild howl, in two twists tore the head off the plump neck.

Two and a half thousand people in the theater cried out as one. Blood spurted up in fountains from the torn arteries in the neck and drenched both shirtfront and tailcoat. The headless body paddled its feet absurdly somehow and sat down on the floor. Hysterical women’s screams were heard in the hall. The cat handed the head to Fagot, who lifted it up by the hair and showed it to the audience, and the head cried out desperately for the whole theater to hear:
“A doctor!”
“Will you go on talking all sorts of drivel in future?” Fagot asked the weeping head menacingly.
“I won’t anymore!” the head croaked.
“For God’s sake, stop tormenting him!” a woman’s voice suddenly rang out from a box, rising above the din, and the magician turned his face toward that voice.
“Well then, citizens, shall we forgive him, or what?” asked Fagot, addressing the hall.
“Forgive him! Forgive him!” came the cries, at first from separate and mostly female voices, and then they merged into a single chorus with the men’s.
“What are your orders, messire?” Fagot asked the masked man.

“Well, now,” the latter responded thoughtfully, “they are people like any other people. They love money, but then that has always been so... Mankind loves money, whatever it may be made of, leather or paper, bronze or gold. Well, they are frivolous... well, what of it... and mercy sometimes knocks at their hearts... ordinary people... On the whole, they remind me of the former ones... only the housing problem has spoiled them...” And he ordered loudly: “Put the head back on.”

The cat, taking more careful aim, jammed the head down onto the neck, and it sat exactly in its place, as though it had never gone anywhere. And, most important, not even a scar was left on the neck. The cat brushed off Bengalsky’s tailcoat and shirtfront with its paws, and the traces of blood vanished from them. Fagot lifted the seated Bengalsky to his feet, shoved a wad of ten-ruble notes into his tailcoat pocket and saw him off the stage with the words:
“Clear off out of here! It’s more fun without you.”
Looking around senselessly and staggering, the master of ceremonies made it only as far as the fire post, and there he was taken ill. He cried out pitifully:
“My head, my head!”
Rimsky was among those who rushed to him. The master of ceremonies was weeping, grabbing at something in the air with his hands, muttering:
“Give me back my head! Give my head back! Take my apartment, take my paintings, only give me back my head!”

A messenger ran for a doctor. They tried to lay Bengalsky down on the sofa in the dressing room, but he began to fight them off and turned violent. They had to call an ambulance. When the unfortunate master of ceremonies had been taken away, Rimsky ran back to the stage and saw that new marvels were taking place on it. Yes, and by the way, whether it was at this moment or a little earlier, the magician, together with his faded armchair, had vanished from the stage, and it must be said that the audience did not notice it at all, carried away by the extraordinary things Fagot was laying out on the stage.
And Fagot, having packed off the injured master of ceremonies, made the following announcement to the audience:
“Now then, now that we’ve got shot of that pest, let’s open a ladies’ shop!”

And at once the floor of the stage was covered with Persian carpets, enormous mirrors appeared, lit from the sides by greenish tubes, and between the mirrors, display windows, in which the spectators, in merry stupefaction, saw Parisian women’s dresses of all colors and styles. That was in some of the windows. In others there appeared hundreds of ladies’ hats, with feathers and without, with buckles and without them, and hundreds of shoes—black, white, yellow, leather, satin, suede, with straps and with little stones. Among the shoes appeared cases of perfume, mountains of handbags of antelope hide, of suede, of silk, and between them whole heaps of oblong little cases of chased gold, the kind that hold lipstick.

A red-haired girl in a black evening dress, who had come from the devil knows where, a girl good in every way if a bizarre scar on her neck had not spoiled her, smiled a proprietor’s smile beside the display windows.

Fagot, grinning sweetly, announced that the firm would exchange, entirely free of charge, ladies’ old dresses and footwear for Parisian models and Parisian footwear likewise. He added the same about handbags and the rest.
The cat began scraping its hind paw, while at the same time making with its front paw certain gestures peculiar to doormen opening a door.
The girl, sweetly though a little huskily, and rolling her r’s, began singing something barely comprehensible but, judging by the women’s faces in the stalls, very tempting:
“Guerlain, Chanel Number Five, Mitsouko, Narcisse Noir, evening gowns, cocktail dresses...”
Fagot writhed, the cat bowed, the girl opened the glass display windows.
“Please!” bawled Fagot. “Without the slightest embarrassment or ceremony!”

The audience was agitated, but so far no one dared to go up on the stage. At last a certain brunette came out of the tenth row of the stalls and, smiling in a way that said she couldn’t care less and didn’t give a hoot anyway, walked over and climbed up onto the stage by the side steps.
“Bravo!” cried Fagot. “I welcome our first customer! Behemoth, an armchair! We’ll begin with the footwear, madame!”

The brunette sat down in the armchair, and Fagot at once tumbled a whole heap of shoes onto the carpet in front of her. The brunette took off her right shoe, tried on a lilac one, stamped on the carpet and examined the heel.
“But won’t they pinch?” she asked thoughtfully. To which Fagot exclaimed in an offended tone:
“Oh, come now, come now!” and the cat miaowed in offense.
“I’ll take this pair, monsieur,” said the brunette with dignity, putting on the second shoe as well.

The brunette’s old shoes were tossed behind a curtain, and she herself proceeded there too, accompanied by the red-haired girl and Fagot, who was carrying several model dresses on hangers. The cat bustled about, helping, and for greater importance hung a tape measure around its neck.

A minute later the brunette came out from behind the curtain in such a dress that a sigh rolled through the whole of the stalls. The brave woman, who had become astonishingly prettier, stopped at the mirror, moved her bare shoulders, touched the hair at the back of her head and twisted around, trying to look at her back.
“The firm begs you to accept this as a souvenir,” said Fagot, and he handed the brunette an open case with a bottle in it.
“Merci,” the brunette answered haughtily, and went down the steps into the stalls. As she walked, spectators jumped up and touched the case.

And now the dam burst completely, and women came at the stage from all sides. In the general excited chatter, giggles and sighs, a man’s voice was heard: “I won’t allow you!” and a woman’s: “Despot and philistine! Don’t break my arm!” Women disappeared behind the curtain, left their dresses there and came out in new ones. A whole row of ladies sat on stools with gilded legs, stamping vigorously on the carpet with their newly shod feet. Fagot went down on his knees, wielding a metal shoehorn; the cat, exhausted under heaps of handbags and shoes, dragged itself from the display windows to the stools and back; the girl with the disfigured neck kept appearing and disappearing and got to the point of rattling away entirely in French, and the astonishing thing was that all the women understood her at half a word, even those of them who did not know a single word of French.

General amazement was caused by a man who had wormed his way onto the stage. He announced that his wife had the flu and that he therefore asked them to pass something on to her through him. As proof that he really was married, the citizen was prepared to show his passport. The solicitous husband’s announcement was met with roars of laughter; Fagot bawled that he believed him like himself, even without a passport, and handed the citizen two pairs of silk stockings, and the cat added a little case of lipstick from himself.

Latecomer women were fighting their way onto the stage, and from the stage flowed the lucky ones, in ball gowns, in pajamas with dragons, in severe afternoon suits, in little hats pulled down over one eyebrow.

Then Fagot announced that, on account of the late hour, the shop would close until tomorrow evening in exactly one minute, and an incredible bustle broke out on the stage. Women hastily grabbed shoes without trying them on at all. One burst behind the curtain like a storm, flung off her suit there and seized the first thing that came to hand—a silk dressing gown covered in enormous bouquets—and, on top of that, managed to snag two cases of perfume.

Exactly a minute later a pistol shot rang out, the mirrors vanished, the display windows and stools sank out of sight, and the carpet melted into the air, as did the curtain. Last of all to vanish was the towering mountain of old dresses and footwear, and the stage was once more severe, empty and bare.
And it was here that a new character entered the action.
A pleasant, resonant and very insistent baritone was heard from box No. 2:

“All the same, citizen artiste, it would be desirable for you to expose without delay to the spectators the technique of your tricks, especially the trick with the paper money. The return of the master of ceremonies to the stage would also be desirable. His fate is causing the spectators concern.”
The baritone belonged to none other than the guest of honor of that evening, Arkady Apollonovich Sempleyarov, chairman of the Acoustics Commission of the Moscow theaters.

Arkady Apollonovich was seated in the box with two ladies: one elderly, expensively and fashionably dressed, and the other young and pretty, dressed more simply. The first of them, as soon came to light when the report was drawn up, was Arkady Apollonovich’s spouse, and the second a distant relative of his, a beginning and promising actress who had come from Saratov and was living in the apartment of Arkady Apollonovich and his spouse.
“Pardon!” responded Fagot. “Begging your pardon, there is nothing to expose here, it is all clear.”
“No, excuse me! An exposure is absolutely necessary. Without it your brilliant numbers will leave a painful impression. The viewing masses demand an explanation.”

“The visual masses,” the insolent buffoon interrupted Sempleyarov, “don’t seem to have announced anything? But, taking into account your deeply respected wish, Arkady Apollonovich, I will, so be it, carry out an exposure. But for that, will you permit one more teeny little number?”
“Why not,” Arkady Apollonovich answered patronizingly, “but there must be an exposure!”
“Very good, very good. And so, allow me to ask you, where were you yesterday evening, Arkady Apollonovich?”
At this inappropriate and even, perhaps, boorish question, Arkady Apollonovich’s face changed, and changed very considerably.
“Yesterday evening Arkady Apollonovich was at a meeting of the Acoustics Commission,” Arkady Apollonovich’s spouse declared very haughtily, “but I do not understand what bearing that has on magic.”

“Oui, madame!” Fagot confirmed. “Naturally, you do not understand. As for the meeting, you are entirely mistaken. Having set off for the said meeting, which, by the way, had not even been scheduled for yesterday, Arkady Apollonovich dismissed his chauffeur outside the building of the Acoustics Commission at Chistye Prudy” (the whole theater went quiet) “and himself took a bus to Yelokhovskaya Street to call on Militsa Andreyevna Pokobatko, an actress of the touring district theater, and spent about four hours visiting her.”
“Oh!” someone exclaimed in anguish in the total silence.
Arkady Apollonovich’s young relative, however, suddenly burst out laughing with a low and terrible laugh.
“It’s all clear!” she exclaimed. “And I suspected it long ago. Now I see why that talentless thing got the part of Louisa!”
And, suddenly swinging back, she struck Arkady Apollonovich on the head with a short, thick lilac umbrella.
But the vile Fagot, who was also Koroviev, shouted:
“There you have it, honored citizens, one of the instances of exposure that Arkady Apollonovich sought so insistently!”
“How dare you, you wretch, touch Arkady Apollonovich?” Arkady Apollonovich’s spouse asked menacingly, rising in the box to her full gigantic height.
A second short surge of satanic laughter seized the young relative.
“If anybody dares to touch him,” she answered, guffawing, “it’s me!”—and for the second time there came the dry crack of the umbrella bouncing off Arkady Apollonovich’s head.
“Police! Take her!” Sempleyarov’s spouse screamed in so terrible a voice that many people’s hearts went cold.
And on top of that the cat sprang out to the footlights and suddenly roared, for the whole theater to hear, in a human voice:
“The séance is over! Maestro! Cut loose with a march!!”

The crazed conductor, without realizing what he was doing, waved his baton, and the orchestra did not begin to play, nor even burst into music, nor even crash into it, but precisely, in the cat’s loathsome expression, cut loose with some incredible march, unlike anything else in its brazenness.
For a moment it seemed as if the barely comprehensible, half-blind but rollicking words of this march had once been heard, under southern stars, in a café chantant:
His Excellency fancied
The birds about the yard,
And pretty girls he chanced on
He took under his guard!!!

Or maybe there were none of these words, but others to the same tune, extremely indecent ones. That is not what matters; what matters is that after all this something like the Babylonian confusion of tongues broke out in the Variety. Police were running to the Sempleyarov box, curious people were climbing onto the barrier, infernal explosions of laughter were heard, furious shouts, drowned by the golden clash of cymbals from the orchestra.

And it could be seen that the stage had suddenly emptied, and that the swindler Fagot, as well as the insolent tomcat Behemoth, had melted into the air and vanished, as the magician in the armchair with the faded upholstery had vanished before them.

chapters.title: 13. The Hero Appears
paragraphs: And so the stranger shook a finger at Ivan and whispered: “Shhh!”

Ivan lowered his legs from the bed and peered. A man of about thirty-eight, clean-shaven, dark-haired, with a sharp nose, anxious eyes and a lock of hair hanging down over his forehead, was cautiously peering into the room from the balcony.

Having made sure that Ivan was alone, and having listened for a while, the mysterious visitor grew bolder and came into the room. Then Ivan saw that the newcomer was dressed in hospital clothes. He had on underwear and slippers on his bare feet, and a brown robe was thrown over his shoulders.
The newcomer winked at Ivan, put a bunch of keys away in his pocket, inquired in a whisper: “May I sit down?”—and, receiving a nod in reply, settled himself in the armchair.
“How did you get in here?” Ivan asked in a whisper, obeying the dry, warning finger. “The balcony grilles are kept locked, aren’t they?”

“The grilles are locked, all right,” the guest confirmed, “but Praskovya Fyodorovna is the dearest person, though, alas, absent-minded. A month ago I pinched a bunch of keys from her and so got the chance to go out onto the common balcony, which runs around the whole floor, and so, now and then, to pay a call on a neighbor.”
“If you can get out onto the balcony, then you can run away. Or is it too high?” Ivan asked with interest.
“No,” the guest answered firmly, “I can’t run away from here, not because it’s high, but because I have nowhere to run to.” And after a pause he added: “So, here we sit?”
“Here we sit,” answered Ivan, peering into the newcomer’s brown and very restless eyes.

“Yes...” Here the guest suddenly grew alarmed. “But I hope you’re not violent? Because, you know, I can’t stand noise, commotion, violence or anything of that kind. Most hateful of all to me is people shouting, whether it’s a cry of suffering, of rage or any other kind of cry. Set my mind at rest, tell me, you’re not violent?”
“Yesterday in a restaurant I socked some type in the mug,” the transformed poet confessed manfully.
“Grounds?” the guest asked sternly.
“Well, to be honest, no grounds,” Ivan answered, embarrassed.

“Disgraceful,” the guest condemned Ivan, and added: “And besides, why do you express yourself like that: ‘socked him in the mug’? After all, it’s not known exactly what a person has, a mug or a face. And, if you think about it, it’s a face after all. So, you know, using your fists... No, you’d better give that up, and for good.”
Having reprimanded Ivan in this way, the guest inquired:
“Profession?”
“Poet,” Ivan admitted, for some reason reluctantly.
The newcomer was upset.
“Oh, what bad luck I have!” he exclaimed, but at once caught himself, apologized and asked: “And what is your name?”
“Bezdomny.”
“Oh dear, oh dear...” said the guest, wincing.
“What, don’t you like my poems?” Ivan asked with curiosity.
“I dislike them terribly.”
“And which ones have you read?”
“I haven’t read any of your poems!” the visitor exclaimed nervously.
“Then how can you say that?”
“Well, what of it,” answered the guest, “as if I hadn’t read the others? However... unless by some miracle? Very well, I’m ready to take it on faith. Are your poems good? You tell me.”
“Monstrous!” Ivan suddenly declared, boldly and frankly.
“Don’t write any more!” the newcomer begged imploringly.
“I promise and I swear!” Ivan pronounced solemnly.
The oath was sealed with a handshake, and just then soft footsteps and voices came from the corridor.
“Shh,” the guest whispered, and, leaping out onto the balcony, closed the grille behind him.

Praskovya Fyodorovna looked in, asked how Ivan was feeling and whether he wished to sleep in the dark or with the light on. Ivan asked for the light to be left on, and Praskovya Fyodorovna withdrew, wishing the patient a good night. And when all was quiet, the guest came back again.

He informed Ivan in a whisper that a new patient had been brought to room 119, some fat man with a purple physiognomy, who kept muttering about some foreign currency in the ventilation and swearing that an unclean force had moved in at their place on Sadovaya.

“He curses Pushkin up hill and down dale and keeps shouting: ‘Kurolesov, encore, encore!’” the guest said, twitching anxiously. Calming down, he sat down again, said: “But anyway, God be with him,” and went on with his conversation with Ivan: “So what was it that landed you here?”
“Pontius Pilate,” Ivan answered, glancing gloomily at the floor.
“What?!” the guest cried, forgetting all caution, and clapped his own hand over his mouth. “What an astounding coincidence! I beg you, I beg you, tell me!”

For some reason feeling trust in the stranger, Ivan, faltering and timid at first, then growing bolder, began to tell the story of the day before at Patriarch’s Ponds. Yes, Ivan Nikolayevich had found a grateful listener in the mysterious thief of keys! The guest did not cast Ivan as a madman; he showed the greatest interest in what he was being told, and, as the story unfolded, he was at last in raptures. Every now and then he interrupted Ivan with exclamations:
“Go on, go on, keep going, I beg you! Only, for the sake of all that’s holy, don’t leave anything out!”

Ivan did not leave anything out, it was easier for him to tell it that way himself, and gradually he got to the moment when Pontius Pilate came out onto the balcony in a white mantle with a blood-red lining.
Then the guest folded his hands as if in prayer and whispered:
“Oh, how I guessed it! Oh, how I guessed it all!”
The listener accompanied the description of Berlioz’s terrible death with an enigmatic remark, and his eyes flashed with malice as he made it:
“I regret only one thing, that it wasn’t the critic Latunsky or the writer Mstislav Lavrovich in this Berlioz’s place.” And he cried out frenziedly, but soundlessly: “Go on!”

The cat paying the conductress amused the guest extraordinarily, and he choked with quiet laughter, watching as Ivan, excited by the success of his narrative, hopped quietly about on his haunches, playing the cat holding the ten-kopeck piece next to its whiskers.
“And so,” Ivan concluded, having told about the incident at Griboyedov’s and grown sad and clouded over, “I ended up here.”
The guest laid a sympathetic hand on the poor poet’s shoulder and said this:

“Unhappy poet! But you yourself, my dear fellow, are to blame for everything. You shouldn’t have behaved so familiarly with him, even rather insolently. And so you’ve paid for it. And you should be thankful that it all cost you comparatively little.”
“But who is he, after all?” Ivan asked, shaking his fists in agitation.
The guest peered at Ivan and answered with a question:
“You won’t get agitated? We are all unreliable people here... There won’t be any calling for the doctor, injections and other fuss?”
“No, no!” Ivan exclaimed. “Tell me who he is!”
“Very well,” the guest answered, and said weightily and distinctly: “Yesterday at Patriarch’s Ponds you met Satan.”
Ivan did not get agitated, as he had promised, but he was all the same most powerfully stunned.
“That can’t be! He doesn’t exist!”

“For pity’s sake! You of all people should be the last to say that. You were, apparently, one of the first to suffer from him. You are sitting, as you yourself understand, in a psychiatric hospital, and yet you keep insisting that he doesn’t exist. Really, it’s strange!”
Thrown off balance, Ivan fell silent.

“As soon as you began describing him,” the guest went on, “I began to guess with whom you had had the pleasure of conversing yesterday. And, really, I am surprised at Berlioz! Now, you, of course, are a virgin soul,” here the guest apologized again, “but he, from what I’ve heard of him, had read at least something! The very first things this professor said dispelled all my doubts. It is impossible not to recognize him, my friend! But then you... you must excuse me again, I’m not mistaken, am I, you are an ignorant man?”
“Indisputably,” agreed the unrecognizable Ivan.
“There you are... why, even the face you described... the different eyes, the eyebrows! Forgive me, but perhaps you have never even heard the opera Faust?”
For some reason Ivan became most dreadfully embarrassed and, his face burning, began muttering something about some trip to a sanatorium in Yalta...

“There you are, there you are... no wonder! But Berlioz, I repeat, astonishes me... He is not only a well-read man but also a very cunning one. Though in his defense I must say that, of course, Woland can throw dust in the eyes of a man even more cunning.”
“What?!” Ivan cried out in his turn.
“Quiet!”
Ivan smacked himself on the forehead with his palm and wheezed:

“I see, I see. He had the letter ‘W’ on his visiting card. Oh-oh-oh, well, there’s a thing!” He was silent for a while in confusion, gazing at the moon floating past beyond the grille, and then he spoke: “So that means he really could have been at Pontius Pilate’s? He was already born back then? And they call me a madman!” Ivan added, pointing indignantly at the door.
A bitter crease appeared by the guest’s lips.

“Let us look the truth in the eye,” and the guest turned his face toward the night luminary racing through a cloud. “You and I are both madmen, there’s no use denying it! You see, he shook you, and you went off your head, since you evidently have the right soil for it. But what you describe really did happen, beyond dispute. Only it is so extraordinary that even Stravinsky, a psychiatrist of genius, did not believe you, of course. Did he examine you?” (Ivan nodded.) “Your companion was at Pilate’s, and at breakfast with Kant, and now he has paid a visit to Moscow.”

“But he’ll get up to the devil knows what here! Somebody has to catch him somehow, don’t they?” The former Ivan, not yet entirely finished off, raised his head in the new Ivan, not altogether confidently, but raised it all the same.

“You’ve already tried, and that’s enough for you,” the guest responded ironically. “I don’t advise others to try either. And as for getting up to things, you may rest assured he will. Ah, ah! But how annoyed I am that it was you who met him and not I! Even though everything in me has burned out and the coals have been covered over with ash, all the same I swear that for that meeting I would give Praskovya Fyodorovna’s bunch of keys, for I have nothing else to give. I am a pauper!”
“But what do you want him for?”
The guest grieved and twitched for a long time, but at last he spoke:

“You see, what a strange story, I am sitting here for the same reason as you, namely because of Pontius Pilate.” Here the guest looked around fearfully and said: “The thing is, a year ago I wrote a novel about Pilate.”
“You’re a writer?” the poet asked with interest.
The guest’s face darkened, and he shook his fist at Ivan; then he said:

“I am a master.” He grew stern and took out of the pocket of his robe a completely greasy black cap with the letter “M” embroidered on it in yellow silk. He put the cap on and showed himself to Ivan both in profile and full face, to prove that he was a master. “She sewed it for me with her own hands,” he added mysteriously.
“And what is your name?”
“I no longer have a name,” the strange guest answered with gloomy contempt. “I renounced it, as I have renounced everything in life in general. Let us forget about it.”
“Then at least tell me about the novel,” Ivan asked delicately.
“If you please, sir. My life, I must say, has not turned out quite in the ordinary way,” the guest began.
...A historian by training, until two years ago he had worked in one of the Moscow museums, and besides that he did translations...
“From what language?” Ivan asked with interest.
“I know five languages besides my own,” answered the guest, “English, French, German, Latin and Greek. Well, and I read a little Italian too.”
“Look at that!” Ivan whispered enviously.
The historian lived a solitary life, having no relatives anywhere and almost no acquaintances in Moscow. And, imagine, one day he won a hundred thousand rubles.

“Picture my amazement,” whispered the guest in the black cap, “when I put my hand into the basket of dirty laundry, and look: it’s the same number as in the newspaper! The bond,” he explained, “they gave me at the museum.”
Having won a hundred thousand, Ivan’s mysterious guest did the following: he bought books, gave up his room on Myasnitskaya...
“Ugh, that cursed hole!” he growled.

...And from a private builder, in a side street near the Arbat, he rented two rooms in the basement of a little house in a little garden. He gave up his job at the museum and began writing a novel about Pontius Pilate.

“Ah, that was a golden age!” the narrator whispered, his eyes shining. “A completely self-contained little apartment, and a hallway besides, and in it a sink with running water,” he stressed, for some reason with particular pride, “little windows right above the little pavement leading from the gate. Opposite, four steps away, by the fence, lilac, a linden and a maple. Ah, ah, ah! In winter I very rarely saw anyone’s black feet in my little window or heard the snow crunching under them. And in my stove a fire was always blazing! But suddenly spring came, and through the dim panes I saw first the bare lilac bushes and then the lilac dressing itself in green. And it was then, last spring, that something happened far more delightful than winning a hundred thousand rubles. And that, you must agree, is an enormous sum of money!”
“That’s true,” Ivan, who was listening attentively, acknowledged.

“I opened the little windows and sat in the second room, quite a tiny one,” the guest began measuring with his hands, “like this: a sofa, and opposite it another sofa, and between them a little table, and on it a beautiful night lamp, and nearer the window, books, and here a little writing desk, and in the first room—an enormous room, fourteen square meters—books, books and the stove. Ah, what a setup I had! The lilac smells extraordinary! And my head would grow light with fatigue, and Pilate was flying to the end...”
“White mantle, red lining! I understand!” Ivan kept exclaiming.

“Precisely! Pilate was flying to the end, to the end, and I already knew that the last words of the novel would be: ‘...the fifth procurator of Judea, the knight Pontius Pilate.’ Well, naturally, I went out for walks. A hundred thousand is an enormous sum, and I had a beautiful suit. Or I would go off to have dinner in some cheap restaurant. There was a wonderful restaurant on the Arbat, I don’t know whether it still exists.”
Here the guest’s eyes opened wide, and he went on whispering, looking at the moon:

“She was carrying repulsive, disturbing yellow flowers in her hands. The devil knows what they’re called, but for some reason they are the first to appear in Moscow. And these flowers stood out very distinctly against her black spring coat. She was carrying yellow flowers! An ugly color. She turned off Tverskaya into a side street and then looked back. Well, you know Tverskaya? Thousands of people were walking along Tverskaya, but I guarantee you that she saw me alone, and looked at me not just anxiously but almost as if in pain. And what struck me was not so much her beauty as the extraordinary loneliness in her eyes, a loneliness no one had ever seen!

“Obeying that yellow sign, I too turned into the side street and followed in her footsteps. We walked along the crooked, dreary side street in silence, I on one side and she on the other. And, imagine, there was not a soul in the street. I was in torment, because it seemed to me that I absolutely had to speak to her, and I was worried that I would not utter a single word, and she would go away, and I would never see her again.
“And, imagine, suddenly she spoke:
“‘Do you like my flowers?’

“I remember distinctly how her voice sounded, rather low, but with catches in it, and, stupid as it is, it seemed to me that an echo struck through the side street and bounced back off the dirty yellow wall. I quickly crossed over to her side and, coming up to her, answered:
“She looked at me in surprise, and suddenly, completely unexpectedly, I understood that all my life I had loved precisely this woman! There’s a thing, eh? You’ll say I’m a madman, of course?”
“I’m not saying anything,” Ivan exclaimed, and added: “I beg you, go on!”
And the guest went on:
“Yes, she looked at me in surprise, and then, having looked, she asked me this:
“‘Don’t you like flowers at all?’
“There was, so it seemed to me, hostility in her voice. I walked beside her, trying to keep in step, and, to my surprise, I did not feel in the least constrained.
“‘No, I do like flowers, only not these,’ I said.
“‘Which ones, then?’
“‘I love roses.’

“Then I was sorry I had said it, because she smiled guiltily and threw her flowers into the gutter. A little at a loss, I picked them up all the same and handed them to her, but she pushed the flowers away with a smirk, and I carried them in my hands.

“So we walked in silence for some time, until she took the flowers out of my hands and threw them onto the roadway, then slipped her hand in its black flared glove through my arm, and we walked on side by side.”
“Go on,” said Ivan, “and please don’t leave anything out!”

“Go on?” the guest asked back. “Well, what came next you could guess yourself.” He suddenly wiped away an unexpected tear with his right sleeve and went on: “Love leaped out in front of us as a murderer leaps out of the ground in a side street, and struck us both at once. That is how lightning strikes, that is how a Finnish knife strikes! She, by the way, insisted afterward that it was not so, that of course we had loved each other long, long before, without knowing each other, without ever having seen each other, and that she had been living with another man... and I, back then... with that, what’s her name...”
“With whom?” asked Bezdomny.
“With that... well... with that... well...” the guest answered, and began snapping his fingers.
“You were married?”
“Well, yes, that’s what I’m snapping about... To that... Varenka... Manechka... no, Varenka... a striped dress, too, the museum... But I don’t remember.

“Well, so, she said that she had gone out that day with yellow flowers in her hands so that I would find her at last, and that if it had not happened, she would have poisoned herself, because her life was empty.
“Yes, love struck us instantly. I knew it that same day, within an hour, when, without noticing the city, we found ourselves on the embankment by the Kremlin wall.

“We talked as though we had parted only yesterday, as though we had known each other for many years. The next day we agreed to meet at the same place, on the Moskva River, and we met. The May sun shone on us. And soon, soon, this woman became my secret wife.

“She came to me every day, and I would begin waiting for her from the morning. This waiting expressed itself in my rearranging the objects on the table. Ten minutes before, I would sit down by the little window and begin listening for the creak of the decrepit gate. And how curious it was: before I met her, few people came into our little yard—to put it simply, nobody came—and now it seemed to me that the whole city was streaming into it. The gate bangs, my heart bangs, and, imagine, at the level of my face, outside the little window, there are invariably somebody’s dirty boots. The knife grinder. Now, who needs a knife grinder in our house? What is there to grind? What knives?

“She came in through the gate once, but before that my heart would pound no fewer than ten times, I’m not lying. And then, when her hour came and the hand showed noon, it would not even stop pounding until, without a knock, almost without a sound, her shoes drew level with the window, shoes with black suede bows fastened with steel buckles.

“Sometimes she would be playful and, stopping at the second little window, tap on the glass with the toe of her shoe. That very second I would be at that window, but the shoe would disappear, the black silk blocking the light would disappear—I would go to let her in.

“Nobody knew about our affair, I guarantee you that, though it never happens that way. Her husband did not know, our acquaintances did not know. In the little old house where that basement belonged to me, they knew, of course, they saw that some woman was coming to see me, but they did not know her name.”
“But who is she?” asked Ivan, extremely interested in the love story.
The guest made a gesture that meant he would never tell anyone that, and went on with his story.

Ivan learned that the master and the unknown woman had fallen in love so deeply that they became completely inseparable. Ivan could already clearly picture the two rooms in the basement of the little house, where there was always twilight because of the lilac and the fence. The shabby red furniture, the bureau with the clock on it that chimed every half hour, and books, books from the painted floor to the sooty ceiling, and the stove.

Ivan learned that his guest and his secret wife, in the very first days of their affair, had come to the conclusion that it was fate itself that had thrown them together on the corner of Tverskaya and the side street, and that they had been created for each other forever.

Ivan learned from the guest’s story how the lovers spent their days. She would come, and first of all put on an apron, and in the narrow hallway, where that very sink was that the poor patient for some reason was so proud of, she would light the kerosene stove on the wooden table, and make breakfast, and lay it out in the first room on the oval table. When the May storms came and water rushed noisily past the half-blind windows into the gateway, threatening to flood their last refuge, the lovers would light the stove and bake potatoes in it. Steam poured from the potatoes, the black potato skins smeared their fingers. Laughter was heard in the little basement; after the rain the trees in the garden shed broken twigs and white clusters.

When the storms ended and the stifling summer came, there appeared in the vase the long-awaited roses that they both loved. The man who called himself the master worked feverishly on his novel, and this novel swallowed up the unknown woman too.
“Really, there were times when I began to be jealous of it,” the night guest who had come from the moonlit balcony whispered to Ivan.

Running her slender fingers with their sharply filed nails into her hair, she reread what had been written endlessly, and, having reread it, she sewed this very cap. Sometimes she squatted by the lower shelves or stood on a chair by the upper ones and wiped the hundreds of dusty spines with a rag. She promised fame, she urged him on, and it was then that she began calling him the master. She waited impatiently for the already promised last words about the fifth procurator of Judea, repeated aloud in a singsong voice particular phrases that she liked, and said that her life was in this novel.

It was finished in the month of August, was given to some obscure typist, and she typed it out in five copies. And at last the hour came when they had to leave their secret refuge and go out into life.

“And I went out into life holding it in my hands, and then my life ended,” the master whispered, and he hung his head, and for a long time the sad black cap with the yellow letter “M” kept nodding. He went on with his story, but it became somewhat incoherent. Only one thing could be understood: that at that time some catastrophe had befallen Ivan’s guest.

“It was my first time in the world of literature, but now, when everything is already over and my ruin is plain to see, I remember it with horror!” the master whispered solemnly, and raised his hand. “Yes, he astounded me extraordinarily, ah, how he astounded me!”
“Who?” Ivan whispered, barely audibly, afraid of interrupting the agitated narrator.

“Why, the editor, I’m telling you, the editor. Yes, so he read it. He looked at me as though my cheek were swollen with a gumboil, kept looking askance into the corner and even giggled in embarrassment. He crumpled the manuscript needlessly and grunted. The questions he asked me seemed insane to me. Saying nothing about the substance of the novel, he asked me who I was and where I had come from, whether I had been writing long, and why nothing had been heard of me before, and he even asked what was, from my point of view, a completely idiotic question: who had put me up to writing a novel on such a strange subject?
“At last I got tired of him, and I asked him point-blank whether he was going to publish the novel or not.

“At this he began to fuss, started mumbling something and declared that he could not decide the question personally, that the other members of the editorial board would have to acquaint themselves with my work, namely the critics Latunsky and Ariman and the writer Mstislav Lavrovich. He asked me to come back in two weeks.
“I came back in two weeks and was received by some girl whose eyes squinted toward her nose from constant lying.”
“That’s Lapshennikova, the editorial secretary,” said Ivan with a smirk; he knew well the world his guest was describing so angrily.

“Maybe,” the latter cut him short. “Well, so, I got my novel back from her, already quite greasy and dog-eared. Trying to keep her eyes from meeting mine, Lapshennikova informed me that the editorial office was supplied with material for two years ahead, and that therefore the question of publishing my novel, as she put it, ‘did not arise.’”
“What do I remember after that?” muttered the master, rubbing his temple. “Yes, red petals fallen on the title page, and also the eyes of my beloved. Yes, those eyes I remember.”

The story of Ivan’s guest was getting more and more muddled, filling up more and more with things left unsaid. He said something about slanting rain and despair in the basement refuge, about going somewhere else as well. He cried out in a whisper that he did not blame her in the least, she who had pushed him into the fight—oh no, he did not blame her!

Further, as Ivan heard, something sudden and strange happened. One day our hero opened a newspaper and saw in it an article by the critic Ariman entitled “An Enemy Sortie,” in which Ariman warned each and every one that he, that is, our hero, had made an attempt to drag into print an apologia for Jesus Christ.
“Ah, I remember, I remember!” cried Ivan. “But I’ve forgotten your name!”

“Let us leave my name alone, I repeat, it no longer exists,” answered the guest. “That isn’t the point. A day later, in another newspaper, another article turned up, signed by Mstislav Lavrovich, in which its author proposed to strike, and strike hard, at Pilatism and at that icon-dauber who had taken it into his head to drag it (that cursed word again!) into print.

“Dumbfounded by this unheard-of word ‘Pilatism,’ I opened a third newspaper. Here there were two articles: one by Latunsky, and the other signed with the letters ‘M. Z.’ I assure you that the works of Ariman and Lavrovich could be considered a joke compared with what Latunsky had written. Suffice it to tell you that Latunsky’s article was entitled ‘A Militant Old Believer.’ I was so absorbed in reading the articles about myself that I did not notice how she (I had forgotten to shut the door) appeared before me with a wet umbrella in her hands and with wet newspapers as well. Her eyes were blazing with fire, her hands were trembling and cold. First she rushed to kiss me, then, in a hoarse voice, banging her hand on the table, she said that she would poison Latunsky.”
Ivan grunted somehow in embarrassment, but said nothing.

“Joyless autumn days set in,” the guest went on. “The monstrous failure with this novel seemed to have taken out a part of my soul. Essentially, I had nothing more to do, and I lived from one meeting with her to the next. And it was at this time that something happened to me. The devil knows what, something Stravinsky has no doubt long since sorted out. Namely, anguish came over me and certain forebodings appeared. The articles, mind you, did not stop. At the first of them I laughed. But the more of them appeared, the more my attitude to them changed. The second stage was the stage of astonishment. Something uncommonly false and unsure could be felt in literally every line of those articles, despite their menacing and confident tone. It kept seeming to me—and I could not get rid of the feeling—that the authors of these articles were not saying what they wanted to say, and that their fury was caused precisely by that. And then, imagine, the third stage set in—the stage of fear. No, not fear of the articles, you understand, but fear of other things that had nothing whatever to do with them or with the novel. For instance, I began to be afraid of the dark. In a word, the stage of mental illness set in. It seemed to me, especially when I was falling asleep, that some very supple and cold octopus was creeping with its tentacles straight and directly toward my heart. And I had to sleep with the light on.

“My beloved changed very much (I did not tell her about the octopus, of course, but she could see that something wrong was happening to me); she grew thin and pale, stopped laughing and kept asking me to forgive her for having advised me to publish an excerpt. She told me to drop everything and go away to the south, to the Black Sea, spending all the money left from the hundred thousand on the trip.

“She was very insistent, and I, so as not to argue (something told me that I would not get to go to the Black Sea), promised her I would do it in the next few days. But she said that she would buy me the ticket herself. Then I took out all my money, that is, about ten thousand rubles, and gave it to her.
“‘Why so much?’ she said in surprise.

“I said something to the effect that I was afraid of thieves and asked her to keep the money for me until my departure. She took it, put it in her handbag, began kissing me and saying that it would be easier for her to die than to leave me alone in such a state, but that she was expected, that she was yielding to necessity, that she would come tomorrow. She begged me not to be afraid of anything.

“That was at dusk, in the middle of October. And she went away. I lay down on the sofa and fell asleep without lighting the lamp. I woke up with the feeling that the octopus was there. Groping in the dark, I barely managed to light the lamp. My pocket watch showed two o’clock in the morning. I had lain down falling ill, and I woke up sick. It suddenly seemed to me that the autumn darkness would squeeze out the windowpanes, pour into the room, and I would choke in it as in ink. I got up a man who was no longer in control of himself. I cried out, and the thought came to me to run to someone, if only to my landlord upstairs. I struggled with myself like a madman. I had strength enough to get to the stove and light the wood in it. When it began to crackle and the stove door rattled, I seemed to feel a little better. I rushed into the hallway and turned on the light there, found a bottle of white wine, uncorked it and began drinking the wine from the bottle. This dulled the fear somewhat—enough, at least, that I did not run to the landlord, and I went back to the stove. I opened the stove door, so that the heat began to scorch my face and hands, and I whispered:
“‘Guess that something terrible has happened to me... Come, come, come!..’

“But no one came. The fire roared in the stove, the rain lashed at the windows. Then the last thing happened. I took out of the desk drawer the heavy copies of the novel and the draft notebooks and began to burn them. It is terribly hard to do, because paper that has been written on burns reluctantly. Breaking my nails, I tore the notebooks apart, stood them upright between the logs, and ruffled the pages with the poker. Every now and then the ash got the better of me, smothering the flames, but I fought it, and the novel, stubbornly resisting, was perishing all the same. Familiar words flashed before me, the yellow crept irresistibly up the pages from the bottom, but the words still showed through even on it. They disappeared only when the paper turned black and I furiously finished them off with the poker.

“At that moment someone began scratching quietly at the window. My heart leaped, and, plunging the last notebook into the fire, I rushed to open the door. Brick steps led up from the basement to the door into the yard. Stumbling, I ran up to it and asked quietly:
“‘Who’s there?’
“And a voice, her voice, answered me:
“‘It’s me...’

“I don’t remember how I managed the chain and the key. As soon as she stepped inside, she pressed herself to me, all wet, with wet cheeks and her hair come loose, trembling. I could utter only a word:

“‘You... you?..’ and my voice broke off, and we ran down the stairs. In the hallway she got out of her coat, and we quickly went into the first room. With a soft cry, she threw out of the stove onto the floor with her bare hands the last thing that remained there, a bundle that had caught fire at the bottom. Smoke filled the room at once. I stamped out the fire with my feet, and she collapsed onto the sofa and wept uncontrollably and convulsively.
“When she had grown calm, I said:
“‘I have come to hate this novel, and I am afraid. I am ill. I am frightened.’
“She stood up and spoke:
“‘God, how ill you are. Why is this, why? But I’ll save you, I’ll save you. What is all this?’
“I saw her eyes swollen from the smoke and from weeping, I felt her cold hands stroking my forehead.
“‘I’ll cure you, I’ll cure you,’ she murmured, digging her fingers into my shoulders, ‘you will restore it. Why, why didn’t I keep one copy at my place!’

“She bared her teeth in fury and said something else, indistinctly. Then, pressing her lips together, she set about gathering up and smoothing out the charred pages. It was some chapter from the middle of the novel, I don’t remember which. She carefully put the sheets together, wrapped them in paper and tied them with a ribbon. All her actions showed that she was full of resolve and had taken herself in hand. She asked for wine and, having drunk it, spoke more calmly.

“‘This is how one has to pay for lying,’ she said, ‘and I don’t want to lie anymore. I would stay with you even now, but I don’t want to do it this way. I don’t want him to be left forever with the memory that I ran away from him in the night. He has never done me any harm... He was called away suddenly, there’s a fire at their factory. But he’ll be back soon. I’ll have it out with him tomorrow morning, tell him that I love another, and come back to you forever. Answer me, perhaps you don’t want that?’
“‘My poor one, my poor one,’ I said to her, ‘I won’t let you do it. Things will go badly with me, and I don’t want you to perish along with me.’
“‘Is that the only reason?’ she asked, and brought her eyes close to mine.
“‘The only one.’
“She became terribly animated, pressed herself to me, winding her arms around my neck, and said:
“‘I am perishing along with you. In the morning I will be with you.’

“And so, the last thing I remember in my life is a strip of light from my hallway, and in that strip of light a loose strand of hair, her beret and her eyes full of resolve. I also remember a black silhouette on the threshold of the outer door, and a white bundle.
“‘I would see you home, but I no longer have the strength to come back alone, I’m afraid.’
“‘Don’t be afraid. Bear it for a few hours. Tomorrow morning I will be with you.’
“Those were her last words in my life... Shhh!” the patient suddenly interrupted himself and raised a finger. “It’s a restless moonlit night tonight.”
He disappeared onto the balcony. Ivan heard little wheels rolling along the corridor; someone sobbed or cried out faintly.

When everything had quieted down, the guest came back and reported that room 120 had also received an occupant. Someone had been brought in, and he kept begging to have his head given back to him. The two companions were silent for a while in alarm, but, having calmed down, they returned to the interrupted story. The guest opened his mouth, but the night was indeed a restless one. Voices could still be heard in the corridor, and the guest began speaking into Ivan’s ear so quietly that what he told became known to the poet alone, except for the first sentence:
“A quarter of an hour after she left me, there came a knock at my window...”

What the patient was whispering into Ivan’s ear evidently agitated him very much. Spasms kept passing across his face. Fear and fury swam and darted in his eyes. The narrator kept pointing somewhere in the direction of the moon, which had long since left the balcony. Only when all sounds from outside had ceased to reach them did the guest move away from Ivan and begin speaking a little louder:

“Yes, so, in the middle of January, at night, in the same coat but with the buttons torn off, I was huddling from the cold in my little yard. Behind me were snowdrifts that had buried the lilac bushes, and in front of me and below, my little windows, faintly lit, with the blinds drawn. I pressed myself to the first of them and listened—a gramophone was playing in my rooms. That was all I could make out, but I could see nothing. After standing there a little, I went out through the gate into the side street. A blizzard was playing in it. A dog that darted under my feet frightened me, and I ran away from it to the other side of the street. The cold, and the fear that had become my constant companion, were driving me to frenzy. I had nowhere to go, and the simplest thing, of course, would have been to throw myself under a tram on the street that my side street ran into. From a distance I could see those light-filled, iced-over boxes and hear their loathsome grinding in the frost. But, my dear neighbor, the whole point was that fear possessed every little cell of my body. And just as I feared the dog, I feared the tram as well. Yes, there is no illness in this building worse than mine, I assure you.”
“But you could have let her know,” said Ivan, sympathizing with the poor patient. “Besides, she has your money, doesn’t she? She’s kept it, of course?”

“Don’t doubt it, of course she has kept it. But you evidently do not understand me. Or, rather, I have lost the ability I once had to describe anything. I don’t much regret it, though, since I will not need it anymore. Before her,” the guest gazed reverently into the darkness of the night, “there would lie a letter from a madhouse. Can one really send letters with an address like that? A mental patient? You are joking, my friend! Make her unhappy? No, I am not capable of that.”

Ivan could not find an objection to this, but the silent Ivan sympathized with his guest, felt compassion for him. And the guest kept nodding his head in its black cap from the torment of his memories, and said this:
“Poor woman... However, I have hope that she has forgotten me...”
“But you could get better...” Ivan said timidly.

“I am incurable,” the guest answered calmly. “When Stravinsky says he will bring me back to life, I don’t believe him. He is humane and simply wants to console me. I don’t deny, though, that I am much better now. Yes, so where was I? The frost, those flying trams... I knew that this clinic had already opened, and I set off for it on foot right across the city. Madness! Outside the city I would probably have frozen to death, but chance saved me. Something had broken down in a truck, I went up to the driver—this was about four kilometers beyond the city gate—and, to my surprise, he took pity on me. The truck was coming here. And he drove me. I got off with frostbitten toes on my left foot. But they cured that. And now this is my fourth month here. And, you know, I find that it is very, very nice here. One mustn’t set oneself grand plans, dear neighbor, truly! I, for instance, wanted to travel all around the globe. Well, it turns out that isn’t to be. I see only an insignificant piece of that globe. I think it isn’t the best thing there is on it, but, I repeat, it isn’t so bad. Summer is coming to us now, ivy will twine on the balcony, so Praskovya Fyodorovna promises. The keys have widened my possibilities. At night there will be the moon. Ah, it has gone! It’s growing cool. The night is tipping past midnight. It’s time for me to go.”
“Tell me, what happened next with Yeshua and Pilate,” Ivan begged. “I implore you, I want to know.”

“Ah, no, no,” the guest answered, twitching painfully. “I cannot remember my novel without shuddering. And your acquaintance from Patriarch’s would have done it better than I could. Thank you for the conversation. Goodbye.”
And before Ivan could collect himself, the grille closed with a soft clink, and the guest was gone.

chapters.title: 14. Glory to the Rooster!
paragraphs: His nerves gave out, as they say, and Rimsky did not wait for the report to be finished but fled to his office. He sat at his desk, staring with inflamed eyes at the magic ten-rouble notes lying in front of him. The financial director’s mind was reeling. Outside, a steady roar rolled on. The audience was pouring out of the Variety building into the street in streams. Suddenly the financial director’s extraordinarily sharpened hearing caught the distinct trill of a police whistle. In itself that sound never promises anything pleasant. And when it was repeated, and a second whistle, more commanding and more prolonged, came to its aid, and then a clearly audible guffawing joined in, and even some sort of hooting and whooping, the financial director understood at once that something else scandalous and nasty had happened in the street. And that this, however much one might like to wave it away, was most intimately connected with the disgusting performance given by the black magician and his assistants. The sensitive financial director was not in the least mistaken.
The moment he glanced out of the window that looked onto Sadovaya, his face twisted, and he did not whisper but hissed:
“I knew it!”

In the bright light of the powerful street lamps he saw on the pavement below him a lady wearing nothing but a slip and a pair of violet knickers. True, the lady had a little hat on her head and an umbrella in her hands.

Around this lady, who was in a state of utter confusion, now crouching down, now making as if to run off somewhere, a crowd surged, giving off that very laughter which sent a chill down the financial director’s spine. Next to the lady some citizen was rushing about, tearing off his summer coat and, in his agitation, quite unable to manage the sleeve, in which his arm had got stuck.

Shouts and roaring laughter came from another spot as well—namely from the left entrance—and, turning his head that way, Grigory Danilovich saw a second lady, in pink underwear. She leapt from the roadway onto the pavement, trying to hide in the doorway, but the audience streaming out blocked her way, and the poor victim of her own frivolity and passion for clothes, deceived by the firm of the vile Fagot, dreamed of only one thing—of sinking through the earth. A policeman was rushing toward the unfortunate woman, drilling the air with his whistle, and behind the policeman hurried some exceedingly merry young men in caps. It was they who were giving off that very laughter and hooting.
A thin, moustached cabby flew up to the first undressed lady and reined in his bony, broken-down horse with a flourish. The moustached man’s face was grinning with joy.
Rimsky struck himself on the head with his fist, spat, and sprang back from the window.

He sat at the desk for some time, listening to the street. The whistling at various points reached its height and then began to die down. The scandal, to Rimsky’s surprise, was somehow cleared up unexpectedly quickly.

The time had come to act; he would have to drink the bitter cup of responsibility. The telephones had been repaired during the third part of the show; he would have to call, report what had happened, ask for help, lie his way out, blame everything on Likhodeyev, shield himself, and so on. Pah, the devil!

Twice the upset director put his hand on the receiver, and twice he took it away again. And suddenly, in the dead silence of the office, the telephone itself burst out ringing right in the financial director’s face, and he started and went cold. “My nerves are in a fine state, though,” he thought, and picked up the receiver. At once he recoiled from it and turned whiter than paper. A quiet, at the same time insinuating and depraved woman’s voice whispered into the receiver:
“Don’t call anyone, Rimsky, or it will go badly...”

The line instantly went empty. Feeling goose bumps crawl down his back, the financial director put down the receiver and for some reason looked round at the window behind him. Through the sparse branches of the maple, still only faintly covered in green, he saw the moon racing through a transparent little cloud. For some reason his eyes fastened on the branches, and Rimsky looked at them, and the longer he looked, the more and more strongly fear took hold of him.

With an effort, the financial director at last turned away from the moonlit window and stood up. There could no longer be any question of telephoning, and now the financial director thought of only one thing—how to get out of the theatre as quickly as possible.

He listened: the theatre building was silent. Rimsky realized that he had long been alone on the whole second floor, and at this thought a childish, irresistible fear seized him.
