“Ah, good.” Woland turned to Margarita: “And so, I ask you... I thank you in advance. Do not lose your head and do not be afraid of anything. Drink nothing but water, or you will grow languid and find it hard. It is time!”
Margarita rose from the rug, and at that moment Koroviev appeared in the doorway.

chapters.title: 23. Satan’s Great Ball
paragraphs: Midnight was approaching; they had to hurry. Margarita saw her surroundings only dimly. What stayed with her were candles and a pool of some sort, set with gems. When Margarita stood on the bottom of this pool, Hella, with Natasha helping her, doused Margarita with some hot, thick, red liquid. Margarita felt a salty taste on her lips and understood that she was being washed in blood. The bloody mantle gave way to another—thick, transparent, pinkish—and Margarita’s head swam from the rose oil. Then Margarita was thrown onto a crystal couch and rubbed with some large green leaves until she shone. At this point the cat burst in and began to help. He squatted at Margarita’s feet and set about rubbing her soles with the air of a man shining boots in the street.

Margarita does not remember who made her slippers out of pale rose petals, or how those slippers fastened themselves with golden buckles. Some force jerked Margarita upright and set her in front of a mirror, and a royal diamond crown glittered in her hair. Koroviev appeared from somewhere and hung on Margarita’s breast a heavy oval-framed image of a black poodle on a heavy chain. This ornament burdened the queen exceedingly. The chain at once began to chafe her neck, and the image kept pulling her to stoop. But something made up to Margarita for the discomfort the chain with the black poodle caused her. This was the deference with which Koroviev and Behemoth now began to treat her.

“Never mind, never mind, never mind!” Koroviev muttered at the door of the room with the pool. “It can’t be helped, it must be done, it must, it must... Allow me, Queen, to give you one last piece of advice. Among the guests there will be all sorts, oh, all sorts indeed, but no one, Queen Margot, is to be shown the least preference! If there is someone you do not like... I understand that of course you will not let it show on your face... No, no, you mustn’t even think it! He’ll notice, he’ll notice that very instant! You must love him, love him, Queen! The hostess of the ball will be repaid a hundredfold for it. And another thing: don’t miss anyone out! At least a little smile, if there’s no time to toss a word, at least the tiniest turn of the head. Anything you like, only not inattention. That makes them waste away...”
Here Margarita, accompanied by Koroviev and Behemoth, stepped out of the pool room into total darkness.
“Me, me,” whispered the cat, “I’ll give the signal!”
“Go ahead!” Koroviev answered in the darkness.

“The ball!” the cat shrieked piercingly, and at once Margarita cried out and shut her eyes for several seconds. The ball fell upon her all at once in the form of light, and with it sound and smell. Swept along on Koroviev’s arm, Margarita found herself in a tropical forest. Red-breasted, green-tailed parrots clung to lianas, hopped along them and screamed deafeningly: “I’m enchanted!” But the forest soon came to an end, and its bathhouse stuffiness gave way at once to the coolness of a ballroom with columns of some yellowish, sparkling stone. This hall, like the forest, was completely empty, and only by the columns stood naked Black men, motionless, with silver bands around their heads. Their faces turned a muddy brown with excitement when Margarita flew into the hall with her retinue, in which Azazello had turned up from somewhere. Here Koroviev let go of Margarita’s arm and whispered:
“Straight at the tulips!”

A low wall of white tulips rose up before Margarita, and beyond it she saw countless lamps under little shades and, in front of them, the white chests and black shoulders of men in tailcoats. Then Margarita understood where the sound of the ball was coming from. The roar of trumpets crashed down on her, and the soaring of violins that burst out from under it drenched her body as if with blood. An orchestra of some hundred and fifty men was playing a polonaise.

The man in a tailcoat who towered in front of the orchestra turned pale when he saw Margarita, broke into smiles, and suddenly, with a sweep of his arms, brought the whole orchestra to its feet. Without breaking off the music for a moment, the orchestra, standing, drenched Margarita in sound. The man above the orchestra turned away from it and bowed low, flinging his arms wide, and Margarita, smiling, waved to him.
“No, not enough, not enough,” Koroviev began to whisper, “he won’t sleep all night. Shout to him: ‘I salute you, king of the waltz!’”

Margarita shouted it and marveled that her voice, full as a bell, rose above the howl of the orchestra. The man started with happiness and laid his left hand on his heart, while with his right he went on waving his white baton at the orchestra.

“Not enough, not enough,” whispered Koroviev. “Look to the left, at the first violins, and nod so that each one thinks you have recognized him personally. There are only world celebrities here. This one, at the first desk—that’s Vieuxtemps. That’s it, very good. Now—on we go!”
“Who is the conductor?” Margarita asked as she flew off.

“Johann Strauss!” cried the cat. “And may they hang me from a liana in the tropical forest if any orchestra like this has ever played at any ball! I invited them! And, mark you, not one fell ill and not one refused.”

In the next hall there were no columns; instead, on one side, there stood walls of red, pink and milk-white roses, and on the other a wall of Japanese double camellias. Between these walls fountains were already spurting and hissing, and champagne seethed with bubbles in three pools, of which the first was a transparent violet, the second ruby, the third crystal. Black men in scarlet headbands dashed about beside them, filling shallow cups from the pools with silver ladles. There turned out to be a gap in the wall of roses, and in it, on a bandstand, a man in a red swallow-tailed coat was working himself into a lather. In front of him a jazz band thundered unbearably loud. As soon as the conductor saw Margarita, he bent so low before her that his hands touched the floor, then straightened up and cried piercingly:
“Hallelujah!”
He slapped himself on one knee—one, then crosswise on the other—two, snatched a cymbal from the hands of the musician at the end of the row, and struck it against a column.

As she flew away, Margarita saw only that the jazz-band virtuoso, battling the polonaise that was blowing at Margarita’s back, was beating his bandsmen over the head with the cymbal, and they were cowering in comic terror.

At last they flew out onto the landing where, as Margarita realized, Koroviev had met her in the darkness with his little lamp. Now the eye was blinded on this landing by the light pouring from crystal clusters of grapes. Margarita was set in her place, and under her left hand she found a low amethyst pillar.
“You can rest your hand on it if it gets very hard,” Koroviev whispered.
Some black-skinned man tossed a cushion under Margarita’s feet with a golden poodle embroidered on it, and on it, obeying someone’s hands, she placed her right foot, bending her knee.

Margarita tried to look around. Koroviev and Azazello stood beside her in ceremonial poses. Next to Azazello were three more young men, who somehow vaguely reminded Margarita of Abadonna. A cold breath blew on her back. Looking around, Margarita saw that hissing wine was gushing from the marble wall behind her and running down into an icy pool. At her left foot she felt something warm and furry. It was Behemoth.

Margarita was high up, and from under her feet a grandiose carpeted staircase went down. Below, so far off that it was as though Margarita were looking through the wrong end of a pair of binoculars, she saw an enormous entrance hall with an absolutely immense fireplace, into whose cold black maw a five-ton truck could easily have driven. The entrance hall and the staircase, flooded with light until it hurt the eyes, were empty. The trumpets now reached Margarita from far away. They stood like this, motionless, for about a minute.
“But where are the guests?” Margarita asked Koroviev.
“They’ll come, Queen, they’ll come, they’ll come any moment. There’ll be no shortage of them. And honestly, I’d rather chop wood than receive them here on the landing.”
“Chop wood, that’s nothing,” the talkative cat chimed in, “I’d rather work as a tram conductor, and there’s no worse job than that in the whole world!”

“Everything must be ready in advance, Queen,” Koroviev explained, his eye glinting through his broken monocle. “Nothing could be nastier than when the first guest to arrive drifts about, not knowing what to do with himself, while his lawful shrew nags him in a whisper for arriving before everyone else. Balls like that belong on the rubbish heap, Queen.”
“Definitely on the rubbish heap,” the cat confirmed.
“No more than ten seconds to midnight,” Koroviev added. “It’s about to begin.”

Those ten seconds seemed extraordinarily long to Margarita. Apparently they had already run out, and absolutely nothing had happened. But then suddenly something crashed down below in the huge fireplace, and out of it leapt a gallows with half-crumbled remains dangling from it. These remains broke loose from the rope, struck the floor, and out of them sprang a handsome dark-haired man in a tailcoat and patent-leather shoes. A small, half-rotted coffin came running out of the fireplace, its lid flew off, and out of it tumbled another set of remains. The handsome man gallantly leapt up to them and offered his crooked arm; the second remains assembled themselves into a naked, fidgety woman in black slippers with black feathers on her head, and then both of them, the man and the woman, hurried up the stairs.

“The first!” exclaimed Koroviev. “Monsieur Jacques and his wife. I commend to you, Queen, one of the most interesting of men. A confirmed counterfeiter, a traitor to the state, but a very decent alchemist. He became famous,” Koroviev whispered in Margarita’s ear, “for poisoning a king’s mistress. And that doesn’t happen to just anyone! Look how handsome he is!”
Margarita, turning pale, her mouth open, gazed down and watched the gallows and the coffin vanish into some side passage of the entrance hall.
“I’m enchanted!” the cat bawled right into the face of Monsieur Jacques as he came up the stairs.
At that moment, down below, a headless skeleton with a torn-off arm appeared out of the fireplace, struck the ground and turned into a man in a tailcoat.
Monsieur Jacques’s wife was already going down on one knee before Margarita and, pale with excitement, kissing Margarita’s knee.
“Queen...” murmured Monsieur Jacques’s wife.
“The queen is enchanted!” cried Koroviev.
“Queen...” the handsome man, Monsieur Jacques, said quietly.
“We are enchanted,” howled the cat.

The young men, Azazello’s companions, smiling lifeless but welcoming smiles, were already edging Monsieur Jacques and his wife aside, toward the cups of champagne the Black men held in their hands. A lone man in a tailcoat came running up the stairs.
“Count Robert,” Koroviev whispered to Margarita, “as interesting as ever. Notice how funny it is, Queen—the reverse case: this one was a queen’s lover and poisoned his wife.”
“We are glad, Count,” cried Behemoth.

Out of the fireplace, one after another, tumbled three coffins, bursting and falling apart, then someone in a black mantle, who was stabbed in the back by the next figure to run out of the black maw. A stifled cry was heard below. A corpse, almost entirely decomposed, came running out of the fireplace. Margarita squeezed her eyes shut, and someone’s hand held a flask of white smelling salts to her nose. Margarita thought it was Natasha’s hand. The staircase began to fill. Now on every step there were men in tailcoats, who looked from a distance completely identical, and naked women with them, who differed from one another only in the color of the feathers on their heads and of their slippers.
Approaching Margarita, hobbling in a strange wooden boot on her left foot, came a lady with eyes cast down like a nun’s, thin, modest, and for some reason with a wide green band around her neck.
“Who is the green one?” Margarita asked mechanically.

“A most charming and most respectable lady,” whispered Koroviev. “I commend her to you: Madame Tofana. She was exceedingly popular among the charming young women of Naples, and of Palermo too, especially among those who had grown tired of their husbands. It does happen, after all, Queen, that a woman grows tired of her husband...”
“Yes,” Margarita answered dully, at the same time smiling at two men in tailcoats who bowed before her one after the other, kissing her knee and her hand.

“Well, there you are,” Koroviev contrived to whisper to Margarita, while at the same time shouting to someone: “Duke! A glass of champagne! I’m enchanted!.. Yes, so, if you please, Madame Tofana entered into the situation of these poor women and sold them a sort of water in little vials. The wife poured this water into her husband’s soup, he ate it, thanked her for her tenderness and felt splendid. True, a few hours later he began to feel very thirsty, then he lay down in bed, and a day later the lovely Neapolitan who had fed her husband the soup was as free as the spring wind.”

“And what is that on her foot?” asked Margarita, never tiring of giving her hand to the guests who had overtaken the hobbling Madame Tofana. “And why that green thing around her neck? Is her neck faded?”

“I’m enchanted, Prince!” Koroviev shouted, and at the same moment whispered to Margarita: “A beautiful neck, but something unpleasant happened to it in prison. On her foot, Queen, is a Spanish boot, and the ribbon is there for this reason: when the jailers learned that some five hundred ill-chosen husbands had left Naples and Palermo for good, in the heat of the moment they strangled Madame Tofana in prison.”

“How happy I am, black queen, that the high honor has fallen to me,” Tofana whispered like a nun, trying to go down on one knee. The Spanish boot got in her way. Koroviev and Behemoth helped Tofana up.
“I am glad,” Margarita answered her, at the same time giving her hand to others.

Now a torrent was flowing up the stairs from below. Margarita no longer saw what was going on in the entrance hall. She raised and lowered her hand mechanically and smiled at the guests, baring her teeth in the same grin each time. The air on the landing was already full of a hum, and from the ballrooms Margarita had left came music, like the sea.

“Now this one is a tedious woman,” said Koroviev, no longer whispering but speaking aloud, since he knew that in the hum of voices he would no longer be heard. “She adores balls, she keeps dreaming of complaining about her handkerchief.”

Among those coming up, Margarita’s eye caught the one Koroviev was pointing to. It was a young woman of about twenty, with a figure of extraordinary beauty, but with somehow restless and importunate eyes.
“What handkerchief?” asked Margarita.

“A chambermaid has been assigned to her,” Koroviev explained, “and for thirty years she has been putting a handkerchief on her night table every night. The moment she wakes, the handkerchief is already there. She has burned it in the stove, she has drowned it in the river, but nothing helps.”
“What handkerchief?” whispered Margarita, raising and lowering her hand.

“A handkerchief with a little blue border. The thing is, when she worked in a café, the owner called her into the storeroom one day, and nine months later she gave birth to a boy, carried him off into the woods, stuffed the handkerchief into his mouth and then buried the boy in the ground. At the trial she said she had nothing to feed the child with.”
“And where is the owner of the café?” asked Margarita.
“Queen,” the cat suddenly creaked from below, “allow me to ask you: what has the owner got to do with it? He didn’t smother the infant in the woods, did he!”
Without ceasing to smile and to wave her right hand, Margarita dug the sharp nails of her left into Behemoth’s ear and whispered to him:
“If you, you scum, ever take it upon yourself to butt into the conversation again...”
Behemoth let out a squeak not at all suited to a ball and wheezed:

“Queen... the ear will swell... Why spoil the ball with a swollen ear?.. I was speaking legally... from the legal point... I’m silent, I’m silent... Consider me not a cat but a fish, only let go of my ear.”
Margarita let go of the ear, and the importunate, gloomy eyes were before her.
“I am happy, Queen and hostess, to be invited to the great ball of the full moon.”
“And I,” Margarita answered her, “am glad to see you. Very glad. Do you like champagne?”
“What are you doing, Queen?!” Koroviev cried into Margarita’s ear, desperately but soundlessly. “There’ll be a jam!”
“I do,” the woman said imploringly, and suddenly began to repeat mechanically: “Frieda, Frieda, Frieda! My name is Frieda, oh Queen!”
“Then get drunk tonight, Frieda, and don’t think about anything,” said Margarita.
Frieda held out both hands to Margarita, but Koroviev and Behemoth very deftly took her by the arms, and she was swallowed up in the crowd.

Now people were coming up from below in a solid wall, as though storming the landing where Margarita stood. Naked women’s bodies rose between the men in tailcoats. Their bodies came floating toward Margarita, swarthy and white and the color of coffee beans and altogether black. In hair that was red, black, chestnut, fair as flax, precious stones played and danced and scattered sparks in the downpour of light. And as though someone had sprinkled the storming column of men with droplets of light, diamond studs spattered light from their shirtfronts. Now every second Margarita felt the touch of lips on her knee, every second she held out her hand to be kissed, and her face had set into a fixed mask of welcome.
“I’m enchanted,” Koroviev chanted monotonously, “we are enchanted... The queen is enchanted...”
“The queen is enchanted...” Azazello twanged behind her back.
“I’m enchanted,” the cat kept crying out.

“A marquise...” Koroviev muttered, “poisoned her father, two brothers and two sisters for an inheritance... The queen is enchanted!.. Madame Minkina... Ah, how lovely! A little highly strung. But why burn the maid’s face with curling tongs? Of course, under those conditions they’ll knife you... The queen is enchanted!.. Queen, a second of your attention! The Emperor Rudolf, sorcerer and alchemist... Another alchemist—hanged... Ah, and here she is! Ah, what a wonderful brothel she kept in Strasbourg!.. We are enchanted!.. A Moscow dressmaker, we all love her for her inexhaustible imagination... she kept a fashion salon and thought up a terribly funny trick: she drilled two little round holes in the wall...”
“And the ladies didn’t know?” asked Margarita.

“Every last one of them knew, Queen,” Koroviev replied. “I’m enchanted!.. This twenty-year-old lad was known from childhood for his strange fancies, a dreamer and an oddball. A girl fell in love with him, and he went and sold her to a brothel...”

From below flowed a river. There was no end of this river in sight. Its source, the huge fireplace, went on feeding it. In this way one hour passed, and a second hour began. Here Margarita began to notice that her chain had grown heavier than it had been. Something strange had happened to her arm too. Now, before raising it, Margarita had to wince. Koroviev’s interesting remarks no longer held Margarita’s attention. The slanting Mongol faces, the white faces and the black all became a matter of indifference to her, at times they merged together, and the air between them for some reason began to quiver and stream. A sharp pain, as if from a needle, suddenly shot through Margarita’s right arm, and, clenching her teeth, she rested her elbow on the pillar. A rustling, as if of wings along the walls, now came from the hall behind her, and it was clear that unheard-of hordes of guests were dancing there, and it seemed to Margarita that even the massive marble, mosaic and crystal floors of that marvelous hall were pulsing rhythmically.

Neither Gaius Caesar Caligula nor Messalina interested Margarita any longer, just as none of the kings, dukes, cavaliers, suicides, poisoners, gallows-birds and procuresses, jailers and cardsharps, executioners, informers, traitors, madmen, sleuths and corrupters interested her. All their names were jumbled in her head, the faces were stuck together into one enormous flat cake, and only one face sat tormentingly in her memory, a face framed by a beard that was truly fiery, the face of Malyuta Skuratov. Margarita’s legs were giving way; every minute she was afraid she would burst into tears. The worst suffering was caused by her right knee, the one being kissed. It had swollen, and the skin on it had turned blue, even though Natasha’s hand had appeared several times beside that knee with a sponge and wiped it with something fragrant. At the end of the third hour Margarita glanced down with utterly hopeless eyes and gave a joyful start: the stream of guests was thinning.

“The laws of arrival at a ball never change, Queen,” Koroviev whispered. “Now the wave will start to ebb. I swear these are the last minutes we have to endure. There’s a group of revelers from the Brocken. They always arrive last. Yes, that’s them. Two drunken vampires... is that all? Ah no, here’s one more. No, two!”
The last two guests were coming up the stairs.

“Why, this is someone new,” said Koroviev, squinting through his eyeglass. “Ah yes, yes. Azazello paid him a visit once and, over a brandy, whispered him a piece of advice on how to get rid of a certain man whose revelations he was terribly afraid of. And so he ordered an acquaintance of his, who depended on him, to spray the walls of the office with poison.”
“What is his name?” asked Margarita.
“Well, honestly, I don’t know myself yet,” Koroviev answered. “I’ll have to ask Azazello.”
“And who is with him?”
“Why, that’s this same most efficient subordinate of his. I’m enchanted!” Koroviev shouted to the last two.
The staircase emptied. Out of caution they waited a little longer. But no one else came out of the fireplace.

A second later, not understanding how it had happened, Margarita found herself in the same room with the pool, and there, bursting at once into tears from the pain in her arm and leg, she collapsed straight onto the floor. But Hella and Natasha, comforting her, again drew her under the shower of blood, again kneaded her body, and Margarita came back to life once more.
“More, more, Queen Margot,” whispered Koroviev, who had appeared beside her. “We must fly round the halls, so that the honored guests don’t feel abandoned.”

And Margarita flew out of the room with the pool again. On the bandstand behind the tulips, where the orchestra of the king of the waltz had played, an ape jazz band was now raging. A huge gorilla with shaggy side-whiskers, a trumpet in its hand, was conducting, stamping heavily in time. Orangutans sat in a row, blowing gleaming trumpets. On their shoulders, riding astride, perched merry chimpanzees with accordions. Two hamadryas baboons with manes like lions’ played grand pianos, and these pianos could not be heard in the thunder and squeal and boom of the saxophones, violins and drums in the paws of gibbons, mandrills and monkeys. On the mirror-like floor countless couples, as if fused together, amazing the eye with the deftness and precision of their movements, all whirling in one direction, moved like a wall, threatening to sweep away everything in their path. Live satin butterflies dived above the dancing hordes, flowers showered down from the ceilings. In the capitals of the columns, whenever the electricity went out, myriads of fireflies lit up, and will-o’-the-wisps floated in the air.

Then Margarita found herself at a pool of monstrous size, bordered by a colonnade. A gigantic black Neptune spewed a broad pink stream from his mouth. An intoxicating smell of champagne rose from the pool. Here unconstrained merriment reigned. The ladies, laughing, kicked off their slippers, handed their bags to their cavaliers or to the Black men running about with sheets in their hands, and with shrieks dived into the pool like swallows. Columns of foam were flung upward. The crystal bottom of the pool glowed with a light from below that pierced the depth of the wine, and silvery swimming bodies could be seen in it. People climbed out of the pool completely drunk. Laughter rang out under the columns and boomed as in a bathhouse.
In all this commotion one woman’s face stayed in her memory, utterly drunk, with senseless eyes that even in their senselessness were pleading, and one word came back to her: “Frieda”!

Margarita’s head began to spin from the smell of wine, and she was about to leave when the cat put on a turn in the pool that held Margarita back. Behemoth worked some sort of spell at Neptune’s mouth, and at once, with a hiss and a roar, the heaving mass of champagne drained out of the pool, and Neptune began to disgorge a wave of dark yellow color that neither sparkled nor foamed. The ladies, squealing and wailing:

“Cognac!” rushed away from the edges of the pool and behind the columns. In a few seconds the pool was full, and the cat, turning three somersaults in the air, crashed down into the swaying cognac. He climbed out snorting, his tie soggy, having lost the gilt from his whiskers and his opera glasses. Only one woman ventured to follow Behemoth’s example, that very same inventive dressmaker, together with her cavalier, an unknown young mulatto. They both dived into the cognac, but at that point Koroviev took Margarita by the arm and they left the bathers.

It seemed to Margarita that she flew past somewhere where she saw mountains of oysters in huge stone ponds. Then she flew over a glass floor with hellish furnaces blazing beneath it and diabolical white cooks dashing about among them. Then somewhere, by now ceasing to take anything in, she saw dark cellars where lamps of some kind were burning, where girls served meat sizzling on red-hot coals, where people drank her health from big mugs. Then she saw polar bears playing accordions and dancing the Kamarinskaya on a stage. A salamander conjurer who did not burn up in the fireplace... And for the second time her strength began to fail.
“One last appearance,” Koroviev whispered to her anxiously, “and we are free.”

Accompanied by Koroviev, she found herself in the ballroom again, but now there was no dancing in it, and the guests were crowding in a countless throng between the columns, leaving the middle of the hall free. Margarita did not remember who helped her up onto the dais that had appeared in the middle of this free space in the hall. When she had climbed onto it, she heard to her surprise a clock striking midnight somewhere, though by her reckoning midnight had long, long since passed. With the last stroke of the clock, which seemed to come from nowhere in particular, silence fell over the crowds of guests.

Then Margarita saw Woland again. He was walking surrounded by Abadonna, Azazello and several others like Abadonna, black and young. Margarita now saw that opposite her dais another dais had been prepared for Woland. But he did not make use of it. What struck Margarita was that Woland had come out for this last great appearance at the ball in exactly the same state he had been in in the bedroom. The same dirty, patched nightshirt hung from his shoulders, and his feet were in worn-down bedroom slippers. Woland had his sword, but he was using this naked sword as a cane, leaning on it.

Limping slightly, Woland stopped by his dais, and at once Azazello was in front of him with a platter in his hands, and on this platter Margarita saw a man’s severed head with the front teeth knocked out. The most complete silence still reigned, and it was broken only once by a doorbell, heard far away and incomprehensible in these circumstances, the kind that rings at a front entrance.

“Mikhail Alexandrovich,” Woland addressed the head quietly, and then the dead man’s eyelids lifted, and in the dead face Margarita, shuddering, saw living eyes, full of thought and suffering. “Everything came true, didn’t it?” Woland went on, looking into the head’s eyes. “The head was cut off by a woman, the meeting did not take place, and I am living in your apartment. That is a fact. And a fact is the most stubborn thing in the world. But now what interests us is what comes next, not this fact, which is already accomplished. You were always an ardent preacher of the theory that once a man’s head is cut off, life in him ceases, he turns to ashes and passes into nonexistence. I am pleased to inform you, in the presence of my guests, although they serve as proof of an entirely different theory, that your theory is both sound and clever. However, all theories are worth one another. Among them there is also one according to which each shall be given according to his faith. So let it come true! You pass into nonexistence, and it will be a joy to me to drink to existence from the cup that you are turning into!”

Woland raised his sword. At once the coverings of the head darkened and shriveled, then fell away in pieces, the eyes disappeared, and soon Margarita saw on the platter a yellowish skull on a golden stand, with emerald eyes and pearl teeth. The top of the skull swung back on a hinge.

“This very second, Messire,” said Koroviev, noticing Woland’s questioning look, “he will appear before you. In this sepulchral silence I can hear his patent-leather shoes creaking and the glass ringing as he puts it down on the table, having drunk champagne for the last time in this life. Ah, here he is.”

A new solitary guest was entering the hall and making his way toward Woland. Outwardly he was no different from the numerous other male guests, except in one respect: the guest was literally reeling with agitation, which could be seen even from far off. Red spots burned on his cheeks, and his eyes darted about in utter alarm. The guest was stunned, and that was entirely natural: everything had astonished him, and above all, of course, Woland’s attire.
Nevertheless the guest was received with exceptional warmth.

“Ah, my dearest Baron Meigel,” Woland addressed the guest with a welcoming smile, while the guest’s eyes were starting out of his head. “I am happy to present to you,” Woland turned to the guests, “the most worthy Baron Meigel, employed by the Entertainment Commission in the post of acquainting foreigners with the sights of the capital.”

Here Margarita froze, because she suddenly recognized this Meigel. She had come across him several times in Moscow theaters and restaurants. “Wait a moment...” thought Margarita, “does that mean he has died too, or what?” But the matter was cleared up at once.

“The dear baron,” Woland went on, smiling joyfully, “was so charming that, on learning of my arrival in Moscow, he telephoned me at once, offering his services in his own specialty, that is, in acquainting me with the sights. It goes without saying that I was happy to invite him to my home.”
At this moment Margarita saw Azazello hand the platter with the skull to Koroviev.

“Oh, by the way, Baron,” said Woland, suddenly lowering his voice confidentially, “rumors have spread about your extraordinary curiosity. They say that, combined with your no less developed talkativeness, it has begun to attract general attention. More than that, wicked tongues have already let fall the words ‘eavesdropper’ and ‘spy.’ And more than that still, there is a supposition that this will bring you to a sad end no later than a month from now. And so, to spare you this agonizing wait, we have decided to come to your aid, taking advantage of the fact that you asked yourself to my home precisely in order to spy and eavesdrop on everything you could.”

The baron turned paler than Abadonna, who was exceptionally pale by nature, and then something strange happened. Abadonna was in front of the baron and took off his glasses for a second. At that same moment something flashed like fire in Azazello’s hands, something popped softly, like a clap of the hands, the baron began to fall backward, and scarlet blood spurted from his chest and flooded his starched shirt and waistcoat. Koroviev held the cup under the pulsing stream and handed the filled cup to Woland. The baron’s lifeless body was by then already on the floor.
“I drink your health, gentlemen,” Woland said quietly, and, raising the cup, touched it to his lips.

Then a metamorphosis took place. The patched shirt and the worn-down slippers vanished. Woland was now in a black chlamys of some kind, with a steel sword at his hip. He quickly came up to Margarita, held the cup out to her and said imperiously:
“Drink!”
Margarita’s head spun, she swayed, but the cup was already at her lips, and voices, though whose she could not make out, whispered in both her ears:
“Don’t be afraid, Queen... Don’t be afraid, Queen, the blood went into the earth long ago. And where it was spilled, grapes are already growing.”

Margarita, without opening her eyes, took a sip, and a sweet current ran through her veins, and a ringing began in her ears. It seemed to her that deafening cocks were crowing, that somewhere a march was being played. The crowds of guests began to lose their shape. Both the men in tailcoats and the women crumbled into dust. Before Margarita’s eyes decay seized the hall, and a smell of the crypt flowed over it. The columns fell apart, the lights went out, everything shrank, and there were no more fountains, tulips or camellias. And there was simply what there was—the jeweler’s widow’s modest drawing room, and a strip of light falling from a door standing ajar. And through that door standing ajar Margarita went in.

chapters.title: 24. The Extraction of the Master
paragraphs: In Woland’s bedroom everything turned out to be as it had been before the ball. Woland sat on the bed in his nightshirt, only Hella was no longer rubbing his leg but laying supper on the table where they had played chess earlier. Koroviev and Azazello, having taken off their tailcoats, sat at the table, and beside them, of course, was the cat, who had refused to part with his tie, even though it had turned into a perfectly filthy rag. Margarita, swaying, came up to the table and leaned on it. Then Woland beckoned her over to him, as he had before, and motioned her to sit beside him.
“Well, have they worn you out terribly?” asked Woland.
“Oh no, Messire,” Margarita answered, though barely audibly.
“Noblesse oblige,” remarked the cat, and poured Margarita some transparent liquid into a tumbler.
“Is this vodka?” Margarita asked weakly.
The cat bounced on his chair in offense.
“Have mercy, Queen,” he wheezed, “would I permit myself to pour a lady vodka? This is pure spirit!”
Margarita smiled and made an attempt to push the glass away.

“Drink boldly,” said Woland, and Margarita at once took the glass in her hand. “Hella, sit down,” Woland ordered, and explained to Margarita: “The night of the full moon is a festive night, and I sup in a close company of my intimates and servants. So, how do you feel? How did this tiring ball go?”
“Stupendously!” Koroviev rattled off. “Everyone is charmed, smitten, crushed! What tact, what skill, what appeal and charm!”

Woland silently raised his glass and clinked it with Margarita’s. Margarita obediently drank, thinking that the spirit would be the end of her on the spot. But nothing bad happened. A living warmth flowed through her stomach, something struck softly at the back of her head, her strength returned, as though she had risen after a long refreshing sleep, and besides that she felt a wolfish hunger. And when she remembered that she had eaten nothing since the morning before, it flared up even more. She began greedily gulping down caviar.
Behemoth cut off a piece of pineapple, salted it, peppered it, ate it, and after that tossed back a second shot of spirit with such dash that everyone applauded.

After the second shot Margarita drank, the candles in the candelabra burned brighter, and the flames in the fireplace grew. Margarita felt no intoxication whatever. Biting into meat with her white teeth, Margarita relished the juice running from it, and at the same time watched Behemoth spreading mustard on an oyster.
“Why not put some grapes on top as well,” Hella said quietly, poking the cat in the ribs.
“I’ll thank you not to teach me,” Behemoth replied. “I’ve sat at table before, don’t you worry, I’ve sat at table!”
“Ah, how pleasant it is to sup like this, by the fireside, without ceremony,” Koroviev quavered, “in a close circle...”
“No, Fagot,” the cat objected, “a ball has its own charm and sweep.”
“There’s no charm in it, and no sweep either, and those idiotic bears, and the tigers in the bar too, nearly gave me a migraine with their roaring,” said Woland.
“Yes, Messire,” said the cat, “if you find there is no sweep, I shall at once begin to hold the same opinion.”
“Watch yourself!” Woland replied to this.
“I was joking,” the cat said meekly, “and as for the tigers, I’ll have them roasted.”
“Tigers can’t be eaten,” said Hella.

“You think so? Then kindly listen,” the cat responded and, screwing up his eyes with pleasure, told how he had once wandered for nineteen days in the desert, and the only thing he had lived on was the meat of a tiger he had killed. Everyone listened with interest to this entertaining narrative, and when Behemoth had finished it, they all exclaimed in chorus:
“Lies!”
“And the most interesting thing about these lies,” said Woland, “is that they are lies from the first word to the last.”
“Oh, is that so? Lies?” exclaimed the cat, and everyone thought he was going to protest, but he only said quietly: “History will judge between us.”
“But tell me,” Margot, revived by the vodka, turned to Azazello, “did you shoot him, that former baron?”
“Naturally,” answered Azazello. “How could he not be shot? He absolutely had to be shot.”
“I was so shaken!” exclaimed Margarita. “It happened so unexpectedly.”
“There was nothing unexpected about it,” Azazello objected, while Koroviev began to howl and whine:
“How could one not be shaken? My own knees started knocking! Bang! Just like that! Baron over on his side!”
“I nearly went into hysterics,” added the cat, licking a spoonful of caviar.
“Here’s what I don’t understand,” said Margarita, and golden sparks from the crystal leapt in her eyes. “Could the music, and all the din of this ball in general, really not be heard outside?”
“Of course it couldn’t be heard, Queen,” Koroviev explained. “It has to be done so that it can’t be heard. One has to be rather careful about it.”
“Well, yes, yes... Only the thing is, that man on the stairs... When Azazello and I came past... And another one by the entrance... I think he was watching your apartment...”

“True, true!” cried Koroviev. “True, dear Margarita Nikolayevna! You confirm my suspicions! Yes, he was watching the apartment! I myself nearly took him for an absent-minded assistant professor or a lover pining on the stairs. But no, no! Something kept gnawing at my heart! Ah, he was watching the apartment! And the other one by the entrance too! And the one in the gateway, the very same thing!”
“But I wonder, what if they come to arrest you?” asked Margarita.

“They’re sure to come, enchanting Queen, sure to!” Koroviev replied. “My heart tells me they’ll come. Not now, of course, but in due course they’ll come without fail. But I suppose there will be nothing interesting about it.”
“Ah, how shaken I was when that baron fell,” said Margarita, evidently still living through the killing, the first she had seen in her life. “You must be a good shot?”
“Fair to middling,” answered Azazello.
“And from how many paces?” Margarita asked Azazello a not entirely clear question.
“Depends what at,” Azazello answered reasonably. “It’s one thing to hit the critic Latunsky’s window with a hammer and quite another to hit him in the heart.”
“In the heart!” Margarita exclaimed, for some reason clutching at her own heart. “In the heart!” she repeated in a hollow voice.
“What critic Latunsky is this?” asked Woland, narrowing his eyes at Margarita.
Azazello, Koroviev and Behemoth lowered their eyes somehow shamefacedly, and Margarita answered, blushing:
“There is a certain critic. This evening I smashed up his whole apartment.”
“Well, there’s a thing! And why was that?”
“He, Messire,” Margarita explained, “destroyed a certain master.”
“But why go to the trouble yourself?” asked Woland.
“Allow me, Messire!” the cat cried joyfully, jumping up.
“Oh, sit down, you,” Azazello growled, getting up. “I’ll pop over there myself right now...”
“No!” exclaimed Margarita. “No, I implore you, Messire, don’t do it!”
“As you wish, as you wish,” replied Woland, and Azazello sat back down in his place.

“So where were we, precious Queen Margot?” said Koroviev. “Ah yes, the heart. He hits the heart,” Koroviev stretched his long finger toward Azazello, “to order, in either atrium of the heart or in either of the ventricles.”
Margarita did not understand at once, and when she did, she exclaimed in surprise:
“But they’re covered up!”
“My dear,” quavered Koroviev, “that’s just the trick of it, that they’re covered up! That’s the whole point! Anyone can hit an exposed object!”

Koroviev took the seven of spades from a drawer in the table, offered it to Margarita and asked her to mark one of the pips with her fingernail. Margarita marked the top right corner one. Hella hid the card under a pillow, calling out:
“Ready!”

Azazello, who was sitting with his back to the pillow, took a black automatic pistol from the pocket of his tailcoat trousers, laid the barrel over his shoulder and, without turning toward the bed, fired, giving Margarita a merry fright. The seven was pulled out from under the shot-through pillow. The pip Margarita had marked was pierced.
“I shouldn’t like to meet you when you have a revolver in your hand,” said Margarita, glancing coquettishly at Azazello. She had a passion for all people who did anything first-rate.

“Precious Queen,” squeaked Koroviev, “I don’t recommend anyone to meet him even if he has no revolver in his hand at all! I give you my word of honor as a former choirmaster and precentor that no one would congratulate the person who met him.”
The cat had sat scowling throughout the shooting demonstration, and suddenly he announced:
“I undertake to beat the record with the seven.”

In reply to this Azazello growled something. But the cat was stubborn and demanded not one revolver but two. Azazello took a second revolver from the second back pocket of his trousers and, twisting his mouth contemptuously, held it out to the braggart together with the first. Two pips on the seven were marked. The cat spent a long time getting ready, with his back to the pillow. Margarita sat with her fingers stuck in her ears and looked at an owl dozing on the mantelpiece. The cat fired both revolvers, whereupon Hella shrieked at once, the dead owl fell from the mantelpiece, and the shattered clock stopped. Hella, one of whose hands was bloodied, seized the cat’s fur with a howl, he seized her hair in return, and, twisted into a ball, they rolled across the floor. One of the goblets fell off the table and broke.
“Drag this rabid she-devil off me!” howled the cat, fighting off Hella, who sat astride him. The combatants were separated, Koroviev blew on Hella’s shot finger, and it healed.
“I can’t shoot when people talk at my elbow!” shouted Behemoth, trying to stick back in its place a huge tuft of fur that had been torn out of his back.
“I’ll wager,” said Woland, smiling at Margarita, “that he pulled that trick on purpose. He’s a decent shot.”

Hella and the cat made peace, and as a token of this reconciliation they kissed. The card was taken out from under the pillow and checked. Not a single pip had been touched except the one Azazello had shot through.
“It can’t be,” the cat insisted, looking through the card at the light of the candelabrum.

The merry supper went on. The candles guttered in the candelabra, and a dry, fragrant warmth spread through the room in waves from the fireplace. Margarita, who had eaten her fill, was overcome by a feeling of bliss. She watched the bluish-gray rings from Azazello’s cigar float off into the fireplace and the cat catch them on the tip of a sword. She did not want to go anywhere, even though by her reckoning it was already late. To judge by everything, the time was getting on for six in the morning. Taking advantage of a pause, Margarita turned to Woland and said timidly:
“I suppose it’s time for me to go... It’s late...”
“What’s your hurry?” Woland asked, politely but rather dryly. The others said nothing, pretending to be absorbed in the smoke rings from the cigar.

“Yes, it’s time,” Margarita repeated, utterly embarrassed by this, and turned around as though looking for a cape or a cloak. Her nakedness suddenly began to make her feel awkward. She got up from the table. Woland silently took his threadbare, greasy dressing gown from the bed, and Koroviev threw it over Margarita’s shoulders.

“Thank you, Messire,” Margarita said barely audibly, and looked at Woland questioningly. In reply he smiled at her politely and indifferently. A black anguish somehow welled up all at once in Margarita’s heart. She felt deceived. No one, apparently, was going to offer her any reward for all her services at the ball, just as no one was keeping her here. And yet it was perfectly clear to her that she had nowhere left to go from here. The fleeting thought that she would have to return to the house set off an inner explosion of despair in her. Should she ask herself, then, as Azazello had temptingly advised in the Alexander Garden? “No, not for anything!” she told herself.
“All the best, Messire,” she said aloud, while thinking to herself: “If only I can get out of here, and then I’ll walk to the river and drown myself.”
“Sit down, now,” Woland suddenly said imperiously.
Margarita’s face changed, and she sat down.
“Perhaps you would like to say something in parting?”

“No, nothing, Messire,” Margarita answered proudly, “except that if you still need me, I am ready and willing to do anything you please. I am not in the least tired and I enjoyed myself very much at the ball. So that if it were still going on, I would willingly offer my knee for thousands of hanged men and murderers to put their lips to.” Margarita was looking at Woland as though through a veil; her eyes were filling with tears.
“Right! You are perfectly right!” Woland cried in a resounding and terrible voice. “That is how it should be!”
“That is how it should be!” Woland’s retinue repeated, like an echo.

“We were testing you,” said Woland. “Never ask for anything! Never for anything, and especially from those who are stronger than you. They will offer of their own accord and give everything of their own accord. Sit down, proud woman.” Woland tore the heavy dressing gown off Margarita, and once again she found herself sitting beside him on the bed. “And so, Margot,” Woland went on, softening his voice, “what do you want for having been my hostess tonight? What do you wish for having spent this ball naked? What value do you set on your knee? What are the damages from my guests, whom you just now called hanged men? Speak! And now speak without constraint, for it is I who have offered.”
Margarita’s heart began to pound; she sighed heavily and began to think something over.

“Well, come on, be bolder!” Woland encouraged her. “Rouse your imagination, spur it on! Merely being present at the scene of the killing of that out-and-out scoundrel of a baron is worth a reward, especially if the person in question is a woman. Well, then?”

Margarita’s breath caught, and she was already about to utter the cherished words she had prepared in her soul, when suddenly she turned pale, opened her mouth and stared. “Frieda! Frieda! Frieda!” some importunate, pleading voice cried in her ears. “My name is Frieda!” And Margarita, stumbling over her words, began:
“So I... may ask... for one thing, then?”
“Demand, demand, my donna,” Woland replied with an understanding smile, “demand one thing.”
Ah, how deftly and distinctly Woland stressed it, repeating Margarita’s own words: “one thing”!
Margarita sighed once more and said:
“I want them to stop bringing Frieda that handkerchief she smothered her child with.”
The cat raised his eyes to heaven and sighed noisily, but said nothing, evidently remembering the ear that had been twisted at the ball.

“In view of the fact,” Woland began, with a smirk, “that the possibility of your having taken a bribe from that fool Frieda is of course entirely ruled out—for that would be incompatible with your royal dignity—I really don’t know what to do. There remains, perhaps, one thing—to get hold of some rags and stuff up all the cracks in my bedroom with them!”
“What are you talking about, Messire?” Margarita asked in astonishment, having listened to these truly incomprehensible words.
“I entirely agree with you, Messire,” the cat broke into the conversation, “rags is just the thing!” And in irritation the cat struck the table with his paw.

“I am talking about mercy,” Woland explained his words, not taking his fiery eye off Margarita. “Sometimes, quite unexpectedly and treacherously, it creeps in through the very narrowest cracks. That is why I speak of rags.”
“And that’s what I’m talking about too!” exclaimed the cat, and, just in case, leaned away from Margarita, covering his sharp ears with paws smeared in pink cream.
“Get out,” Woland told him.

“I haven’t had my coffee yet,” replied the cat. “How can I leave? Can it be, Messire, that on a festive night the guests at table are divided into two grades? Some of the first freshness, and the others, as that sad skinflint of a barman put it, of the second?”
“Be quiet,” Woland ordered him, and, turning to Margarita, asked: “You are, by all appearances, a person of exceptional kindness? A person of high morals?”

“No,” Margarita answered forcefully, “I know that one can speak to you only frankly, and I will tell you frankly: I am a frivolous person. I asked you for Frieda only because I was careless enough to give her firm hope. She is waiting, Messire, she believes in my power. And if she is left deceived, I shall be in a terrible position. I shall have no peace all my life. It can’t be helped! That’s just how it turned out.”
“Ah,” said Woland, “that is understandable.”
“So will you do it?” Margarita asked quietly.

“By no means,” Woland answered. “The thing is, dear Queen, that a slight muddle has occurred here. Each department must attend to its own business. I don’t dispute that our possibilities are rather great; they are far greater than some not very sharp-sighted people suppose...”
“Yes, far greater,” the cat could not help putting in, evidently proud of these possibilities.

“Be quiet, the devil take you!” Woland told him, and went on, addressing Margarita: “But simply, what sense is there in doing what is supposed to be done by another—as I put it—department? And so I shall not do it; you will do it yourself.”
“But will it come true if I do it?”
Azazello cast an ironic sidelong look at Margarita with his crooked eye, imperceptibly shook his red head and snorted.
“Oh, just do it, what torment,” Woland muttered, and, turning the globe, began to peer at some detail on it, evidently attending to other business as well during his conversation with Margarita.
“Well, Frieda...” Koroviev prompted.
“Frieda!” Margarita cried piercingly.
The door flew open, and a disheveled, naked woman, though now without any sign of drink, ran into the room with frenzied eyes and stretched out her arms to Margarita, who said majestically:
“You are forgiven. They will not bring you the handkerchief anymore.”
Frieda let out a wail, fell face down on the floor and lay with her arms outstretched in the shape of a cross before Margarita. Woland waved his hand, and Frieda vanished from sight.
“Thank you, and farewell,” said Margarita, and rose.

“Well now, Behemoth,” Woland began, “let us not profit from the act of an impractical person on a festive night.” He turned to Margarita. “So that doesn’t count, since I did nothing. What do you want for yourself?”
A silence fell, and it was broken by Koroviev, who began whispering in Margarita’s ear:
“Diamond donna, this time I advise you to be a little more sensible! Otherwise fortune may slip away, you know.”
“I want my lover, the master, to be given back to me at once, this very second,” said Margarita, and her face was distorted by a spasm.

At this a wind burst into the room, so that the flames of the candles in the candelabra lay down flat, the heavy curtain at the window was swept aside, the window flew open, and far up on high appeared the moon, full, but not a morning moon, a midnight one. From the windowsill a greenish kerchief of night light lay down on the floor, and in it appeared Ivanushka’s night visitor, the one who called himself the master. He was in his hospital clothes—a robe, slippers and the black cap he never parted with. His unshaven face twitched in a grimace, he glanced sidelong at the candle flames with a madman’s fear, and the stream of moonlight seethed around him.

Margarita recognized him at once, moaned, clasped her hands and ran to him. She kissed him on the forehead, on the lips, pressed herself to his prickly cheek, and the tears she had held back so long now ran down her face in streams. She uttered only one word, repeating it senselessly:
“You... you... you...”
The master moved her away from him and said dully:

“Don’t cry, Margot, don’t torment me. I am gravely ill.” He grasped the windowsill with his hand, as though about to leap onto it and flee, bared his teeth, peering at those seated there, and cried out: “I’m frightened, Margot! My hallucinations have started again...”
Sobs choked Margarita; she whispered, choking on her words:
“No, no, no... don’t be afraid of anything... I’m with you... I’m with you...”

Koroviev deftly and unobtrusively pushed a chair toward the master, and he sank onto it, while Margarita threw herself on her knees, pressed herself against the sick man’s side, and grew still like that. In her agitation she did not notice that her nakedness had somehow suddenly come to an end; she was now wearing a black silk cloak. The sick man lowered his head and began to stare at the ground with gloomy, sick eyes.
“Yes,” Woland began after a silence, “they’ve given him a good going-over.” He ordered Koroviev: “Give this man something to drink, knight.”
Margarita begged the master in a trembling voice:
“Drink it, drink it! Are you afraid? No, no, believe me, they will help you!”
The sick man took the glass and drank what was in it, but his hand trembled, and the empty glass smashed at his feet.
“For luck! For luck!” Koroviev whispered to Margarita. “Look, he’s already coming to himself.”
Indeed, the sick man’s gaze was no longer so wild and restless.
“But is it you, Margot?” asked the moonlit visitor.
“Don’t doubt it, it’s me,” answered Margarita.
“Another!” ordered Woland.
After the master had drained the second glass, his eyes became alive and full of understanding.
“There now, that’s another matter,” said Woland, narrowing his eyes. “Now let us talk. Who are you?”
“I am no one now,” answered the master, and a smile twisted his mouth.
“Where have you come from just now?”
“From the house of sorrow. I am mentally ill,” the newcomer answered.
Margarita could not bear these words and wept again. Then, wiping her eyes, she cried out:
“Terrible words! Terrible words! He is a master, Messire, I warn you of that! Cure him, he is worth it!”
“Do you know who you are speaking to now,” Woland asked the newcomer, “whose house you are in?”
“I do,” answered the master. “My neighbor in the madhouse was that boy, Ivan Bezdomny. He told me about you.”

“Why, of course, of course,” responded Woland. “I had the pleasure of meeting that young man at Patriarch’s Ponds. He very nearly drove me mad myself, proving to me that I don’t exist! But you do believe that it really is me?”
“I have to believe it,” said the newcomer, “but of course it would be far more comforting to consider you the product of a hallucination. Forgive me,” the master added, catching himself.
“Well, if it’s more comforting, then go ahead and consider me so,” Woland replied politely.
“No, no!” Margarita said in fright, shaking the master by the shoulder. “Come to your senses! It really is he before you!”
Here too the cat butted in:

“And I really do look like a hallucination. Note my profile in the moonlight.” The cat climbed into the shaft of moonlight and wanted to say something more, but he was asked to be quiet, and, replying: “All right, all right, I’m prepared to be quiet. I shall be a silent hallucination,” he fell silent.
“But tell me, why does Margarita call you the master?” asked Woland.
The other smiled wryly and said:
“That is a forgivable weakness. She has too high an opinion of the novel I wrote.”
“What is the novel about?”
“It is a novel about Pontius Pilate.”

Here again the little tongues of the candle flames swayed and leapt, the dishes rattled on the table, and Woland burst into thunderous laughter, but it frightened no one and surprised no one. Behemoth for some reason applauded.

“About what, about what? About whom?” Woland began, when he had stopped laughing. “Now, of all times? That’s stupendous! And you couldn’t find another subject? Let me have a look,” and Woland held out his hand, palm up.
“Unfortunately I cannot do that,” answered the master, “because I burned it in the stove.”
“Forgive me, but I don’t believe you,” Woland replied. “That cannot be. Manuscripts don’t burn.” He turned to Behemoth and said: “Come on, Behemoth, let’s have the novel.”

The cat instantly leapt up from his chair, and everyone saw that he had been sitting on a thick stack of manuscripts. With a bow the cat handed the top copy to Woland. Margarita trembled and cried out, stirred to tears again:
“There it is, the manuscript! There it is!”
She rushed to Woland and added rapturously:
“All-powerful! All-powerful!”

Woland took the copy he had been handed, turned it over, laid it aside and stared at the master in silence, without a smile. But the master, for no knowable reason, sank into anguish and unrest, rose from the chair, wrung his hands and, turning to the distant moon and shuddering, began to mutter:
“Even at night, by the moon, I have no peace... Why have they disturbed me? O gods, gods...”
Margarita clutched at the hospital robe, pressed herself to him, and began muttering herself, in anguish and in tears:
“God, why isn’t the medicine helping you?”
“Never mind, never mind, never mind,” whispered Koroviev, wriggling around the master, “never mind, never mind... Another little glass, and I’ll keep you company...”
And the little glass winked, sparkled in the moonlight, and that little glass helped. The master was seated in his place again, and the sick man’s face took on a calm expression.
“Well, now everything is clear,” said Woland, and tapped the manuscript with a long finger.

“Perfectly clear,” the cat confirmed, forgetting his promise to become a silent hallucination. “Now the main line of this opus is clear to me through and through. What’s that you say, Azazello?” he turned to the silent Azazello.
“I say,” Azazello twanged, “that it would be a good thing to drown you.”

“Have mercy, Azazello,” the cat replied, “and don’t put the idea into my master’s head. Believe me, every night I would appear to you in the same moonlit garb as the poor master, and nod to you, and beckon you to follow me. How would you like that, O Azazello?”
“Well, Margarita,” Woland joined in the conversation again, “tell me everything you need, then.”
Margarita’s eyes flashed, and she turned to Woland imploringly:
“May I have a whisper with him?”
Woland nodded, and Margarita, pressing close to the master’s ear, whispered something to him. He could be heard answering her:
“No, it’s too late. I want nothing more in life. Except to see you. But again I advise you—leave me. You will be lost with me.”

“No, I won’t leave you,” answered Margarita, and turned to Woland: “I ask you to return us to the basement in the side street off the Arbat, and for the lamp to be lit, and for everything to be as it was.”
At this the master laughed and, putting his arms around Margarita’s curly head, the curls of which had long since come undone, said:

“Ah, don’t listen to the poor woman, Messire. Another man has been living in that basement for a long time now, and in general it never happens that everything becomes as it was.” He laid his cheek against his beloved’s head, put his arms around Margarita, and began to murmur: “Poor thing, poor thing...”
“It never happens, you say?” said Woland. “That is true. But we shall try.” And he said: “Azazello!”

At once a citizen came crashing down from the ceiling onto the floor, bewildered and close to frenzy, in nothing but his underwear, but for some reason holding a suitcase and wearing a cap. The man was trembling and cowering with fear.
“Mogarych?” Azazello asked the man who had dropped from the sky.
“Aloisy Mogarych,” the man answered, trembling.
“Was it you who, after reading Latunsky’s article on this man’s novel, wrote a complaint about him, reporting that he kept illegal literature at home?” asked Azazello.
The newly arrived citizen turned blue and dissolved in tears of repentance.
“You wanted to move into his rooms?” Azazello twanged, as warmly as he could.
The hiss of an infuriated cat was heard in the room, and Margarita, howling:
“Know what a witch is, know it!” sank her nails into Aloisy Mogarych’s face.
Pandemonium followed.
“What are you doing?” the master cried out in anguish. “Margot, don’t disgrace yourself!”
“I protest, it’s no disgrace!” bawled the cat.
Koroviev pulled Margarita away.
“I put in a bathtub...” cried the bloodied Mogarych, his teeth chattering, and in his terror he began babbling some nonsense, “just whitewash... vitriol...”
“Well, it’s a good thing you put in a bathtub,” said Azazello approvingly, “he needs to take baths.” And he shouted: “Out!”
Then Mogarych was turned upside down and carried out of Woland’s bedroom through the open window.
The master goggled, whispering:

“Well, this, I daresay, beats what Ivan was telling me!” Utterly shaken, he looked around and at last said to the cat: “But excuse me... was it you... was it you, sir...” He faltered, not knowing how to address a cat. “Are you that same cat who got on the tram?”

“It was I,” the flattered cat confirmed, and added: “It is pleasant to hear you address a cat so politely. For some reason cats are usually spoken to with familiarity, though no cat has ever drunk Bruderschaft with anyone.”
“For some reason it seems to me that you are not very much of a cat...” the master answered hesitantly. “They’ll miss me at the hospital anyway,” he added timidly to Woland.
“Now why should they miss you!” Koroviev reassured him, and some papers and books turned up in his hands. “Is this your case history?”
“Yes.”
Koroviev flung the case history into the fireplace.
“No document, no person,” Koroviev said with satisfaction. “And is this your landlord’s house register?”
“Ye-es...”

“Who is registered in it? Aloisy Mogarych?” Koroviev blew on the page of the house register. “Presto, he’s gone, and, kindly note, he never was. And if the landlord is surprised, tell him he dreamed Aloisy. Mogarych? What Mogarych would that be? There never was any Mogarych.” Here the laced and sealed register evaporated from Koroviev’s hands. “And there it is, already back in the landlord’s desk.”

“You were right to say,” said the master, struck by the neatness of Koroviev’s work, “that if there’s no document, there’s no person. That’s exactly it, I’m the one who doesn’t exist—I have no document.”

“I beg your pardon,” cried Koroviev, “now that’s precisely a hallucination. Here it is, your document,” and Koroviev handed the master a document. Then he rolled up his eyes and whispered sweetly to Margarita: “And here is your property, Margarita Nikolayevna,” and he handed Margarita a notebook with charred edges, a dried rose, a photograph and, with particular care, a savings book. “Ten thousand, just as you were pleased to deposit it, Margarita Nikolayevna. We have no need of what belongs to others.”
“My paws would wither sooner than I’d touch what belongs to others,” the cat exclaimed, puffing himself up, as he danced on the suitcase to cram all the copies of the ill-fated novel into it.
“And your little document too,” Koroviev went on, handing Margarita a document, and then, turning to Woland, he reported respectfully: “That is all, Messire!”
“No, not all,” replied Woland, tearing himself away from the globe. “Where, my dear donna, would you have me put your retinue? I personally have no need of it.”
Here Natasha ran in through the open door, naked as she was, clasped her hands and cried to Margarita:
“Be happy, Margarita Nikolayevna!” She nodded her head at the master and turned to Margarita again: “I knew all along where you were going, you know.”
“Housemaids know everything,” remarked the cat, raising his paw significantly. “It’s a mistake to think they’re blind.”
“What do you want, Natasha?” asked Margarita. “Go back to the house.”

“Darling Margarita Nikolayevna,” Natasha began imploringly, and went down on her knees, “beg them,” she glanced sidelong at Woland, “to let me stay a witch. I don’t want to go back to the house anymore! I won’t marry an engineer or a technician either! Monsieur Jacques proposed to me at the ball last night.” Natasha unclenched her fist and showed some gold coins.
Margarita turned a questioning gaze on Woland. He nodded. Then Natasha threw her arms around Margarita’s neck, gave her loud kisses and, with a triumphant cry, flew out of the window.
In Natasha’s place appeared Nikolai Ivanovich. He had regained his former human shape, but was extremely gloomy and even, perhaps, irritated.
“Here is someone I shall let go with particular pleasure,” said Woland, looking at Nikolai Ivanovich with disgust, “with exceptional pleasure, so superfluous is he here.”
“I most earnestly request to be issued a certificate,” Nikolai Ivanovich began, looking around wildly, but with great persistence, “stating where I spent last night.”
“For what purpose?” the cat asked sternly.
“For the purpose of presenting it to the police and to my wife,” Nikolai Ivanovich said firmly.
“We do not usually issue certificates,” the cat replied, scowling, “but for you, so be it, we’ll make an exception.”
And before Nikolai Ivanovich could collect himself, the naked Hella was already sitting at a typewriter, and the cat was dictating to her:

“I hereby certify that the bearer hereof, Nikolai Ivanovich, spent the said night at Satan’s ball, having been brought there in the capacity of a means of transport... Open a bracket, Hella! In the bracket write ‘hog.’ Signature—Behemoth.”
“And the date?” squeaked Nikolai Ivanovich.

“We don’t put dates; with a date the paper becomes invalid,” the cat responded, dashed off his signature, got a stamp from somewhere, breathed on it according to all the rules, stamped the word “Payed” on the paper and handed the paper to Nikolai Ivanovich. After that Nikolai Ivanovich vanished without a trace, and in his place there appeared another unexpected person.
“And who is this?” Woland asked squeamishly, shielding his eyes from the candlelight with his hand.
Varenukha hung his head, sighed and said quietly:
“Let me go back. I can’t be a vampire. Why, that time with Hella I nearly hounded Rimsky to death! And I’m not bloodthirsty. Let me go.”
“What raving is this?” asked Woland, wrinkling his face. “What Rimsky would that be? What is this nonsense?”
“Don’t trouble yourself, Messire,” Azazello responded, and turned to Varenukha: “No being rude on the telephone. No lying on the telephone. Understood? You won’t do it anymore?”
Everything went cloudy in Varenukha’s head with joy, his face beamed, and, not knowing what he was saying, he began to babble:
“By the true... that is, I mean to say, Your Maj... right after lunch...” Varenukha pressed his hands to his chest, gazing at Azazello imploringly.
“All right, home with you,” Azazello replied, and Varenukha melted away.
“Now leave me alone with them, all of you,” Woland ordered, pointing to the master and Margarita.
Woland’s order was carried out instantly. After a certain silence Woland turned to the master:
“So, then, back to the Arbat basement? But who will write? And the dreams, the inspiration?”

“I have no more dreams, and no inspiration either,” answered the master. “Nothing around me interests me except her.” He again laid his hand on Margarita’s head. “They have broken me, I am bored, and I want to go to the basement.”
“And your novel? Pilate?”
“I hate it, that novel,” answered the master. “I have been through too much because of it.”

“I implore you,” Margarita begged plaintively, “don’t talk like that. Why do you torment me? You know I have put my whole life into this work of yours.” Margarita added, turning to Woland: “Don’t listen to him, Messire, he has been tormented too much.”
“But surely one must describe something?” said Woland. “If you have exhausted that procurator, well, start portraying this Aloisy, at least.”
The master smiled.
“Lapshennikova wouldn’t print that, and besides, it isn’t interesting.”
“And what will you live on? You’ll have to go begging.”
“Gladly, gladly,” answered the master, drew Margarita to him, put his arm around her shoulders and added: “She’ll come to her senses and leave me...”

“I don’t think so,” Woland said through his teeth, and went on: “So the man who composed the story of Pontius Pilate is going off to a basement, intending to settle down there by the lamp and go begging?”
Margarita drew away from the master and began to speak very heatedly:
“I did everything I could, and I whispered the most tempting thing to him. And he refused it.”

“I know what you whispered to him,” Woland objected, “but that is not the most tempting thing. And to you I will say,” he turned to the master with a smile, “that your novel will bring you more surprises yet.”
“That is very sad,” answered the master.
“No, no, it’s not sad,” said Woland. “Nothing terrible will happen anymore. Well, Margarita Nikolayevna, everything is done. Have you any complaint against me?”
“How can you, oh, how can you, Messire!”
“Then take this from me as a keepsake,” said Woland, and drew from under the pillow a small golden horseshoe studded with diamonds.
“No, no, no, why on earth should I!”
“Do you wish to argue with me?” asked Woland with a smile.
Since her cloak had no pocket, Margarita put the horseshoe in a napkin and tied it in a knot. Here something astonished her. She looked around at the window, in which the moon was shining, and said:
“But here’s what I don’t understand... How is it that it’s midnight and still midnight, when it ought to have been morning long ago?”
“It is pleasant to hold back a festive midnight a little,” answered Woland. “Well, I wish you happiness!”
Margarita stretched out both hands to Woland as if in prayer, but did not dare approach him, and exclaimed quietly:
“Farewell! Farewell!”
“Until we meet again,” said Woland.

And Margarita in the black cloak and the master in the hospital robe went out into the corridor of the jeweler’s widow’s apartment, where a candle was burning and Woland’s retinue was waiting for them. When they set off down the corridor, Hella carried the suitcase containing the novel and Margarita Nikolayevna’s small belongings, and the cat helped Hella. At the door of the apartment Koroviev bowed and vanished, and the others went to see them off down the stairs. The stairs were empty. As they passed the third-floor landing, something thudded softly, but nobody paid any attention to it. At the very front doors of entrance six Azazello blew upward, and they had only just stepped out into the courtyard, which the moon did not reach, when they saw a man in boots and a cap asleep on the steps, and evidently sleeping the sleep of the dead, and also a big black car standing by the entrance with its headlights off. Through the windshield the silhouette of a rook could be dimly seen.
They were already about to get in when Margarita exclaimed quietly in despair:
“God, I’ve lost the horseshoe!”
“Get in the car,” said Azazello, “and wait for me. I’ll be back in a moment, I’ll just sort out what’s what.” And he went off into the entrance.

And what was what was this: some time before Margarita and the master came out with their escort, a dried-up little woman with a can and a bag in her hands had come out onto the stairs from apartment No. 48, which was situated under the jeweler’s widow’s. This was the very Annushka who on Wednesday, to Berlioz’s misfortune, had spilled sunflower oil by the turnstile.

Nobody knew, and probably nobody ever will know, what this woman did in Moscow or what means she lived on. All that was known of her was that she could be seen every day, now with a can, now with a bag, and sometimes with a bag and a can together—either at the kerosene shop, or at the market, or under the gateway of the building, or on the stairs, but most often in the kitchen of apartment No. 48, where this Annushka lived. Besides that, and above all, it was known that wherever she was or appeared, a row would at once break out in that place, and besides that, that she bore the nickname “the Plague.”

Annushka the Plague for some reason got up extremely early, and today something had got her up long before dawn, just after midnight. A key turned in the door, Annushka’s nose poked out of it, and then the whole of her poked out too; she slammed the door behind her and was already about to set off somewhere when a door crashed on the landing above, someone came tumbling down the stairs and, running into Annushka, flung her aside so that she struck the back of her head against the wall.

“Where the devil are you rushing to in nothing but your drawers?” shrieked Annushka, clutching the back of her head. The man in nothing but his underwear, with a suitcase in his hand and a cap on his head, his eyes shut, answered Annushka in a wild, sleepy voice:
“The water heater! The vitriol! What the whitewash alone cost me.” And, bursting into tears, he barked: “Out!”

Here he rushed off, not further down the stairs, but back up—to where the windowpane had been kicked out by the economist’s foot—and through this window he flew out into the courtyard feet first. Annushka even forgot about the back of her head; she gasped and dashed to the window herself. She lay down on her stomach on the landing and stuck her head out into the courtyard, expecting to see on the asphalt, lit by the courtyard lamp, a man with a suitcase smashed to death. But there was absolutely nothing on the asphalt in the courtyard.

It remained to suppose that the sleepy and strange individual had flown out of the building like a bird, leaving no trace behind him. Annushka crossed herself and thought: “Yes, that’s apartment number fifty for you, all right! It’s not for nothing people talk!.. Some apartment, that!..”

She had not finished thinking this when the door upstairs banged again, and a second someone came running down from above. Annushka pressed herself against the wall and saw some rather respectable citizen with a little beard, but with a face that, as it seemed to Annushka, was ever so slightly piggish, slip past her and, like the first, leave the building through the window, again without the slightest thought of smashing himself on the asphalt. Annushka had by now forgotten the purpose of her outing and stayed on the stairs, crossing herself, moaning and talking to herself.
A third man, without a beard, with a round shaven face, in a Tolstoy blouse, ran down from above a short time later and flitted out of the window in exactly the same way.

To Annushka’s credit it must be said that she was inquisitive, and she decided to wait a little longer to see whether there would be any new miracles. The door upstairs was opened again, and now a whole party began to come down from above, not running, but in the ordinary way, as all people walk. Annushka ran away from the window, went down to her own door, opened it in a flash, hid behind it, and in the crack she had left her eye, frenzied with curiosity, glimmered.

Someone, either sick or not sick, but strange, pale, overgrown with a beard, in a black cap and some sort of robe, was coming down with unsteady steps. He was being led carefully by the arm by some little lady in a black cassock, as it seemed to Annushka in the half-dark. The little lady was either barefoot or in some sort of transparent slippers, foreign, evidently, torn to shreds. Pah! Slippers, indeed! Why, the little lady’s naked! Yes, of course, the cassock’s thrown straight over her naked body! “Some apartment, that!” Everything in Annushka’s soul was singing in anticipation of what she would tell the neighbors tomorrow.

Behind the strangely dressed little lady came a completely naked little lady with a small suitcase in her hand, and beside the suitcase an enormous black cat was bustling about. Annushka very nearly squeaked something out loud, rubbing her eyes.

Bringing up the rear of the procession was a short, limping foreigner with a crooked eye, without a jacket, in a white evening waistcoat and a tie. This whole party filed past Annushka and on down. Here something thudded on the landing.

Hearing the footsteps die away, Annushka slid out from behind the door like a snake, set her can against the wall, dropped on her stomach on the landing and began to grope about. In her hands she found a little napkin with something heavy in it. Annushka’s eyes nearly popped out of her head when she unwrapped the little bundle. Annushka held the precious object right up to her eyes, and those eyes burned with a fire that was positively wolfish. A blizzard formed in Annushka’s head:

“I know nothing, I’ve seen nothing!.. To my nephew? Or saw it into pieces?.. The little stones can be picked out... And one little stone at a time: one to Petrovka, another to the Smolensky market... And—I know nothing and I’ve seen nothing!”

Annushka hid her find in her bosom, grabbed her can and was already about to slip back into the apartment, putting off her trip into town, when there rose up before her, sprung from the devil knows where, that same man with the white chest and no jacket, who whispered quietly:
“Hand over the little horseshoe and the little napkin.”
“What little napkin-horseshoe would that be?” asked Annushka, pretending very skillfully. “I don’t know about any little napkin. What’s the matter with you, citizen, are you drunk or something?”

Without another word the white-chested man, with fingers as hard as the handrails of a bus and just as cold, squeezed Annushka’s throat so that he cut off all access of air to her chest completely. The can fell from Annushka’s hands onto the floor. After keeping Annushka without air for a while, the jacketless foreigner took his fingers from her neck. Gulping in air, Annushka smiled.
