“I like speed myself,” Margarita was saying excitedly, “I like speed and nakedness... Like from a Mauser: bang! Oh, how he shoots!” Margarita cried, turning to the master. “A seven under the pillow, and any pip you like!” Margarita was beginning to get drunk, and it made her eyes blaze.

“And again I forgot,” Azazello shouted, slapping himself on the forehead. “I’m completely run off my feet! Why, Messire has sent you a present”—here he addressed himself specifically to the master—“a bottle of wine. Kindly note, it is the very wine that the procurator of Judea drank. Falernian wine.”

Quite naturally, such a rarity drew great attention from both Margarita and the master. Out of a piece of dark funeral brocade Azazello extracted a jug completely covered in mold. They sniffed the wine, poured it into glasses, looked through it at the light in the window, which was fading before the storm. They saw everything turn the color of blood.
“Woland’s health!” exclaimed Margarita, raising her glass.

All three put their lips to their glasses and each took a big gulp. At once the pre-storm light began to go out in the master’s eyes, his breath caught, and he felt that the end was coming. He still saw Margarita, deathly pale, helplessly stretching out her arms to him, drop her head onto the table and then slide down to the floor.

“Poisoner...” the master still managed to cry out. He wanted to snatch a knife from the table to strike Azazello with it, but his hand slid helplessly off the tablecloth, everything around the master in the basement turned black, and then disappeared altogether. He fell on his back and, as he fell, cut the skin of his temple on the corner of the desk.

When the poisoned pair had gone still, Azazello went into action. First of all he flew out the window, and in a few moments he was at the private house where Margarita Nikolayevna had lived. Always precise and meticulous, Azazello wanted to check that everything had been carried out as it should be. And everything turned out to be in perfect order. Azazello saw a gloomy woman, who was waiting for her husband to come back, come out of her bedroom, suddenly turn pale, clutch at her heart and, crying out helplessly:
“Natasha! Somebody... come here!” fall to the floor in the drawing room before she reached the study.

“All in order,” said Azazello. A moment later he was beside the stricken lovers. Margarita lay with her face buried in the little rug. With his iron hands Azazello turned her toward him like a doll and peered into her face. Before his eyes the poisoned woman’s face was changing. Even in the gathering storm dusk one could see her temporary witch’s squint vanish, and the cruelty and wildness of her features. The dead woman’s face brightened and at last softened, and her bared teeth were no longer predatory but simply a woman’s grimace of suffering. Then Azazello unclenched her white teeth and poured into her mouth a few drops of the very same wine he had poisoned her with. Margarita sighed, began to rise without Azazello’s help, sat up and asked weakly:
“What for, Azazello, what for? What have you done to me?”
She saw the master lying there, shuddered and whispered:
“I didn’t expect this... murderer!”
“Oh, no, no,” Azazello answered, “he’ll get up in a moment. Oh, why are you so nervous!”

Margarita believed him at once, so convincing was the red-haired demon’s voice. She jumped up, strong and alive, and helped him give the man on the floor some wine. Opening his eyes, he looked up darkly and with hatred repeated his last word:
“Poisoner...”
“Ah! An insult is the usual reward for a job well done,” replied Azazello. “Can you really be blind? Then hurry up and see!”
At this the master rose, looked about him with a gaze that was alive and clear, and asked:
“What does this new thing mean?”

“It means,” Azazello answered, “that it is time for us to go. The storm is already thundering, do you hear? It’s getting dark. The horses are pawing the ground, the little garden is shuddering. Say goodbye to the basement, say goodbye quickly.”
“Ah, I understand,” said the master, looking around, “you have killed us, we are dead. Oh, how clever that is! How timely! Now I understand everything.”

“Oh, come now,” Azazello replied, “is it you I hear? Why, your beloved calls you the master; why, you think, so how can you be dead? Do you really have to sit in a basement in a shirt and hospital drawers in order to consider yourself alive? That’s ridiculous!”
“I understood everything you said,” cried the master, “don’t go on! You are a thousand times right!”

“Great Woland,” Margarita began to echo him, “great Woland! He thought of something much better than I did. Only the novel, the novel,” she shouted to the master, “take the novel with you, wherever you fly!”
“No need,” the master replied, “I know it by heart.”
“But you won’t forget a word... not a single word of it?” Margarita asked, pressing herself to her lover and wiping the blood from his cut temple.
“Don’t worry! Now I will never forget anything again,” he replied.
“Then fire!” cried Azazello. “Fire, with which everything began and with which we end it all.”

“Fire!” Margarita shouted terribly. The little basement window banged, and the wind blew the blind aside. The sky thundered, merrily and briefly. Azazello thrust his clawed hand into the stove, pulled out a smoking brand and set fire to the tablecloth on the table. Then he set fire to a stack of old newspapers on the sofa, and after that to a manuscript and the curtain at the window.
The master, already intoxicated by the ride to come, tossed some book from the shelf onto the table, ruffled its pages in the burning tablecloth, and the book flared up with a merry flame.
“Burn, burn, old life!”
“Burn, suffering!” shouted Margarita.

The room was already swaying in crimson columns, and together with the smoke the three ran out through the door, climbed the stone steps and came out into the little courtyard. The first thing they saw there was the landlord’s cook sitting on the ground; beside her lay scattered potatoes and several bunches of onions. The cook’s state was understandable. Three black horses were snorting by the shed, quivering, sending up fountains of earth. Margarita mounted first, then Azazello, and last the master. The cook, with a groan, was about to raise her hand to make the sign of the cross, but Azazello shouted menacingly from the saddle:

“I’ll cut your hand off!” He whistled, and the horses, breaking the branches of the lindens, soared up and plunged into a low black cloud. At once smoke came pouring out of the little basement window. From below came the cook’s weak, pitiful cry:
“Fire!..”
The horses were already racing over the roofs of Moscow.

“I want to say goodbye to the city,” the master shouted to Azazello, who was galloping in front. The thunder ate the end of the master’s sentence. Azazello nodded and put his horse into a gallop. A cloud was flying swiftly toward the riders, but it was not yet spattering rain.

They flew over a boulevard and saw the little figures of people scattering to hide from the rain. The first drops were falling. They flew over smoke, all that was left of Griboyedov’s. They flew over the city, which darkness was already flooding. Lightning flashed above them. Then the roofs gave way to greenery. Only then did the rain pour down and turn the riders into three huge bubbles in the water.

Margarita already knew the sensation of flight, but the master did not, and he marveled at how quickly they reached their goal, the one he wanted to say goodbye to, since there was no one else for him to say goodbye to. Through the veil of rain he at once recognized the building of Stravinsky’s clinic, the river, and the pine wood on the other bank that he had studied so very well. They came down in a clearing in a grove not far from the clinic.
“I’ll wait for you here,” Azazello shouted, cupping his hands to his mouth, now lit up by the lightning, now disappearing in the gray veil, “say your goodbyes, but quickly!”

The master and Margarita leaped from their saddles and flew, flickering like watery shadows, across the clinic garden. A moment later the master, with a practiced hand, was moving aside the balcony grille of room No. 117. Margarita followed him. They went in to Ivanushka, invisible and unnoticed, amid the crashing and howling of the storm. The master stopped by the bed.

Ivanushka lay motionless, just as he had when he first watched a storm in this house of his repose. But he was not crying as he had that time. When he had taken a good look at the dark silhouette that had burst in on him from the balcony, he raised himself, held out his hands and said joyfully:
“Ah, it’s you! And I’ve been waiting and waiting for you. And here you are, my neighbor.”
To this the master replied:
“I’m here! But I can’t be your neighbor any longer, unfortunately. I am flying away forever, and I have come to you only to say goodbye.”
“I knew it, I guessed it,” Ivan replied quietly, and asked: “Did you meet him?”
“Yes,” said the master. “I came to say goodbye to you because you were the only person I have talked to lately.”
Ivanushka brightened and said:

“It’s good that you dropped in here. I’ll keep my word, you know: I won’t write any more little verses. I’m interested in something else now”—Ivanushka smiled and looked with mad eyes somewhere past the master—“I want to write something else. Lying here all this time, you know, I’ve understood a great deal.”
The master was stirred by these words and began to speak, sitting down on the edge of Ivanushka’s bed:
“Now that’s good, that’s good. You write the sequel about him!”
Ivanushka’s eyes flashed.
“But won’t you do it yourself?” Here he hung his head and added thoughtfully: “Ah, yes... why am I asking?” Ivanushka glanced sidelong at the floor and looked frightened.
“Yes,” said the master, and his voice seemed unfamiliar and hollow to Ivanushka, “I won’t be writing about him any more. I will be busy with something else.”
A distant whistle cut through the noise of the storm.
“Do you hear?” asked the master.
“It’s the storm...”
“No, they’re calling me, it’s time for me to go,” the master explained, and rose from the bed.
“Wait! One more word,” Ivan begged. “Did you find her? Has she stayed faithful to you?”

“Here she is,” the master replied, and pointed at the wall. The dark Margarita separated herself from the white wall and came up to the bed. She looked at the young man lying there, and grief could be read in her eyes.
“Poor boy, poor boy,” Margarita whispered soundlessly, and bent over the bed.

“How beautiful she is,” Ivan said without envy, but with sadness and a kind of quiet tenderness. “See how well everything has turned out for you. But it’s not like that for me.” Here he thought and added thoughtfully: “Though, then again, maybe it is like that...”

“It is, it is,” Margarita whispered, and bent right down to him, “there, I’ll kiss you on the forehead, and everything will be as it should be for you... you can believe me on that, I have seen everything already, I know everything.”
The young man lying there put his arms around her neck, and she kissed him.
“Farewell, disciple,” the master said barely audibly, and began to melt into the air. He vanished, and with him Margarita vanished too. The balcony grille closed.

Ivanushka grew restless. He sat up in bed, looked around anxiously, even moaned, began talking to himself, got up. The storm was raging harder and harder and had evidently stirred up his soul. He was also troubled because beyond the door his hearing, now used to constant quiet, caught restless footsteps, muffled voices behind the door. He called out, nervous by now and trembling:
“Praskovya Fyodorovna!”
Praskovya Fyodorovna was already coming into the room, looking at Ivanushka questioningly and anxiously.
“What? What is it?” she asked. “Is the storm upsetting you? Well, never mind, never mind... We’ll help you in a minute. I’ll call the doctor right away.”

“No, Praskovya Fyodorovna, there’s no need to call the doctor,” said Ivanushka, looking anxiously not at Praskovya Fyodorovna but at the wall. “There’s nothing particularly wrong with me. I understand things now, don’t be afraid. You’d do better to tell me,” Ivan asked warmly, “what happened just now next door, in room one hundred and eighteen?”
“In eighteen?” Praskovya Fyodorovna asked back, and her eyes darted about. “Why, nothing happened there.” But her voice was false; Ivanushka noticed it at once and said:

“Ah, Praskovya Fyodorovna! You’re such a truthful person... You think I’m going to start raging? No, Praskovya Fyodorovna, that won’t happen. You’d do better to tell me straight. I feel everything through the wall, you know.”

“Your neighbor has just passed away,” Praskovya Fyodorovna whispered, unable to overcome her truthfulness and kindness, and looked at Ivanushka in fright, clothed all over in the light of a lightning flash. But nothing terrible happened to Ivanushka. He merely raised a finger significantly and said:
“I knew it! I assure you, Praskovya Fyodorovna, that just now in the city one more person passed away. I even know who”—here Ivanushka smiled mysteriously—“it’s a woman.”

chapters.title: 31. On the Sparrow Hills
paragraphs: The storm had been carried off without a trace, and a many-colored rainbow, arching across the whole of Moscow, stood in the sky, drinking water from the Moskva River. High up, on a hill between two groves, three dark silhouettes could be seen. Woland, Koroviev and Behemoth sat in the saddles of black horses, gazing at the city spread out beyond the river, with the broken sun glittering in thousands of west-facing windows, and at the gingerbread towers of the Novodevichy Convent.
There was a rushing noise in the air, and Azazello, with the master and Margarita flying in the black tail of his cloak, came down together with them beside the waiting group.

“I had to trouble you, Margarita Nikolayevna and master,” Woland began after a short silence, “but please don’t hold it against me. I don’t think you will regret it. Well, then,” he turned to the master alone, “say goodbye to the city. It’s time for us to go.” Woland pointed with his hand in its black flared gauntlet to where countless suns were melting the glass beyond the river, where above those suns hung the mist, smoke and steam of a city baked all day long.

The master threw himself out of the saddle, left the others sitting there and ran to the edge of the hill’s steep drop. His black cloak dragged along the ground behind him. The master began to look at the city. In the first moments a wrenching sadness crept up to his heart, but very quickly it gave way to a sweetish anxiety, a wandering gypsy restlessness.

“Forever! I must take that in,” the master whispered, and licked his dry, cracked lips. He began to listen to himself and to note precisely everything that was happening in his soul. His agitation turned, as it seemed to him, into a feeling of deep and mortal grievance. But this was unstable; it vanished and for some reason gave way to a proud indifference, and that in turn to a presentiment of lasting peace.

The group of riders waited for the master in silence. The group of riders watched the long black figure at the edge of the drop gesticulating, now raising its head as if trying to cast its gaze across the whole city and look beyond its edges, now hanging its head as if studying the trampled, stunted grass underfoot.
The silence was broken by Behemoth, who had grown bored.
“Permit me, maître,” he began, “to give a farewell whistle before the ride.”
“You may frighten the lady,” Woland replied, “and besides, don’t forget that all your outrages for today are already over.”

“Oh no, no, Messire,” Margarita responded, sitting sidesaddle like an Amazon, her hand on her hip and her pointed train hanging down to the ground, “permit him, let him whistle. Sadness has seized me before the long road. Isn’t it true, Messire, that it’s quite natural, even when a person knows that happiness awaits him at the end of that road? Let him make us laugh, or else I’m afraid it will all end in tears, and everything will be spoiled before the road!”

Woland nodded to Behemoth, who grew very lively, jumped from the saddle to the ground, put his fingers in his mouth, puffed out his cheeks and whistled. Margarita’s ears rang. Her horse reared up, dry branches came showering down from the trees in the grove, a whole flock of crows and sparrows flew up, a column of dust was swept toward the river, and one could see several caps being blown off the passengers into the water from a river tram passing the landing stage.

The master flinched at the whistle but did not turn around; instead he began gesticulating still more restlessly, raising his hand to the sky as if threatening the city. Behemoth looked around proudly.
“That was whistled, I don’t dispute it,” Koroviev remarked condescendingly, “it was whistled indeed, but, to speak impartially, it was whistled very middlingly!”
“I’m not a choirmaster, after all,” Behemoth replied with dignity, pouting, and unexpectedly winked at Margarita.
“Here, let me have a go, for old times’ sake,” said Koroviev, rubbing his hands and blowing on his fingers.
“But watch it, watch it,” came Woland’s stern voice from his horse, “no tricks that cause bodily harm!”

“Messire, believe me,” Koroviev responded, putting his hand to his heart, “just for a joke, purely for a joke...” Here he suddenly stretched upward as if he were made of rubber, made some cunning figure out of the fingers of his right hand, twisted himself up like a screw, and then, suddenly unwinding, whistled.

Margarita did not hear this whistle, but she saw it, while she and her hot-blooded horse were thrown some seventy feet to one side. Beside her an oak tree was torn out by the roots, and the ground was covered with cracks all the way to the river. A huge slab of the bank, together with the landing stage and the restaurant, was dumped into the river. The water in it boiled and surged up, and onto the opposite bank, green and low-lying, a whole river tram was flung with its passengers completely unharmed. A jackdaw killed by Fagot’s whistle was hurled at the feet of Margarita’s snorting horse.
This whistle startled the master. He clutched his head and ran back to the group of companions waiting for him.
“Well, then,” Woland addressed him from the height of his horse, “are all the accounts settled? Has the leave-taking been done?”
“Yes, it has,” the master replied, and, now calm, looked Woland straight and boldly in the face.
And then over the hills, like a trumpet call, rolled Woland’s terrible voice:
“It’s time!!” And Behemoth’s shrill whistle and guffaw.

The horses tore forward, and the riders rose upward and galloped off. Margarita felt her frenzied horse champing and pulling at the bit. Woland’s cloak billowed out over the heads of the whole cavalcade, and that cloak began to cover the darkening vault of the evening sky. When for a moment the black covering was blown aside, Margarita turned in full gallop and saw that behind them there were no longer the many-colored towers with an airplane wheeling above them, and that the city itself had long since gone too: it had sunk into the earth and left only mist behind it.

chapters.title: 32. Forgiveness and Eternal Refuge
paragraphs: Gods, my gods! How sad the evening earth is! How mysterious the mists over the marshes. Whoever has wandered in those mists, whoever has suffered much before death, whoever has flown over this earth bearing a burden beyond his strength, knows it. The one who is weary knows it. And without regret he leaves the mists of the earth, its little marshes and its rivers; with a light heart he gives himself into the hands of death, knowing that she alone...

Even the magical black horses had tired, and carried their riders slowly, and the inevitable night began to overtake them. Sensing it at his back, even the irrepressible Behemoth fell quiet and, gripping the saddle with his claws, flew on silent and serious, his tail fluffed out.

Night began to cover the forests and meadows with a black kerchief; night lit sad little lights somewhere far below, lights that were now neither interesting nor needed by Margarita or the master, strangers’ lights. Night was overtaking the cavalcade, sifting down on it from above and scattering here and there in the saddened sky the white specks of stars.

Night thickened, flew alongside, caught the riders by their cloaks and, tearing them from their shoulders, exposed the deceptions. And when Margarita, fanned by the cool wind, opened her eyes, she saw how the appearance of all those flying toward their goal was changing. And when the full crimson moon began to rise toward them from behind the edge of the forest, all the deceptions vanished, and the unstable sorcerer’s clothing fell into the marsh and drowned in the mists.

It is hardly likely that anyone would now have recognized Koroviev-Fagot, the self-styled interpreter for the mysterious consultant who needed no interpreting at all, in the one who was now flying directly beside Woland, at the right hand of the master’s beloved. In place of the one who had left the Sparrow Hills in torn circus clothes under the name of Koroviev-Fagot, there now galloped, the gold chain of his bridle softly ringing, a dark-violet knight with a most somber face that never smiled. He rested his chin on his chest, he did not look at the moon, he took no interest in the earth; he was thinking of something of his own as he flew beside Woland.
“Why has he changed so?” Margarita asked Woland quietly, over the whistling of the wind.

“This knight once made an unfortunate joke,” Woland replied, turning toward Margarita his face with its quietly burning eye. “His pun, which he composed while talking about light and darkness, was not entirely good. And after that the knight had to go on joking a little more and a little longer than he had expected. But tonight is a night when accounts are settled. The knight has paid his account and closed it!”

Night tore off Behemoth’s fluffy tail too, stripped off his fur and flung its tufts across the marshes. The one who had been a cat, entertaining the prince of darkness, now turned out to be a slim youth, a demon page, the best jester that has ever existed in the world. Now he too had fallen quiet and flew soundlessly, turning his young face up to the light pouring from the moon.

At the side of them all, the steel of his armor gleaming, flew Azazello. The moon had changed his face too. The absurd, ugly fang had vanished without a trace, and the crooked eye had turned out to be false. Both of Azazello’s eyes were alike, empty and black, and his face was white and cold. Now Azazello flew in his true form, as the demon of the waterless desert, the demon-killer.

Margarita could not see herself, but she saw clearly how the master had changed. His hair now showed white in the moonlight and was gathered behind into a braid, and it flew in the wind. When the wind blew the cloak away from the master’s legs, Margarita saw on his jackboots the little stars of his spurs, now dimming, now flaring up. Like the demon youth, the master flew without taking his eyes off the moon, but he smiled at it as if at someone well known and dearly loved, and, from a habit acquired in room No. 118, he was muttering something to himself.

And finally, Woland too flew in his true guise. Margarita could not have said what the reins of his horse were made of, and she thought that perhaps they were chains of moonlight, and the horse itself only a mass of darkness, and the mane of that horse a storm cloud, and the rider’s spurs the white specks of stars.

So they flew in silence for a long time, until the very landscape below began to change. The sad forests sank into the earthly gloom and drew the dull blades of the rivers down with them. Below, boulders appeared and began to glint, and between them gaped black chasms into which the light of the moon did not reach.

Woland reined in his horse on a stony, joyless, flat summit, and then the riders moved on at a walk, listening to their horses’ shoes crushing flints and stones. The moon flooded the platform with green and bright light, and Margarita soon made out in this deserted place an armchair, and in it the white figure of a seated man. Perhaps this seated man was deaf, or too deeply sunk in thought. He did not hear the stony ground shudder under the weight of the horses, and the riders, without disturbing him, came up close to him.

The moon helped Margarita well; it shone better than the very best electric lantern, and Margarita saw that the seated man, whose eyes seemed blind, was rubbing his hands in short movements and fixing those same unseeing eyes on the disk of the moon. Now Margarita saw too that beside the heavy stone chair, on which some sparks glittered in the moonlight, lay a dark, enormous dog with pointed ears, and that it, like its master, was gazing anxiously at the moon. At the seated man’s feet lay the shards of a broken jug, and a black-red puddle that never dried spread out there.
The riders halted their horses.

“They have read your novel,” Woland began, turning to the master, “and said only one thing: that, unfortunately, it is not finished. So I wanted to show you your hero. For nearly two thousand years he has been sitting on this platform and sleeping, but when the full moon comes, as you see, he is tormented by insomnia. It torments not only him but his faithful guardian, the dog. If it is true that cowardice is the gravest vice, then the dog, perhaps, is not guilty of it. The only thing the brave dog was ever afraid of was thunderstorms. Well, then, the one who loves must share the fate of the one he loves.”
“What is he saying?” asked Margarita, and her perfectly calm face was veiled by a haze of compassion.

“He is saying,” came Woland’s voice, “one and the same thing. He is saying that even by moonlight he has no peace, and that he has a bad post. That is what he always says when he is not asleep, and when he sleeps, he sees one and the same thing: a moonlit road, and he wants to walk along it and talk with the prisoner Ha-Notsri, because, as he claims, he did not finish saying something that time, long ago, on the fourteenth day of the spring month of Nisan. But, alas, for some reason he never manages to get out onto that road, and no one comes to him. Then, what can one do, he has to talk to himself. Still, one does need some variety, and to his speech about the moon he often adds that more than anything in the world he hates his immortality and his unheard-of fame. He claims that he would gladly exchange his lot for that of the ragged vagrant Levi Matvei.”
“Twelve thousand moons for one moon once long ago, isn’t that too much?” asked Margarita.
“Is the business with Frieda being repeated?” said Woland. “But, Margarita, do not trouble yourself here. Everything will be right; the world is built on that.”

“Let him go!” Margarita suddenly cried out piercingly, the way she had once cried out when she was a witch, and at that cry a stone broke loose in the mountains and went flying down the ledges into the abyss, filling the mountains with its crashing. But Margarita could not have said whether it was the crash of the fall or the crash of satanic laughter. Be that as it may, Woland was laughing, glancing at Margarita, and saying:

“There’s no need to shout in the mountains; he is used to landslides anyway, and it won’t disturb him. You need not ask for him, Margarita, because the one he so longs to talk with has already asked for him.” Here Woland turned again to the master and said: “Well, then, now you can finish your novel with a single sentence!”

The master seemed to have been waiting for this already while he stood motionless, looking at the seated procurator. He cupped his hands into a megaphone and shouted so that the echo went leaping across the deserted, treeless mountains:
“Free! Free! He is waiting for you!”

The mountains turned the master’s voice into thunder, and that same thunder destroyed them. The accursed rocky walls fell. Only the platform with the stone chair remained. Above the black abyss into which the walls had gone, a boundless city lit up, with gleaming idols reigning over it, above a garden that had grown lush over the many thousands of these moons. Straight to this garden stretched the moonlit road the procurator had waited for so long, and the first to rush running along it was the dog with the pointed ears. The man in the white cloak with the blood-red lining rose from the chair and shouted something in a hoarse, broken voice. It was impossible to make out whether he was weeping or laughing, or what he was shouting. One could see only that, following his faithful guard, he too ran swiftly along the moonlit road.
“Am I to go there, after him?” the master asked anxiously, touching the reins.
“No,” Woland replied, “why chase in the footsteps of what is already finished?”

“Then over there?” asked the master, and he turned and pointed back, to where the city they had just left had woven itself together in the rear, with the convent’s gingerbread towers and the sun smashed to pieces in the glass.

“No again,” Woland replied, and his voice thickened and flowed over the rocks. “Romantic master! The one whom the hero you invented, and whom you yourself have just set free, so longs to see, has read your novel.” Here Woland turned to Margarita: “Margarita Nikolayevna! One cannot help believing that you tried to devise the very best future for the master, but truly, what I am offering you, and what Yeshua asked for on your behalf, yes, on yours, is better still. Leave the two of them together,” Woland was saying, leaning from his saddle toward the master’s and pointing after the departed procurator, “let us not disturb them. And perhaps they will come to some agreement.” Here Woland waved his hand toward Yershalaim, and it went out.

“And there too,” Woland pointed to the rear, “what is there for you to do in a little basement?” Here the broken sun in the glass went out. “What for?” Woland went on, persuasively and gently. “Oh, thrice-romantic master, do you really not want to stroll with your beloved by day under cherry trees that are beginning to blossom, and in the evening listen to the music of Schubert? Will you really not find it pleasant to write by candlelight with a goose quill? Do you really not want, like Faust, to sit over a retort in the hope that you will manage to fashion a new homunculus? There, go there! A house and an old servant are already waiting for you there, the candles are already burning, and soon they will go out, because you will at once meet the dawn. Along this road, master, along this one! Farewell! It is time for me to go.”

“Farewell!” Margarita and the master answered Woland in a single cry. Then the black Woland, keeping to no road at all, plunged into the chasm, and after him, with a roar, his retinue came crashing down. There were no more rocks around them, no platform, no moonlit road, no Yershalaim. The black horses had vanished too. The master and Margarita saw the promised dawn. It was beginning right there, directly after the midnight moon. The master walked with his beloved in the radiance of the first morning rays across a mossy stone footbridge. They crossed it. The stream was left behind the faithful lovers, and they walked along a sandy road.

“Listen to the soundlessness,” Margarita was saying to the master, and the sand rustled under her bare feet, “listen and enjoy what you were never given in life: silence. Look, there ahead is your eternal home, which you have been given as a reward. I can already see the Venetian window and the climbing vine; it rises right up to the roof. Here is your home, here is your eternal home. I know that in the evening those you love will come to you, those who interest you and who will not disturb you. They will play for you, they will sing for you, you will see what light there is in the room when the candles are burning. You will fall asleep wearing your greasy, eternal cap, you will fall asleep with a smile on your lips. Sleep will strengthen you, you will begin to reason wisely. And you will no longer be able to drive me away. I will be the one to guard your sleep.”

So Margarita spoke as she walked with the master toward their eternal home, and it seemed to the master that Margarita’s words were flowing just as the stream left behind them had flowed and whispered, and the master’s memory, his restless memory pierced all over by needles, began to fade. Someone was setting the master free, as he himself had just set free the hero he had created. That hero had gone into the abyss, gone irrevocably: the son of the astrologer king, forgiven on the night before the Resurrection, the cruel fifth procurator of Judea, the knight Pontius Pilate.

chapters.title: Epilogue
paragraphs: But all the same, what happened next in Moscow, after Woland left the capital at sunset on Saturday evening, vanishing with his retinue from the Sparrow Hills?

That for a long time a heavy hum of the most incredible rumors went on throughout the capital, spreading very quickly to remote backwaters of the provinces too, hardly needs saying. It is sickening even to repeat these rumors.

The writer of these truthful lines himself, while traveling to Feodosia, heard a story on the train about how in Moscow two thousand people had walked out of a theater stark naked, in the literal sense of the word, and in that state had gone home in taxicabs.

The whisper “The unclean powers...” was heard in the lines outside dairy shops, in streetcars, in stores, in apartments, in kitchens, on trains both suburban and long-distance, at stations and halts, at dachas and on beaches.

The most developed and cultured people, of course, took no part whatever in these stories about the unclean powers that had visited the capital, and even laughed at them and tried to bring the storytellers to reason. But a fact, as they say, is still a fact, and it simply cannot be brushed aside without explanation: someone had been to the capital. The charred embers left of Griboyedov’s alone, and much else besides, confirmed it all too eloquently.
Cultured people adopted the investigation’s point of view: it had been the work of a gang of hypnotists and ventriloquists in superb command of their art.

Measures to catch it, both in Moscow and beyond, were of course taken at once and energetically, but, to great regret, they produced no results. The one who called himself Woland, with all his minions, had disappeared, and never returned to Moscow, and did not appear anywhere else either, and gave no sign of himself in any way. Quite naturally, the supposition arose that he had fled abroad, but he did not turn up anywhere there either.

The investigation of his case went on for a long time. After all, whatever one may say, this was a monstrous case! Not to mention the four burned-down buildings and the hundreds of people driven out of their minds, there were people killed as well. Of two this can be said for certain: of Berlioz and of that unfortunate employee of the Bureau for Acquainting Foreigners with the Sights of Moscow, the former Baron Meigel. They, after all, had been killed. The charred bones of the second were discovered in apartment No. 50 on Sadovaya Street after the fire was put out. Yes, there were victims, and those victims demanded an investigation.
But there were other victims too, even after Woland had left the capital, and these victims, sad as it is to say, were black cats.

About a hundred of these peaceful animals, devoted and useful to man, were shot or exterminated by other means in various places around the country. Some fifteen cats, sometimes in a badly mutilated state, were delivered to police stations in various towns. In Armavir, for example, one of these entirely innocent beasts was brought into the police by some citizen with its front paws tied together.

The citizen had lain in wait for this cat at the moment when the animal, with a furtive look (but what can one do if cats have such a look? It is not because they are depraved, but because they are afraid that some creature stronger than they, dogs and people, might do them some harm or injury. Both are very easy to do, but there is no honor in it, I assure you. No, none whatever!), yes, so with a furtive look the cat was about to dart into the burdock for some reason.
Throwing himself on the cat and tearing the tie from his neck to bind it, the citizen muttered venomously and menacingly:
“Aha! So now you’ve graced us with a visit here in Armavir, have you, Mister Hypnotist? Well, nobody’s afraid of you here. And don’t pretend to be dumb. We know what kind of bird you are!”

The citizen led the cat to the police, dragging the poor beast by its front paws, which were trussed with a green tie, and making sure with little kicks that the cat walked on its hind legs without fail.
“You,” shouted the citizen, accompanied by whistling boys, “stop it, stop playing the fool! It won’t work! Kindly walk the way everybody walks!”

The black cat only rolled its martyred eyes. Deprived by nature of the gift of speech, it could not justify itself in any way. For its rescue the poor beast is indebted first of all to the police, and besides that to its owner, a respectable old widow. As soon as the cat had been delivered to the station, it was established there that the citizen smelled most powerfully of spirits, as a result of which his testimony was at once called into doubt. Meanwhile the old woman, having learned from the neighbors that her cat had been nabbed, ran off to the station and got there in time. She gave the cat the most flattering references, explained that she had known it for five years, since it was a kitten, vouched for it as for herself, and proved that it had never been noticed in anything bad and had never been to Moscow. It had been born in Armavir, and there it had grown up and learned to catch mice.
The cat was untied and returned to its owner, though not before it had tasted grief, having learned in practice what a mistake and a slander are.

Besides the cats, some minor unpleasantnesses befell certain people. Several arrests took place. Among others, the following were detained for a short time: in Leningrad, the citizens Volman and Volper; in Saratov, Kiev and Kharkov, three Volodins; in Kazan, a Volokh; and in Penza, for no reason at all that anyone could tell, the chemistry Candidate of Sciences Vetchinkevich. True, he was enormously tall and a very swarthy brunet.
In various places, besides that, nine Korovins, four Korovkins and two Karavayevs were caught.
A certain citizen was taken off the Sevastopol train, bound hand and foot, at Belgorod station. This citizen had taken it into his head to entertain his fellow passengers with card tricks.

In Yaroslavl, right at lunchtime, a citizen came into a restaurant carrying a Primus stove which he had just collected from the repair shop. As soon as the two doormen saw him in the cloakroom, they abandoned their posts and ran, and after them all the customers and staff ran out of the restaurant. In the process the cashier’s entire takings vanished in some incomprehensible way.
There was much more besides; you can’t remember it all. There was a great ferment of minds.

Again and again one must do the investigation justice. Everything was done not only to catch the criminals but also to explain everything they had perpetrated. And all of it was explained, and one cannot but acknowledge these explanations to be both sensible and irrefutable.

Representatives of the investigation and experienced psychiatrists established that the members of the criminal gang, or perhaps one of them (suspicion fell mainly on Koroviev), were hypnotists of unprecedented power, capable of showing themselves not in the place where they actually were but in imaginary, displaced positions. Besides this, they could freely suggest to those who came up against them that certain things or people were where they actually were not, and, conversely, could remove from the field of vision things or people that were in fact within that field of vision.

In the light of such explanations absolutely everything is clear, even the thing that most disturbed the citizens, the seemingly inexplicable invulnerability of the cat fired upon in apartment No. 50 during the attempts to take it into custody.

There was no cat on the chandelier, naturally; nobody even thought of firing back; they were shooting at an empty space, while Koroviev, having suggested that the cat was misbehaving on the chandelier, could freely have been standing behind the backs of the men shooting, grimacing and relishing his enormous but criminally misused capacity for suggestion. It was he too, of course, who set fire to the apartment by spilling gasoline.

Styopa Likhodeyev, of course, never flew to any Yalta (a stunt like that is beyond even Koroviev) and sent no telegrams from there. After he fainted in the jeweler’s widow’s apartment, frightened by Koroviev’s trick of showing him a cat with a pickled mushroom on a fork, he lay there until Koroviev, mocking him, pulled a felt hat on him and sent him off to Moscow airfield, having first suggested to the representatives of the criminal investigation department who were meeting Styopa that Styopa would climb out of the airplane arriving from Sevastopol.

True, the Yalta criminal investigation department insisted that it had received a barefoot Styopa and had sent telegrams about Styopa to Moscow, but not a single copy of those telegrams could be found in the files, from which the sad but completely unshakable conclusion was drawn that the gang of hypnotists possessed the ability to hypnotize at enormous distances, and moreover not only individual persons but whole groups of them. Under these conditions the criminals could drive people with the most stable psychological makeup out of their minds.

What is there to say about such trifles as a deck of cards in someone else’s pocket in the stalls, or ladies’ dresses that vanished, or a meowing beret and the like! Tricks of that sort can be pulled by any professional hypnotist of middling power on any stage, including the simple trick of tearing off the master of ceremonies’ head. A talking cat is also sheer nonsense. To present people with such a cat, it is enough to have mastered the first rudiments of ventriloquism, and hardly anyone will doubt that Koroviev’s art went considerably beyond those rudiments.

No, the point here is not decks of cards at all, nor the forged letters in Nikanor Ivanovich’s briefcase. Those are all trifles! It was he, Koroviev, who drove Berlioz under the streetcar to certain death. It was he who drove the poor poet Ivan Bezdomny out of his mind, who made him dream and see in tormenting visions ancient Yershalaim and the waterless, sun-scorched Bald Mountain with three men hanging on posts. It was he and his gang who made Margarita Nikolayevna and her housemaid, the beautiful Natasha, disappear from Moscow. Incidentally, the investigation looked into this matter with special care. It needed to be established whether these women had been abducted by the gang of murderers and arsonists or had run off with the criminal company of their own free will. Basing itself on the absurd and muddled testimony of Nikolai Ivanovich, and taking into account the strange and insane note Margarita Nikolayevna had left her husband, a note in which she writes that she is going off to become a witch, and considering the circumstance that Natasha had disappeared leaving all her clothes behind, the investigation came to the conclusion that both mistress and maid had been hypnotized, like many others, and abducted by the gang in that state. The thought also arose, and probably a perfectly correct one, that the criminals had been attracted by the beauty of both women.

But one thing remained completely unclear to the investigation: the motive that drove the gang to abduct from the psychiatric clinic a mental patient who called himself the master. This could not be established, any more than the abducted patient’s surname could be obtained. And so he vanished forever under a dead label: “Number one hundred and eighteen, from Building One.”
And so almost everything was explained, and the investigation ended, as in general everything ends.

Several years passed, and the citizens began to forget Woland, and Koroviev, and the rest. Many changes took place in the lives of those who had suffered at the hands of Woland and his minions, and however small and insignificant these changes may be, they should still be noted.

Georges Bengalsky, for instance, after spending three months in the hospital, recovered and was discharged, but he had to give up his job at the Variety, and at the busiest time, too, when the public was flocking for tickets: the memory of black magic and its exposure proved very tenacious. Bengalsky left the Variety because he understood that appearing every evening before two thousand people, being inevitably recognized and invariably subjected to jeering questions about which he liked better, with his head or without it, was too painful.

Besides, the master of ceremonies had lost a considerable dose of the cheerfulness so necessary in his profession. He was left with an unpleasant, burdensome habit: every spring, at the full moon, he would fall into a state of anxiety, suddenly clutch at his neck, look around in fright and weep. These fits would pass, but all the same, while he had them, he could not carry on with his former work, and the master of ceremonies retired and began to live on his savings, which, by his modest reckoning, ought to last him fifteen years.

He left and never again met Varenukha, who had won universal popularity and affection for his responsiveness and courtesy, unbelievable even among theater administrators. Free-pass seekers, for instance, never called him anything but their father and benefactor. Whatever the hour, whoever telephoned the Variety, a soft but sad voice was always heard on the line: “Yes, I’m listening,” and when asked to call Varenukha to the phone, the same voice would hastily answer: “At your service.” But then how Ivan Savelyevich suffered for his courtesy!

Styopa Likhodeyev no longer has to talk on the telephone at the Variety. Immediately after his discharge from the clinic, where Styopa spent eight days, he was transferred to Rostov, where he was appointed manager of a large grocery store. Rumor has it that he has completely stopped drinking port and drinks only vodka infused with blackcurrant buds, which has made him much healthier. They say he has become taciturn and keeps away from women.

Stepan Bogdanovich’s removal from the Variety did not bring Rimsky the joy he had so greedily dreamed of for several years. After the clinic and Kislovodsk, the financial director, now old, very old, with a shaking head, submitted his resignation from the Variety. What is interesting is that the resignation was brought to the Variety by Rimsky’s wife. Grigory Danilovich himself could not find the strength to visit, even in daytime, the building where he had seen the cracked windowpane flooded with moonlight and the long arm groping its way toward the lower latch.

Having left the Variety, the financial director joined the children’s puppet theater in Zamoskvorechye. In this theater he no longer had to deal with the most esteemed Arkady Apollonovich Sempleyarov on matters of acoustics. The latter was transferred in two shakes to Bryansk and appointed manager of a mushroom procurement station. Muscovites now eat salted saffron milk caps and pickled porcini and cannot praise them enough, and are extraordinarily pleased about this transfer. It is all in the past now, and one may say that things never went right for Arkady Apollonovich with the acoustics, and however hard he tried to improve them, they stayed just as they had been.

Among those who broke with the theater, apart from Arkady Apollonovich, one must also count Nikanor Ivanovich Bosoy, although he had no connection with theaters except a love of free tickets. Nikanor Ivanovich not only does not go to any theater, either for money or for free, but even changes countenance at any talk of the theater. To no lesser, indeed to a greater degree, he has come to hate, besides the theater, the poet Pushkin and the talented actor Savva Potapovich Kurolesov. The latter to such a degree that last year, seeing in the newspaper a black-bordered announcement that Savva Potapovich had been struck down by a stroke at the very height of his career, Nikanor Ivanovich turned so purple that he nearly followed Savva Potapovich himself, and roared: “Serves him right!” What is more, that same evening Nikanor Ivanovich, on whom the death of the popular actor had brought a mass of painful memories, got horribly drunk all alone, with only the full moon lighting up Sadovaya for company. And with every glass the accursed chain of hateful figures grew longer before him, and in that chain were Sergei Gerardovich Dunchil, and the beauty Ida Gerkulanovna, and that red-haired owner of fighting geese, and the candid Nikolai Kanavkin.

Well, and what happened to those people? Oh, come now! Nothing whatever happened to them, nor can anything happen, because they never really existed, just as the likable actor who was the master of ceremonies never existed, nor the theater itself, nor Porokhovnikov’s old skinflint of an aunt, rotting foreign currency in her cellar, and certainly there were no golden trumpets and no insolent cooks. Nikanor Ivanovich only dreamed all that under the influence of that rotten Koroviev. The only living person who flew into that dream was precisely Savva Potapovich, the actor, and he got mixed up in it only because he had lodged himself in Nikanor Ivanovich’s memory thanks to his frequent performances on the radio. He existed, but the rest did not.

So then, perhaps there was no Aloisy Mogarych either? Oh, no! He not only existed but exists to this day, and precisely in the post Rimsky gave up, that is, the post of financial director of the Variety.

Coming to his senses about twenty-four hours after his visit to Woland, on a train somewhere near Vyatka, Aloisy realized that, having left Moscow for some reason in a fit of mental derangement, he had forgotten to put on his trousers, but had instead, for no comprehensible purpose, stolen the landlord’s house register, which he had no use for whatever. Paying the conductor a colossal sum, Aloisy acquired from him an old and greasy pair of trousers and turned back from Vyatka. But, alas, he could no longer find the landlord’s little house. The decrepit old junk had been licked clean away by fire. But Aloisy was an extremely enterprising man. Two weeks later he was already living in a splendid room in Bryusov Lane, and a few months later he was already sitting in Rimsky’s office. And just as Rimsky had once suffered because of Styopa, so now Varenukha was tormented because of Aloisy. Ivan Savelyevich dreams of only one thing, that this Aloisy be removed from the Variety somewhere out of sight, because, as Varenukha sometimes whispers among close friends, “he has supposedly never in his life met such a scoundrel as this Aloisy, and supposedly he expects anything whatever from this Aloisy.”

However, perhaps the administrator is biased. No shady dealings have been noticed on Aloisy’s part, or indeed any dealings at all, unless, of course, one counts the appointment of somebody else in place of the barman Sokov. As for Andrei Fokich, he died of liver cancer in the clinic of the First Moscow State University some nine months after Woland’s appearance in Moscow...
Yes, several years have passed, and the events truthfully described in this book have healed over and faded from memory. But not for everyone, not for everyone!

Every year, as soon as the festive spring full moon comes round, toward evening a man of about thirty or a little over thirty appears under the lindens at Patriarch’s Ponds. A reddish-haired, green-eyed, modestly dressed man. This is a research fellow of the Institute of History and Philosophy, Professor Ivan Nikolayevich Ponyrev.

When he comes under the lindens, he always sits down on the very bench where he sat that evening when Berlioz, long since forgotten by everyone, saw for the last time in his life the moon breaking into pieces.

Now, whole, white at the start of the evening and then golden, with a dark dragon-horse on it, it floats over the former poet, Ivan Nikolayevich, and at the same time stands in one place at its height.

Ivan Nikolayevich knows everything; he knows and understands it all. He knows that in his youth he fell victim to criminal hypnotists, was treated afterward and was cured. But he also knows that there is something he cannot master. He cannot master this spring full moon. As soon as it begins to approach, as soon as the luminary that once hung higher than two five-branched candlesticks begins to grow and fill with gold, Ivan Nikolayevich becomes restless and nervous, loses his appetite and sleep, and waits for the moon to ripen. And when the full moon comes, nothing can keep Ivan Nikolayevich at home. Toward evening he goes out and walks to Patriarch’s Ponds.
Sitting on the bench, Ivan Nikolayevich by now talks to himself openly, smokes, squints now at the moon, now at the turnstile he remembers so well.
Ivan Nikolayevich spends an hour or two like this. Then he gets up and, always by one and the same route, through Spiridonovka, with empty, unseeing eyes, walks to the lanes of the Arbat.

He walks past the kerosene shop, turns where the crooked old gas lamp stands, and creeps up to a railing behind which he sees a luxuriant garden, not yet in leaf, and in it a Gothic mansion, painted by the moon on the side where the bay with its triple window juts out, and dark on the other.

The professor does not know what draws him to the railing or who lives in that mansion, but he knows that at the full moon there is no point fighting himself. Besides, he knows that in the garden beyond the railing he will inevitably see one and the same thing.

He sees an elderly, respectable man sitting on a little bench, with a small beard, wearing a pince-nez, and with faintly piggish features. Ivan Nikolayevich always finds this inhabitant of the mansion in one and the same dreamy pose, his gaze turned to the moon. Ivan Nikolayevich knows that, having admired the moon, the seated man will without fail shift his eyes to the windows of the bay and fix them there, as if expecting them to be flung open any moment and something extraordinary to appear on the windowsill.

Everything that follows Ivan Nikolayevich knows by heart. At this point one must be sure to hide deeper behind the railing, for any moment now the seated man will begin to turn his head restlessly, to catch at something in the air with wandering eyes, to smile rapturously, and then he will suddenly clasp his hands in some sweet anguish, and then he will simply mutter, rather loudly:
“Venus! Venus!.. Oh, what a fool I am!..”

“Gods, gods!” Ivan Nikolayevich will begin to whisper, hiding behind the railing and never taking his kindling eyes off the mysterious stranger. “There’s another victim of the moon... Yes, another victim, like me.”
And the seated man will go on with his speeches:
“Oh, what a fool I am! Why, why didn’t I fly away with her? What was I afraid of, the old ass! I got myself a certificate! Well, put up with it now, you old cretin!”
This will go on until a window bangs in the dark part of the mansion, something whitish appears in it, and an unpleasant female voice rings out:
“Nikolai Ivanovich, where are you? What sort of fancies are these? Do you want to catch malaria? Come and have your tea!”
At this, of course, the seated man will come to and answer in a lying voice:
“The air, I wanted a breath of air, my darling! The air is so very good!”
And then he will get up from the bench, furtively shake his fist at the window closing below, and trudge into the house.

“He’s lying, he’s lying! Oh gods, how he lies!” mutters Ivan Nikolayevich, walking away from the railing. “It’s not the air at all that draws him into the garden; he sees something at this spring full moon, on the moon and in the garden, up on high. Oh, what I would give to get into his secret, to know what Venus it is that he lost and now fumbles for in the air with his hands, fruitlessly, trying to catch her!”

And the professor comes home quite ill by now. His wife pretends not to notice his state and hurries him off to bed. But she herself does not go to bed; she sits by the lamp with a book and looks with bitter eyes at the sleeper. She knows that at dawn Ivan Nikolayevich will wake with an agonized cry, will begin to weep and thrash about. That is why there lies before her on the tablecloth under the lamp a syringe made ready beforehand in spirit, and an ampoule of liquid the color of strong tea.

The poor woman, bound to a gravely sick man, is now free and can fall asleep without fear. After the injection Ivan Nikolayevich will sleep till morning with a happy face and will see dreams unknown to her, but sublime and happy ones.

What wakes the scholar and brings him to his pitiful cry on the night of the full moon is always one and the same thing. He sees an unnatural noseless executioner who, leaping up and giving a kind of grunting whoop, stabs with a spear into the heart of Gestas, tied to a post and out of his mind. But it is not so much the executioner who is terrible as the unnatural lighting in the dream, which comes from a sort of storm cloud that boils and bears down on the earth, as happens only during world catastrophes.

After the injection everything changes before the sleeper. From the bed to the window stretches a broad moonlit road, and onto this road climbs a man in a white cloak with a blood-red lining, and he begins to walk toward the moon. Beside him walks a young man in a torn chiton and with a disfigured face. The two are talking heatedly about something, arguing, wanting to come to an agreement about something.

“Gods, gods!” says the man in the cloak, turning his haughty face to his companion. “What a vulgar execution! But tell me, please,” and here his face turns from haughty to imploring, “it never happened, did it! I beg you, tell me, it never happened?”
“Why, of course it never happened,” his companion answers in a hoarse voice, “you imagined it.”
“And can you swear to that?” the man in the cloak begs ingratiatingly.
“I swear!” answers his companion, and for some reason his eyes are smiling.

“I need nothing more!” the man in the cloak cries out in a broken voice, and climbs higher and higher toward the moon, drawing his companion with him. Behind them walks a calm and majestic, gigantic dog with pointed ears.

Then the moonlit path boils up, a river of moonlight begins to gush from it and floods out in all directions. The moon reigns and plays, the moon dances and frolics. Then in the stream a woman of boundless beauty takes shape and leads toward Ivan by the hand a man overgrown with a beard, who looks around timidly. Ivan Nikolayevich recognizes him at once. It is that number one hundred and eighteen, his night visitor. In his dream Ivan Nikolayevich stretches out his hands to him and asks avidly:
“So that, then, is how it ended?”
“That is how it ended, my disciple,” answers number one hundred and eighteen, and the woman comes up to Ivan and says:
“Of course, that is how. Everything has ended, and everything ends... And I will kiss you on the forehead, and everything will be as it should be for you.”
She bends down to Ivan and kisses him on the forehead, and Ivan reaches toward her and peers into her eyes, but she retreats, retreats and goes away with her companion toward the moon...

Then the moon begins to rage; it brings torrents of light crashing straight down on Ivan, it splashes light in all directions, a moonlight flood begins in the room, the light sways, rises higher, floods the bed. That is when Ivan Nikolayevich sleeps with a happy face.

In the morning he wakes up silent, but completely calm and well. His needle-pricked memory grows quiet, and until the next full moon no one will trouble the professor: neither the noseless killer of Gestas, nor the cruel fifth procurator of Judea, the knight Pontius Pilate.
